articles.title: Defense Without Limits
articles.body:
Defense Without Limits
Iranian officials say Tehran will place no limits on hitting aggressors and their regional backers in case of a renewed US-Israeli attack
TEHRAN – The tone of the enemy toward Iran has sharply escalated again, with senior American and Israeli officials openly speaking of finishing the job and some analysts warning a new round of war is near, while Iranian political and military officials say the country is fully ready for a severe and unrestricted response.
An informed Iranian source told Press TV that Iran has prepared for an all-out, multi-layered and comprehensive war. According to the source, Tehran has made a firm decision that in reaction to any aggression, assassination and terror, it will respond without any limitation or restraint and will crush with full force the accessible interests and targets of the aggressors and their supporters in the region.
From Tehran's point of view, the source said, the US will not launch an attack without Israel, nor Israel without the US, and talk of their independence from each other in a war against Iran resembles a bitter joke. The explicit threats by American officials and the Zionist regime to attack Iran, the source added, have provided the legal and moral license for Iran to adopt necessary defensive measures.
"We will soon finish the job"
On Sunday, US President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that Iran had been "systematically destroyed, both militarily and financially, and unless they change their ways, rapidly, we will soon finish the job."
In the same post, Trump gave his "complete and total endorsement" to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel's October 27 parliamentary election, suggesting Washington could take on the fight itself if Netanyahu failed to stay in power: with the "wrong Leader" in Israel, "America will have to do this work ourselves."
Trump did not specify what action he had in mind. Earlier this month he had said the US would not attack Iran before the November 3 US midterm elections and had spoken of "productive discussions." His latest comments came after he and Netanyahu discussed a possible new military operation, according to Axios, which reported last week that Netanyahu raised intelligence suggesting Tehran was rebuilding its nuclear program. Trump has also raised the possibility of striking the underground Pickaxe Mountain complex near Natanz.
At a campaign rally in Kansas on Monday, Trump said the US was in a position to walk away from the war now, describing Iran as devastated and adding: "They're not going to have a nuclear weapon."
Netanyahu matched the tone. In a briefing with Israeli journalists on Sunday, he declared that bringing down the Islamic Republic remained a key objective and that he had directed all security agencies to pursue it: "We must bring this regime down once and for all."
Presenting an updated security doctrine, he said, as reported by Israel Hayom: "The objectives I set do not depend on American approval. To the extent necessary, we will also act independently. We have done so before, and if necessary, we will do so again. We are prepared to take the initiative. We must prevent the enemy from delivering the first blow."
He described confronting Iran as his "life's mission," claimed "90% of the job is done" by pointing to economic pressure and protests, and responded to Trump's endorsement with: "Together we will complete the mission!" In a video of a phone call released Monday, he told Trump: "Donald, we have a job to finish, you said it, and we'll finish it together."
In an interview with Fox News on October 18, Netanyahu warned Iran is developing intercontinental ballistic missiles capable of reaching US cities and seeking nuclear warheads, saying: "You are the real target." He listed as his first priority if reelected: "First, we will achieve the complete elimination of the Iranian threat to Israel, to America, and to the entire world."
Unannounced visit and election countdown
The rhetoric moved with military signals. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth paid an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, October 19, meeting Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz at Ovda Air Base in the Negev. Spokesman Doron Spielman said they discussed "the threats in the region" and offensive-defensive cooperation. The Pentagon gave no details.
On Tuesday, Hegseth told US troops in the Central Command area: "I got to see some of our warfighters — they're preparing and ready to ensure that Iran never has a nuclear weapon," adding they were "ready to go."
Israel canceled soldiers' leave from Thursday ahead of the vote. Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir said forces were on "a high level of alertness and readiness" against "external interference." Netanyahu told i24NEWS on Tuesday that Iran and its proxies could try to disrupt the October 27 election.
"Either a deal or an attack"
The Financial Times reported on Wednesday, October 21, citing a person familiar with Israeli planning, that renewed US-Israeli strikes in the coming weeks are "not an unreasonable scenario." Three sources said Netanyahu urged the military earlier this month to prepare a multi-day offensive including nuclear sites, planned for the weekend of October 10, which did not proceed after Trump opposed action before the US midterms. One source said: "There will either be a deal or an attack."
White House deputy spokesperson Anna Kelly told the FT the US "will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections." The New York Times quoted Raz Zimmt of Tel Aviv's INSS as saying: "The baseline expectation in Iran, and in Israel, is that it's a matter of when the war restarts, not if." He added a strike alone would likely not achieve Washington's goals but might give Trump "an image of victory and a way out."
Ready for war, ready for diplomacy
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iraq's Al-Ekhbariya chanel that Iran entered three rounds of talks and all three led to war. "We were in the midst of negotiations and in the end it was proven that the Americans cannot be trusted. In the third round, we reached an understanding with Trump, but Trump himself violated it and adhered to it for only two weeks."
After more than eight months, Washington has achieved none of its objectives, he said, calling that a strategic failure for the US and a strategic success for Iran. America is now in a deep quagmire, resorting to military threats, sanctions and pressure on neighbors not to cooperate with Tehran, without result. "Iran will never surrender, neither to sanctions nor to military threats. The only solution is diplomacy and a negotiated solution."
"Every possibility exists, including that the Americans and the Zionist regime will start another war. But we are in full readiness. We are fully prepared to defend ourselves and will stand until the last moment," Araghchi said. "When I say we are ready for war, it does not mean we want war. It is a message to do calculations and not enter that war again. We are as ready for diplomacy as we are for war."
The main deterrent, he argued, is that readiness: Americans know war cannot deliver their goals. In the two wars, they "fell into Israel's trap, more precisely Netanyahu's trap. Netanyahu will do anything for his personal goal, not for America, Israel or anyone else."
In a Financial Times essay titled "The false assumptions about us are dangerous," Araghchi wrote that a way forward requires Washington to accept it has "no military options." Trump entered the war on "fundamentally erroneous assumptions," being wrongly told Iranian forces are unprepared, despite lessons learned since 2025. "In June 2025 and February 2026, they bombed us while we were negotiating. And in June this year, shortly after an agreement was signed by Presidents Pezeshkian and Trump, we were attacked a third time. How can we trust a US president again?"
He recalled presenting a Seven-Day Plan via mediators at the UN General Assembly under which the US would do nothing it had not already agreed to: the Strait of Hormuz would reopen on Day 6, talks for a final deal on Day 7. He cited Moody's that the war has cost US consumers $265 billion this year, about $2,000 per household, half from energy prices, plus damaged bases and equipment losses. Further escalation, he warned, would put civilian lives, regional states and the world economy at great risk and bring "even greater strategic failure."
Defense without restraint
Armed Forces General Staff spokesman Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi replied to Trump and Netanyahu: "We tell the child-killing twins, Trump and Netanyahu: you are on the slope of decline, and with boasting you will not save yourselves from the swamp of death."
New Defense Minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi, approved Sunday with 237 votes, wrote he devoted his first working hour to the IRGC Aerospace Force and Army air defense: "For us, responding to threats is not a rhetorical contest; it is turning threats into greater readiness. We are focused on our targets with new technologies; we eat dust but we will not give away soil."
National Security Commission Chairman Ebrahim Azizi wrote on X: "Regardless of your election results, we have no doubt about your hostility. We are ready, in response to any operational mistake, to wipe you off the map."
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei wrote Wednesday on X, reacting to the US Secretary of State's call to condemn Iran over Persian Gulf insecurity: "In less than nine months, they attacked Iran twice in the middle of negotiations; they slaughtered our children in Minab, killed our daughters in Lamard, assassinated our leaders, and intensified sanctions; and now, after blatantly violating the understanding they signed, while claiming victory, they ask the world to condemn Iran." The world, he said, is paying for US-Israeli law-breaking, from regional turmoil to energy insecurity. "You cannot set fires, throw the region into chaos, then stand as plaintiff and ask others to condemn the victim."
Ball in Washington's court
Tehran sees a deadlock not easily broken. The gap over the balance of conflict, US pressure to force submission before the midterms, Iran's tighter control of Hormuz and action against violating vessels, oil above $110 after two tankers carrying 4 million barrels hit mines — one burning, one halted — the criticized diesel deal with Russia, and Hegseth's secret talks with Netanyahu alongside UAE officials all point to continued tension.
 
While unofficial sources speak of a Pakistan-Qatar proposal, Tehran believes Trump seeks to pass the midterms, not end a costly war whose declared goals keep changing. Iran does not doubt Islamabad's sincerity, but the ball, officials say, is in Washington's court. Until the US abandons the illusion of forcing surrender and imposing unilateral terms, by negotiation or aggression, the conflict will not end.

articles.title: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine
articles.body:
Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine in the war against Russia
Over the past week, Ukraine has received a stark reminder of its growing dependence on uninterrupted access to Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield networks in its drone-heavy war against Russia, now in its fifth year.
Ukraine has a fraction of Russia's resources, but its aggressive development of drone warfare on defensive and offensive fronts has helped it endure an onslaught from its much bigger adversary, which invaded Ukraine in early 2022. That was true until last week, when Ukraine reported a throttling of the Starshield network that was causing its drones to stop midflight and fall out of the sky.
The two SpaceX networks operate on a constellation of thousands of low-Earth satellites — Starlink is the commercial version, while Starshield is a military product licensed to the U.S. government and its partners, among them Ukraine.
Kyiv's reliance on drones has made Starlink and Starshield nearly indispensable to its arsenal. When Ukraine experienced a disruption to those networks, it lost the shield of interceptors and drones that offered some protection against Russian drone and missile strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes Musk throttled Starshield at the request of U.S. officials, though the world's richest man has denied any role and said it's the U.S. government that controls the military-grade network. President Trump has also denied he's responsible for slowing the network.
However, CBS News reported Tuesday that Musk was behind the disruption, which occurred after he spoke with administration officials multiple times seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter, according to sources familiar with the situation.
There has also been conflicting information about whether full access to the networks has been restored. As of Wednesday afternoon, Starlink remained throttled, Zelenskyy's office confirmed.
Here's what's known about Starshield and Starlink — and their role in the Ukraine war.
What happened in Ukraine?
On Oct. 13, Ukraine's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment, making it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones, officials and soldiers told CBS News.
Ukrainian soldiers said they noticed "speed limits" had been imposed on their use of SpaceX's Starshield internet dishes, the military-grade Starlink dishes that Ukrainians strap onto their drones so remote pilots can maintain their connection with the unmanned aircraft as they fly toward Russian targets.
Access was restricted by turning off dishes on Ukrainian drones flying above a certain speed, causing them to fall out of the sky. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense sources said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions without informing them beforehand.
Zelenskyy said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Russian Shahed attack drones.
What are Starshield and Starlink?
Starshield, the military-grade satellite network, runs on the same constellation of satellites as its civilian sister, Starlink, but has fewer technical limitations and more advanced security features. Both are operated by Musk's company SpaceX.
The U.S. government pays SpaceX to license the use of Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia.
There is no working alternative to Starlink, as no direct competitor approaches Starlink's coverage of 11,150 satellites. Amazon Leo aims to compete, but at this point, it has under 400 satellites in low Earth orbit and has been hampered by the launchpad explosion of a Blue Origin rocket in May.
Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr (43.5 mph) speed cap, which is the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates exceeding the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable.
Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr (99.4 mph). Starshield-equipped strike drones cruise at 160 km/h or more, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes.
During the throttling over the last week, Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr (55.9 mph), making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
On Oct. 15, some Ukrainian officials said that the Starshield restrictions had been lifted. But Zelenskyy told NBC News on Sunday the maximum speed was still 161 km/hr.
Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that the service was "still limited," but he added that Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him he would "work with his team on this to unblock" it.
Is Ukraine using Starshield or Starlink?
It uses both. Starlink has been providing internet service to Ukrainian civilians and military forces since 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, according to Reuters.
Initially funded by private donors and a U.S. foreign aid contract, SpaceX won a Pentagon contract to pay for Starlink for Ukraine in 2023, along with a contract for 500 Starshield terminals.
In August 2024, SpaceX signed another Defense Department contract to expand Starshield usage to 3,000 terminals for the front lines, Bloomberg reported.
Beyond communicating with and guiding drones over long distances, Starshield also serves another function: It connects every sensor and weapon system on the battlefield. Disruptions to the service have an impact that can be compared to an office having to function without being able to connect to Wi-Fi.
Ukraine's military uses Starlink for general battlefield communications, and Ukrainian civilians rely on it for communications needs, too.
On the Russian side, the Kremlin had also been using Starlink until February, when SpaceX cut off its access. As a result, Ukraine gained more than 150 square miles of territory.
Musk and throttling Ukraine's access to Starshield
CBS News reported Tuesday that a decision by Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, though it remains unclear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed.
Musk had spoken with administration officials multiple times, seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter, sources said. He has in the past expressed distaste for the perception that his company could be seen as profiting from the Ukraine war.
The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some Trump administration officials, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon had specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.
The president said Monday he was seeking information about who had ordered the slowdown. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday denied the Pentagon had manipulated the service, saying, "We haven't made any directives or anything like that."
Can Elon Musk stop the use of Starlink and Starshield?
Musk has not admitted to imposing restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starshield.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," the world's richest person wrote on X.
He added that Starlink is a "commercial service," writing that it is "limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action."
Rubio, however, seemed to attribute the network constraints to Musk.
"The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk," Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Wednesday.
Within a few minutes, though, he seemed to concede that Starshield was different: "We don't control what a private company — how they decide their product can be used. Now, if they're in a contract with the United States military, like Starshield, that's a different matter, because that's something we are purchasing and using for our use."
Intelligence-sharing
At around the same time as the Starlink and Starshield disruptions, Ukraine also did not receive warnings from U.S. intelligence about major Russian strikes.
Ukraine relies on a mixture of American sensors, aircraft, surveillance and human intelligence to map Russian positions and launch sites.
The early warning system, which is distinct from the SpaceX products, notifies Ukraine when Russia has launched a ballistic missile in its direction. It failed in at least two instances, on Oct. 13 and Oct. 18.
On Oct. 13, Zelenskyy said Ukraine "received no advance warning" when Russia launched a ballistic missile barrage. That overnight attack targeted energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv and Kharkiv, killing six people and leaving some 600,000 without power.
Ukrainian sources said U.S. officials said the warning system had failed due to "bad weather." Ukrainian officials expressed doubt about that explanation and accused the U.S. of "playing" with the system. By 3 a.m., that system seemed to have been restored.
Then on Monday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been hit by another wave of Russian missile and drone strikes, "and again, there was no warning from partners."
A senior Pentagon official told CBS News Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."
By Wednesday, however, the warning system appeared to have been restored: "Now intelligence works. Thank you so much. That was crucial for us," Zelenskyy said on Fox News.
Rising pressure to end the war
Deliveries of key Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine have also slowed, Ukraine has said.
Rubio on Tuesday called interceptors the "most in-demand product right now in the defense field," and said that "when a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States, it's not because we're denying. We have our own needs, too."
"There's nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine," he said. "It's simply a balance between our obligations."
Mr. Trump has grown impatient with the more than four-year-long war. He has sought to portray the ongoing Ukraine war as the reason for high energy prices and has vented his frustration with Zelenskyy more frequently in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to end it.
He waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. And Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week.
Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire.
Mr. Trump told reporters Tuesday that Russia keeps "grinding away" and is more capable of sustaining casualties than Ukraine, arguing "it's time" for Zelenskyy to make a deal.

articles.title: U.S. and Israel prepare for a new war with Iran
articles.body:
- President Trump said the U.S. is not negotiating with Iran and that “something” will happen “fairly soon,” as plans for renewed strikes take shape.
- U.S. troops are leaving bases in Jordan, Qatar and Kuwait, and Israeli jets flew a mock strike mission to Iran’s border.
The United States and Israel are moving toward a new war with Iran within days, as President Donald Trump said Washington is no longer negotiating with Tehran and that “something” will happen “fairly soon,” while U.S. troops pull out of exposed bases across the Middle East and Israeli fighter jets rehearse a strike on Iran at the edge of its airspace.
The troop withdrawals, embassy staff cuts and large-scale air activity over the region closely resemble the buildup that came just before the war began in late February, and they put the next round of fighting on a timeline measured in days rather than months, with the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections now less than two weeks away.
“No, I think we’re not negotiating… we are going to have something, one way or the other. It’ll happen fairly soon,” said President Donald Trump on Oct. 21.
The remarks mark a sharp turn from Trump’s pledge on Oct. 8 that the United States would not attack Iran before the midterms, and they come as Washington and Jerusalem finalize plans for what officials described to The New York Times as a short but intensive operation against Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities and missile and drone arsenals. Options presented to Trump include strikes on tunnel entrances at nuclear sites such as Pickaxe Mountain and on the strategic islands of Kharg, which handles most of Iran’s oil exports, and Qeshm, NBC News reported, while officials quoted by the Times said there is a chance he could order strikes before the end of this month.
On the ground, the U.S. military has quietly moved troops out of bases in Jordan, Qatar and Kuwait in recent days, two U.S. officials and two people familiar with the matter told NBC News, and one official said getting forces out of harm’s way is part of planning as Trump weighs restarting major combat operations. The State Department has ordered staff reductions at the U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks on the kingdom including strikes on civilian airports, and chiefs of mission at several other posts across the region have been told to operate with fewer personnel, in moves that sources compared directly with the drawdowns at the start of the war in February.
“We regularly move U.S. service members and assets to optimize mission readiness,” a U.S. Central Command spokesperson said.
Israel has already rehearsed the opening move of a new campaign, sending dozens of fighter jets and refueling aircraft along a route through Syrian and Iraqi airspace consistent with a strike on Iran and turning them back only as they approached the Iranian border, Axios reporter Barak Ravid reported, citing sources who described it as a massive power projection operation. Israel told Washington the flight was an exercise and a show of force, but the sortie was followed overnight by large-scale tactical aircraft activity over the region that defense writer Tyler Rogoway said looked like a dry run for a large integrated operation, in which commanders put much of the real strike force in position to rehearse before the order to execute is given.
Such rehearsals also force Iran to switch on its air defenses as if a full attack were coming, which lets U.S. and Israeli intelligence detect, classify and pinpoint radars and missile sites that would have to be suppressed, destroyed or avoided on the first night of an offensive, Rogoway noted, and that kind of targeting picture is far sharper when Iranian crews are on high alert than during routine surveillance.
Tensions are climbing at sea as well, after the naval arm of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said its forces hit four vessels it accused of illegal oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf and that three more ships struck mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, warning that continued provocations could bring a wider response against U.S. bases in the region. Iran’s neighbors are bracing for the fallout, with Saudi Arabia already under a sustained Houthi missile and drone campaign that has led Britain to send Royal Air Force Typhoons to guard Saudi cities and Türkiye to prepare forces for deployment to the kingdom under its new defense pact with Riyadh and Pakistan.

articles.title: Iran reveals ‘offensive’ doctrine, US issues alert: Is war imminent?
articles.body:
Iran reveals ‘offensive’ doctrine, US issues alert: Is war imminent?
US orders diplomatic staff out of Saudi Arabia amid escalating conflict and reports of potential US and Israeli strikes on Iran.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says renewed attacks by the United States could prompt Tehran to invade neighbouring countries and hit bases used in US military operations as part of its new “offensive” strategy.
The warning on Wednesday came amid escalating attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a global energy chokepoint, and uncertainty over diplomatic efforts to end the nearly eight-month war.
“Our defence doctrine was previously defensive; we used to say that if a country attacks us, we will respond. Now we say that if a country attacks us, we will both respond and launch an offensive,” IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebi said.
Washington ordered some diplomatic personnel to leave Saudi Arabia amid attacks from Yemen’s Houthis while US President Donald Trump has signalled that a decision on the conflict could come soon.
According to media reports, the US and Israel are planning potential attacks on Iran in the coming weeks.
As negotiations seem stalled and both sides exchange threats, could the region be heading towards another military escalation?
What is Iran’s new doctrine?
The IRGC on Wednesday announced a shift towards an “offensive and asymmetrical” defence doctrine, threatening to invade countries that launch attacks against it.
Mohebi said Tehran would no longer limit its military operations to retaliatory strikes.
Mohebi stressed that Iran’s missile stockpile has increased 1.5 times since the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025. He did not provide specific figures.
“The quality of the missiles has improved significantly, and their range, destructive power and accuracy in hitting targets have increased,” the spokesman said.
Moreover, Mohebi said Iranian forces were in the “stage of preparing to unveil the ‘father of all bombs’. This is something new for the enemy.”
Meanwhile, attacks in the Strait of Hormuz continued unabated.
The IRGC’s navy said on Thursday that four vessels it accused of being involved in illegal oil transfers were struck and caught fire in the northern Gulf. Three other vessels hit mines west of the strait, it added.
Before the war, one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz. While shipments through the strait are still below those levels, oil shipments from the region returned to pre-war levels last month as exporters found alternative ways to ship out their oil and gas, including using pipelines.
However, a flurry of recent attacks in the key waterway and the fighting between Yemen’s Houthis and its Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, which has resulted in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, have once again sent oil prices surging. Brent crude climbed above $110 a barrel on Thursday amid fears of further disruptions to regional energy supplies.
Why the shift?
Iran’s shift towards an offensive military doctrine reflects Tehran’s determination to make future US-Israeli attacks significantly more costly, according to analysts.
Negar Mortazavi, senior fellow at the Centre for International Policy, told Al Jazeera that Tehran was drawing lessons from the wars of 2025 and 2026 after its previous strategy of retaliation failed to prevent repeated attacks.
“Tehran now wants to establish a new equation: Any future attack on Iran will come at a much higher cost for the aggressors,” she told Al Jazeera.
Unable to match conventional US military capabilities, Iran is increasingly relying on asymmetric warfare, including missiles, drones and its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, Mortazavi explained.
She said Tehran was pursuing a broader strategy aimed at imposing military, economic and political costs on Washington, including potentially influencing the November 3 US midterm elections.
“Iran wants to teach Washington a lesson: Attacking Iran comes with a high price, one that can even cost elections,” Mortazavi said, referring to US surveys that are predicting electoral losses for Trump’s Republican Party.
She added that Iranian officials were closely monitoring the elections, believing the economic fallout from the war could damage the Republican Party’s prospects of retaining control of Congress.
“The long-term objective is to establish deterrence so that future American administrations think twice before daring to attack Iran again,” she said.
Political analyst Rami Khouri said the doctrine was also intended to ensure that the consequences of attacks extend to the US, Israel and regional countries supporting their military operations.
“That’s one part of the strategy, that the suffering and the damage have to be equal and reciprocal,” Khouri, nonresident senior fellow at the Arab Center, told Al Jazeera.
Khouri argued that Tehran was also seeking to challenge what it views as longstanding Western domination of the region.
“The Iranians are actually working to try to end the colonial period,” he said.
He added that Iran’s strategy could extend the economic consequences of conflict far beyond the Middle East, affecting energy supplies, transportation, insurance costs and shipments of essential goods.
“The pain is going to go way beyond just the Middle East and Israel and the US and will hurt people in other parts of the world,” Khouri said.
What has the US said about resuming the war?
Trump has offered conflicting signals about Washington’s next steps.
On Wednesday, he said the US was no longer negotiating with Tehran and suggested developments were imminent. “We are going to have something one way or the other that’ll happen fairly soon,” he told reporters.
He also said Washington could end the war immediately but wanted a lasting outcome. “It’ll end very soon. We could leave now, but we want to make sure it lasts for a long time,” Trump said at a campaign rally in South Carolina.
Trump previously pledged not to attack Iran before the November 3 elections.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this week that reaching a peace agreement is extremely difficult and insisted that Iran must stop targeting commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
In recent weeks, Iran’s enrichment of uranium has re-emerged as a point of contention.
Rubio has maintained that Washington will reject any agreement allowing Iran to develop nuclear weapons, which require highly enriched uranium. “The United States will not support any deal that creates a pathway for Iran to ever have a nuclear weapon,” he said on Wednesday.
Tehran insisted its right to enrichment is guaranteed under the Non-Proliferation Treaty.
Iran has offered a seven-day plan to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for Washington ending its blockade of Iranian ports, easing sanctions and unfreezing Iranian assets.
Meanwhile, the US Department of State on Wednesday ordered nonemergency personnel and their families to leave Saudi Arabia after recent Houthi attacks.
The US embassy in Riyadh has warned of further attacks while American officials told the Reuters news agency that family members could be withdrawn from other Gulf missions.
State Department spokesman Tommy Piggott said departure orders for mission personnel across the Gulf have not been ordered, saying the current orders were for “employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only”.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reiterated on Sunday his pledge to topple Iran’s government, saying it was key to preventing it from rebuilding its nuclear programme and the “axis of resistance”, further raising prospects of an escalation.
Netanyahu made the comments as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister is locked in a tough battle to remain in power in Tuesday’s elections.
Is war imminent?
Analysts warned that renewed US-Israeli attacks on Iran are increasingly possible with both sides preparing for another confrontation despite the continued possibility of diplomacy.
“Another round of war seems to be approaching,” Mortazavi said.
“Both sides appear to be preparing for renewed confrontation while escalating tensions in the Strait of Hormuz increase the risk of a wider conflict,” she said.
Mortazavi added that the elections in the next two weeks in the US and Israel could influence the timing of military action but warned that the current trajectory appeared to favour escalation over negotiations.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, on Wednesday said, “Everyone must know that any action against Iran comes at a cost.”
“If diplomacy can create this understanding, we prefer diplomacy, but if the war continues, Iran has the necessary means to sustain its response,” Rezaei said, according to the IRNA news agency.
Echoing Mortazavi, Khouri warned that another confrontation could be approaching although he said US threats might still be part of a negotiating strategy.
“I think imminent conflict is on the cards, but I don’t know if war is the right word to use,” Khouri told Al Jazeera.
He said renewed strikes could target Iran’s critical infrastructure, including electricity networks, transportation systems, bridges and essential services.
“We’re probably going to get some severe attacks on a few targets that will try to make life in Iran very difficult,” he said.
However, Khouri cautioned that Iran’s ability to withstand another major military offensive while inflicting comparable damage on its adversaries remained uncertain.
“It’s not clear if Iran has the ability to withstand major new assaults against it,” he said, while stressing that Tehran was unlikely to surrender to military pressure.

articles.title: Gulf nations brace for possible return to all-out war between US and Iran
articles.body:
The volatility around the Israeli and US midterm elections is fueling fears of renewed US-Israeli strikes on Iran in a short and intensive military campaign to push Tehran into concessions, with Iran vowing a devastating response against the Gulf nations.
The Gulf countries and the wider Middle East are bracing for a possible resumption of hostilities in the Iran war amid multiple simultaneous warnings and media reports of increasing intensity and detail, coupled with a massive US military build-up in the Gulf and Israeli and Iranian armies placed on high alert, raising fears of an imminent escalation with devastating consequences for the region.
Against the backdrop of growing speculation over the last weeks that the US and Israel may launch a new attack against Iran before or after the mid-term elections in the US and next week’s elections in Israel, a new US Department of State travel alert issued on Wednesday evening was relayed by news agencies and wider media as an urgent signal as to the imminence of war restarting, with the Gulf nations bearing the brunt of a potentially larger conflict.
The US Department of State announced that it ordered non-essential US government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as “the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area.”
Several news outlets reported that families of embassy staff in the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar, and Bahrain were also ordered to leave, quoting multiple diplomatic sources.
US Department of State spokesperson Tommy Pigott said these reports were “inaccurate."
“The US Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only,” as a result of the growing Houthi attacks, Pigott said in a post on X.
The US Saudi warning follows a Middle East-wide red alert issued by Washington on Monday to US citizens in 12 countries across the Middle East, warning their citizens in Israel, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, the UAE, Yemen and Iran, citing risks of potential attacks on US interests.
War vs elections
With days before Israel’s close elections in which prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu could lose power, and ahead of next month’s US midterm elections in which war-linked high prices have sparked voter anger, there are growing concerns and speculations that US-Israeli attacks on Iran could resume.
The US has been rebuilding a massive strike force in the Gulf by sending more military assets to the region, including a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops, to join the largest US naval and air force in the Middle East since the invasion of Iraq in 2003.
Iran has been warning for weeks that it has reorganised its defence capabilities and that any attack would be matched with what they called a devastating response against US interests and civilian infrastructure across the region, which would be far worse than their previous attacks on the Gulf nations and longer in time too.
Iranian officials and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) are preparing for war, having declared their “100% certainty” that the US and Israel will attack them again.
According to reports in Iran, Tehran activated its so-called Mosaic Defence doctrine by which Iran would operate in a decentralised way, by giving local commanders a list of targets to keep fighting even if the central command is destroyed.
In parallel with the US Department of State alert on Wednesday, the New York Times and other media reported that the US and Israel have developed specific plans for new strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections.
US President Donald Trump declared recently that any considerations for a new attack on Iran would be made after the US midterm elections.
According to the New York Times report, which quoted US officials, targets would likely include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and arsenals of missiles and drones, with the objective of pushing Iran into a deal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu earlier this week on an unannounced trip in Israel to discuss “the threats in the region.”
Speaking at an IDF officer graduation ceremony on Wednesday night, Netanyahu said that the Tehran regime has to be finally overthrown.
The Israeli premier justified this by stating that Iran's Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei "decided to follow in his father's footsteps (to attempt) once again to develop the bombs of death."’
The younger Khamenei, who has been selected as the new supreme leader following his father Ali Khamenei's killing in the US-Israeli strikes on Tehran in the opening salvo of the war on 28 February, is yet to be seen in public amid continued reports questioning his health condition.
Earlier this week, US media reported that dozens of Israeli fighter jets and refuelling aircraft reportedly flew towards the Iranian border before turning back, calling the sorties a military exercise and a "show of force," according to the Times of Israel newspaper.
According to media reports, US officials have questioned Israel's fighter jet deployment, believing the purpose of the exercise was to test Iranian air defence units and provoke them to open fire.
In parallel, Israeli media reported that Israeli security officials warned the government that an attack on Iran could be perceived as political interference in the election next week.
Israel’s opposition leader Yair Lapid told the Israeli media that “based on the information available to me, there is absolutely no reason to attack Iran or anywhere else before the elections.”
Calls for extreme caution amid uncertainty
Meanwhile on Thursday, seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz after being hit by Iran or striking naval mines, Tehran said, a markedly high number as tensions wind upward over concerns about a return to all-out war.
Iran still asserts control over the waterway, a central point of leverage in any talks with the US over the war.
During his state visit to Qatar, French President Emmanuel Macron issued a stern warning on Wednesday about the Gulf's fragile security situation, urging “extreme caution” to avoid escalating tensions that could reignite conflict, after talks with Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.
Macron told the media that he was “very cautious because no one can tell how the situation will evolve in the next days and weeks."
"No one can ignore that we are in a period that despite everything can lead to tensions: elections in Israel, the midterm elections in the United States, and so during this time efforts and initiatives must be doubled to avoid that these tensions don’t result in a resumption of conflict,” the French president explained.
"There is a lot of uncertainty and measures taken by one side and the other that I would not comment on."
Nevertheless, the US-Iran exchanges continue through international mediators, with Qatar and Pakistan leading the efforts to find a diplomatic breakthrough.
The US has previously applied pressure and threats on Iran to push for concessions and reach a deal.
A return to all-out war would again endanger civilians throughout the region and complicate global deliveries of oil, natural gas and related products like fertiliser from the region and likely bring another spike in energy prices around the world.

articles.title: Ukraine faces a new Russian cruise missile called Filin
articles.body:
- Ukrainian military intelligence published a 3D model and component breakdown of Russia’s Filin cruise missile, first used against Ukraine in late summer 2026.
- The ground-launched missile has a claimed range of up to 1,200 km and contains 35 American and 22 Chinese components.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency has published a detailed breakdown of Filin, a new Russian ground-launched cruise missile that Moscow began firing at Ukraine in late summer 2026. According to the agency, the missile combines a composite airframe and a Russian jet engine with onboard electronics built largely from American and Chinese parts.
The Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine’s Defense Ministry, known as HUR, released an interactive 3D model of the missile, its main assemblies and a catalog of its electronic components on the agency’s War & Sanctions portal. The agency did not say how many Filin missiles Russia has launched, which targets they hit or how investigators obtained the parts they examined.
Filin, Russian for “eagle owl,” is made by AO NPO Molniya, a company within Russia’s state-owned Tactical Missiles Corporation. HUR described the missile as the latest product of a Russian effort to build relatively cheap jet-powered strike weapons that launch from the ground instead of from aircraft or warships.
The missile is 3.5 meters (11.5 feet) long and has a wingspan of 3 meters (9.8 feet), with a maximum launch weight of 210 kg (463 pounds). Its fuselage is made of carbon fiber and fiberglass composites, and some of its parts are produced by 3D printing, an approach that can cut manufacturing time and cost compared with traditional machined components.
Russia claims Filin can reach a top speed of 800 km/h (497 mph) and fly up to 1,200 km (746 miles), although HUR’s specification sheet gives the range as 600 to 1,200 km (373 to 746 miles), which suggests the figure depends on the configuration. The missile can fly at very low altitude, where ground-based radar has a harder time detecting incoming threats, or climb as high as 6 km (19,700 feet).
Filin comes in versions with either a 50 kg (110-pound) or a 100 kg (220-pound) warhead, and HUR lists three warhead types: high-explosive fragmentation, penetrating and thermobaric. A thermobaric warhead first disperses an explosive cloud and then ignites it, producing a longer and more powerful blast wave than a conventional charge of similar weight.
The missile is fired from a ground launcher with the help of a solid-fuel booster, which pushes it up to flying speed before its small jet engine takes over for the cruise to the target.
HUR’s investigation also links Filin closely to Russia’s long-range attack drone program. The missile’s onboard equipment is produced by OOO PLAZ, which also makes equipment for the Garpiya, or “Harpy,” drone, a modification of the Geran-2 built in several series by the Izhevsk Electromechanical Plant Kupol. The Geran-2 itself is Russia’s version of the Iranian-designed Shahed-136, and HUR said electronic units from Filin and Garpiya share a similar layout and similar markings.
For guidance, Filin relies on a Chinese-made inertial navigation system, which tracks the missile’s position using onboard motion sensors without any outside signal. It works alongside a 16-channel Kometa satellite navigation module, a jam-resistant receiver made by Russia’s VNIIR-Progress that has repeatedly turned up in Russian drones and guided bombs recovered in Ukraine.
HUR said Filin’s electronics resemble those found in other Russian missiles and drones, but with a larger share of Chinese parts and with the same design solutions reused across different units and circuit boards. Investigators counted 35 American components and 22 Chinese ones in the missile’s onboard equipment.
The identified suppliers include Texas Instruments, Analog Devices, NXP Semiconductors and STMicroelectronics, along with Chinese firms such as WinChipHead and Mornsun. Production markings on some parts date from 2021 and 2022, including an Ethernet switch chip made in May 2022, three months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
Filin’s engine, by contrast, is Russian: an R500 turbojet built by OOO Reynolds. HUR had previously identified the same engine in Russia’s S-71K Kover air-launched cruise missile and in the S-71M Monokhrom.

articles.title: Russia frees retired US schoolteacher in goodwill gesture as Putin meets Witkoff
articles.body:
Russia frees retired US schoolteacher in goodwill gesture as Putin meets Witkoff
- Russia freed retired US schoolteacher Stephen Hubbard, 74, and sent him back to the United States after talks between Vladimir Putin and US envoy Steve Witkoff.
- Witkoff called the talks “constructive” and said more US-Russia-Ukraine discussions are planned, with a possible high-level meeting in mid-November.
- Hubbard’s release drew praise from Trump officials and anger in Washington, while his family and lawyer said his conviction for “mercenary activity” was false.
AI generated
ST PETERSBURG, Russia - Russia freed Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired US schoolteacher in custody since 2022, from prison on Oct 21 and took him to St Petersburg to fly back to the United States, after talks that Washington said were a step towards ending the war in Ukraine.
Russian President Vladimir Putin made the announcement at a meeting in St Petersburg with US envoy Steve Witkoff, who later said the talks will continue towards planned technical-level discussions involving the US, Russia and Ukraine.
Witkoff thanked Putin for Hubbard’s release and called the Russian leader a “humanitarian”, in footage of the exchange, a remark that drew sharp rebuke from Republican and Democratic lawmakers given Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The prisoner release comes as US President Donald Trump’s recent gestures toward Moscow, including a deal to buy Russian diesel and a waiver of new sanctions, have already sparked bipartisan pushback in the US Congress and worry in European capitals.
Putin’s spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, said Putin had freed Hubbard at the request of US President Donald Trump, and had also taken into account the American’s poor health.
“The president sends his thanks, our whole nation sends their thanks, because of Stephen Hubbard,” Witkoff told Putin in a meeting shown on state TV. “Because of you he’s going home to his family.”
In a video shared with Reuters, Hubbard, wearing a dark fleece and clean-shaven, is seen in an undisclosed location in Russia shaking Witkoff’s hand and thanking him.
Later, Trump posted a picture of Hubbard appearing inside a plane with others and holding an American flag. Trump told reporters late on Oct 21 that Hubbard had landed and that he would be visiting the White House “over the next day or so”.
Hubbard’s son, Joseph Coleman, told Reuters in a voice message that he spoke briefly by phone with his father before he boarded the airplane in Russia.
“Today, he seemed light in his step, a sense of happiness in his voice”, Coleman said.
Three-way meeting planned on war
Witkoff called the talks with Putin “constructive” and said in a post on X that he had also met Ukrainian and European leaders in Oslo to advance Trump’s mission to end the war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he supported the US proposal for three-way talks with Russia and the US at the level of negotiators to be held as soon as possible, preferably by early November.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere, who met Witkoff, had earlier said the talks will likely happen in mid-November and focus on a potential post-conflict security structure.
On the evening of Oct 21, officials in Kyiv said Russian forces attacked the capital city with ballistic missiles that damaged homes and a petrol station and caused injuries.
‘Humanitarian’
Witkoff’s praise for Putin over Hubbard’s release was scorned by some in Washington.
“Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian.’ What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say,” Republican US Senator Thom Tillis said in an X post directed at the US envoy.
Trump, asked about Witkoff’s “humanitarian” comment earlier on Oct 21, told reporters at the White House: “Well, I guess you have to say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man, who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life, out. But I wouldn’t say anything one way or the other.”
The US “gave nothing in exchange” for the prisoner release, Trump said, adding “we’re getting closer” to settling the war.
“He is the happiest man around,” Trump said of Hubbard.
“This was very surprising to him, but I did it, it really took place on a phone call at the end of last week with President Putin, so we appreciate it very much. And his family is extremely happy.”
Family, lawyer disputed conviction
Hubbard, a native of Michigan, had been serving a prison sentence of six years and 10 months in Russia following a conviction for mercenary activity in a closed-door trial.
He was arrested in April 2022 in the eastern Ukrainian city of Izyum, where Russian prosecutors alleged he had been manning a Ukrainian military checkpoint.
Prosecutors said Hubbard had joined a Ukrainian territorial defence unit, received training, weapons and ammunition, and was promised US$1,000 a month.
Russian state media reported he pleaded guilty to the charges. But De Luca previously told Reuters that Hubbard had told him the charges against him were false and that he was not in any combat or military unit.
In a 2024 interview with Reuters, Hubbard’s sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, also disputed the idea that her brother took up arms for any government, calling him “so non-military” and pointing out his advanced age.
De Luca on Oct 21 thanked Trump, Witkoff and other US officials for securing the release, calling it “a dividend earned along the hard road to peace”.
As of Oct 21, Hubbard was the only US prisoner held by Russia who was designated by Washington as “wrongfully detained”.
The Trump administration secured the release last year of another American jailed in Russia, schoolteacher Marc Fogel, who had been serving a 14-year prison term for drug smuggling. REUTERS

articles.title: Press review: Russia-US-Ukraine peace hopes rise as Moscow offers Iran-US mediation
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. The prospects for peace and trilateral talks between Russia, the US and Ukraine following the October 21 St. Petersburg meeting; Moscow’s willingness to mediate between Tehran and Washington; and Russia’s potential agreement with the US to start shipping fertilizers alongside diesel. These stories topped Thursday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Media: Chances of peace and Russia-US-Ukraine talks following St. Petersburg meeting
US efforts to end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine have resumed, perhaps the main visible and indisputable outcome of the October 21 talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg. The envoy left Russia with news of the release of an American citizen from a Russian prison and Moscow’s assurances that the proposals he brought would be reviewed. In addition, Putin expressed readiness to launch trilateral talks in the Russia-US-Ukraine format. The talks are scheduled for mid-November, after the US congressional elections, which are likely to bring significant changes.
Witkoff’s visit to St. Petersburg wrapped up a busy diplomatic round, international affairs expert Nikolay Novik told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. The St. Petersburg talks were preceded by consultations in Oslo. Witkoff and Kushner, who participated remotely, met with Zelensky, European leaders, and EU and NATO representatives there, the expert recalled. "It is likely that Witkoff presented an updated plan to end the conflict and a proposal for direct talks involving Trump and Zelensky. There may also have been discussions about a meeting between Putin, Trump, and Xi Jinping in China during the APEC summit on November 18-19: Washington doesn’t need a technical pause, but rather an outcome from the summit that can be presented as a tangible result," Novik said.
At the same time, the package of conditions that the US envoy might have brought - if these were the ones recently mentioned in the Western media - does not suit Russia, Russian International Affairs Council President Dmitry Trenin told Vedomosti. According to the expert, Moscow agreed to discuss not so much the settlement itself as possible ways to establish a security framework for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends. "By 2027, we will most likely still be in the midst of ongoing hostilities, though the US administration had certainly hoped to achieve tangible results by the end of this year," Trenin noted. The expert stressed that the future prospects of the negotiation process, including the development of specific terms, will be determined by the actual situation on the battlefield.
The current round of talks differs from previous ones because the agenda will include the issue of security guarantees for both Russia and Ukraine, an issue that was not included in negotiations with Kiev following the Istanbul consultations, Nikolay Silayev, a leading researcher at the MGIMO Institute of International Relations, said. However, the expert does not expect the upcoming negotiations with Ukraine to conclude any differently from the previous ones. "The main reason for the lack of confidence in a breakthrough is the public statements made by Ukrainian and European officials. Their position remains the same: an unconditional ceasefire," he stressed.
Izvestia: Russia ready to mediate between Tehran and Washington
Moscow is prepared to act as a mediator in settling the conflict between the US and Iran, provided both parties are interested. Talks between Washington and Tehran have reached an impasse, partly due to the unresolved question of Iran’s nuclear program. Russia previously proposed transporting Iran’s enriched uranium to its territory, but this initiative has yet to receive support.
The eight-month conflict between the US and Iran has stalled. Washington’s initial plan to quickly topple the country’s government has failed. Passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains difficult, and diplomats have yet to make progress toward resolving the conflict. Under these circumstances, Russia could assume the role of mediator. Moscow is ready to take such a step, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko told Izvestia. "If all parties express interest, then we are ready [to act as mediators]," he noted. "We previously offered our services regarding how the Iranian nuclear program could be resolved, but our proposals have not yet been supported," the senior diplomat said.
Thanks to its good relations with both Iran and Israel, Russia occupies a unique position as a universal intermediary in the Middle East, political analyst Alexander Kargin said. Moreover, Moscow is currently pursuing a negotiating track with the US as well. The expert noted that Pakistan, another potential mediator, has no diplomatic relations with Israel at all, whereas Russia does not face this problem.
Russian mediation would at least help establish a ceasefire, paving the way for a comprehensive resolution of the crisis, Kargin said. The analyst expects that, ultimately, the practical necessity of Moscow’s involvement will prevail, and the parties will bring Russia into the negotiations. At the same time, according to him, the parties to the conflict have diametrically opposed views on the nuclear program. While Russia’s proposal to remove the uranium would be ideal, heightened tensions in the Middle East are preventing the parties from making even the smallest compromises, Kargin stressed.
Izvestia: Russia may begin exporting fertilizers to US alongside diesel
Russia is ready to supply mineral fertilizers and fuel to the US, but expanding fertilizer exports would require a reallocation of shipments: currently, about 69% of fertilizer production is exported, experts said. Russian President Vladimir Putin has discussed the prospect of supplying fertilizers to the US market on a significant scale. In addition, the first shipment of 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel fuel is scheduled to leave for the US on October 22, with other countries set to receive shipments by the end of the year.
During a meeting with US special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on October 21, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that Moscow could supply fertilizers to the American market in large quantities. However, it is difficult to gauge potential export volumes, since a significant portion of Russian production is already under contract with foreign buyers, Denis Prikhodko, an equity market analyst at Alfa-Capital Asset Management, told Izvestia. According to him, shipments will increase gradually, primarily through the redistribution of export flows among foreign markets rather than through higher production.
Increasing fertilizer and diesel fuel shipments to the US market could help bring down prices for these products both in the US and globally, which is especially important for agricultural producers. Such agreements with Russia would benefit both the Donald Trump administration and the Russian authorities, Igor Yushkov, a leading analyst at the National Energy Security Fund, stressed.
The European factor is also relevant. According to political scientist and German studies expert Yegor Belyachkov, the current leadership of most European countries will likely react negatively to an agreement between Russia and the US on fertilizer supplies, just as they did with the diesel deal. This approach directly reflects European countries' policy in recent years, under which the slightest compromise between Moscow and Washington prompts EU nations to attempt to block such agreements. Brussels could do so by tightening sanctions against Russia and coordinating with American Democrats, the expert said.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Possibility of routing Persian Gulf oil around Strait of Hormuz
New pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz and lead to seaports outside the Persian Gulf will address the problem of supplying Middle Eastern oil to the global market. In five years, the strait may become obsolete for oil trade as shipments are redirected along new routes. This is not the first attempt to find alternative ways to deliver oil from Persian Gulf countries. Previously, this idea was also proposed by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. According to him, the construction of oil pipelines will render the Strait of Hormuz "a worthless piece of water" in as little as two to three years.
Bypass routes are currently more profitable, not because transporting oil via pipeline is inexpensive, but because of the increased costs linked to transit through the Strait of Hormuz, Maxim Malkov, a Kept partner and head of the firm’s oil and gas practice, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta. Before the crisis, tanker transit cost the same as or less than pipeline transport, while now, that balance has reversed, the expert noted. However, maritime transport is cheaper in peacetime. The cost of pumping oil through a pipeline is up to five times higher than the cost of moving it by oil tanker per kilometer, Oleg Abelev, head of the analytical department at the Rikom-Trust investment company, pointed out.
Existing alternative routes do not resolve the problem because their combined capacity is less than half of the volumes that previously passed through the Strait of Hormuz, Malkov emphasized. Moreover, the Red Sea poses its own risks, such as Houthi attacks, and there are virtually no alternatives to tankers for transporting refined petroleum products, the expert noted. But even if the existing infrastructure that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz is expanded and new oil pipelines are built in parallel, the economic viability of these projects will be questionable, economist Boris Kopeikin stressed. If the situation in the region stabilizes in the long term, oil will once again follow the traditional route, through the Strait of Hormuz, he said.
At the same time, the main advantage of alternative routes is the diversification of risks. They reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz and allow exports to continue in the event of shipping restrictions, but they do not guarantee complete supply security, Ivan Timonin, a senior manager at the Implementa consulting firm, said. According to Abelev, pipelines are no safer than maritime transport. They are vulnerable to drone and missile attacks, and protecting them along their entire length is quite difficult. Unlike seagoing vessels, a pipeline is stationary and its location is precisely known. It cannot be replaced or rerouted. Maritime transport offers greater flexibility. Oil pipelines for the Persian Gulf states are an expensive insurance policy, not a cheap alternative, the expert stressed.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: French authorities trying to ease protests with talks and concessions
Ahead of another round of large-scale protests scheduled for the weekend, the authorities are trying to reach a deal with the protesters. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu met with union representatives on October 21. The meeting produced no results; the government did not receive any promises to call off the protests. In fact, a general strike has been announced.
Nevertheless, Lecornu remains undeterred. The government has proposed an aid program for businesses affected by the unrest. Following his trip to the Persian Gulf states, President Emmanuel Macron issued a statement saying that he had secured additional fuel shipments to bring down prices in the country. The authorities are hoping these measures will have a rapid effect.
Rather than resorting to force, the French authorities have decided to address the wave of protests sweeping the country through persuasion. They have chosen to respond to the demonstrators’ main demands. Perhaps there is no other option: last weekend, more than half a million French citizens took to the streets across the country. The protests are no longer limited to schoolchildren and their parents who are dissatisfied with the education system. Labor unions are actively participating in the protests, which are directed against the rising cost of living and ultimately against the economic policies of the current president and government.
At the same time, the situation in the country is gradually returning to normal, although this will take some time, Tatyana Zvereva, a professor at the World Economy and World Politics Faculty of the Russian National Research University Higher School of Economics, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. "The composition of the protesters is complex. It includes high school students, members of the ‘Yellow Vests’ movement, and others, including members of fringe political organizations," she noted. According to the expert, the French authorities are pursuing two main lines of action. On the one hand, they are restoring order, which society as a whole expects. The far-right National Rally party has been particularly vocal in demanding this. On the other hand, the authorities are negotiating with moderate protesters.
"The logic is this: the most aggressive protesters must be held accountable, and positive-minded citizens must be reached out to by addressing their socio-economic demands. However, the second point is much more difficult to achieve. Therefore, it seems unlikely that we can expect quick results from the negotiations. But dialogue can help defuse the situation and let off some steam," Zvereva emphasized.
TASS is not responsible for the material quoted in these press reviews

articles.title: Britain undersells its nuclear contribution to NATO
articles.body:
Britain is unique among allies in declaring its existing nuclear forces to NATO, but despite nuclear capabilities consuming over a fifth of the defence budget the Ministry of Defence does not maximise the political and economic value of that commitment, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, examined nuclear deterrence in the High North as part of its inquiry.
Dhesi said: “The High North poses a major strategic challenge for the UK’s security. This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage.”
Its conclusion states: “The United Kingdom has committed to acquiring a sub-strategic nuclear capability to enhance deterrence, although how this aligns with the security of the High North is less clear. To ensure the capability is effective it will probably be necessary for the RAF to occasionally rehearse forward deploying the nuclear-capable F-35A aircraft to the High North. Recipient countries will, therefore, need to be fully aligned and supportive of Britain’s extended deterrence strategy. Uniquely, the UK already declares its existing nuclear forces to NATO, but despite consuming over a fifth of the defence budget the MOD does not maximise the political and economic value of this considerable financial and military commitment.”
According to the most recent departmental annual report and accounts cited by the committee, spending on nuclear capabilities accounts for £14.45 billion of the total defence budget of £69.61 billion.
Britain agreed in 2025 to purchase twelve F-35A fighter aircraft for the Royal Air Force, giving it a sub-strategic nuclear capability and joining NATO’s Dual Capable Aircraft programme, with the Defence Investment Plan allocating £2.1 billion up to 2030 for the total British F-35 fleet. The committee notes that while the aircraft will be flown by RAF pilots, approval to use the nuclear weapons carried by those jets would in any crisis remain under American control.
The report asks how Britain will operate the new capability, including whether the aircraft would deploy to allied countries during peacetime to practise their wartime nuclear role, and how concern about the enduring level of American commitment to European security is addressed by carrying a weapon that remains under American sovereign control during any crisis.
France and Britain each hold around three hundred nuclear warheads, against an American stockpile the report puts at around 3,700 operational weapons. Under the July 2025 Northwood Declaration the two countries agreed to create a Nuclear Steering Group to provide political direction and coordinate across nuclear policy, capabilities and operations, and President Macron announced changes to French nuclear doctrine in March 2026 which included moving towards forward deterrence.
That resulted in bilateral agreements with NATO countries including Denmark and Norway in the High North, allowing French nuclear aircraft to deploy temporarily to their territory for exercises and joint missions. French nuclear assets will not be shared and French nuclear decision making will remain sovereign.
The committee records that France has generated considerable publicity around its agreements, strengthening its international profile on security matters and offering a platform to engage on wider issues including defence export sales.
Its recommendation asks the department to provide the committee with a classified briefing on how it intends to enhance nuclear deterrence through the new sub-strategic capability, including any discussions with regional allies on extended deterrence in the High North and the forward deployment of the capability, and states that given the financial burden of operating the deterrent the department should remind allies more frequently of the unique nuclear capability Britain declares to NATO.

articles.title: ‘No Kings’ protests reflect a crisis of imperial plutocracy in the US
articles.body:
‘No Kings’ protests reflect a crisis of imperial plutocracy in the US
ARIZONA- The most obvious focus of the current “No Kings” protests lies in US citizens’ immediate “bread and butter issues”: brutal cuts to education, social security, and health care ($1 trillion in cuts to Medicaid and Childre’s Health Insurance); massive inflation that makes it hard to feed families, pay outrageous costs for health insurance, and endure the exorbitant price of fuel precipitated by the perfidious war on Iran, launched for a second time since June, 2025, in the midst of negotiations.
Beyond that initial layer is the severe reduction and even obliteration of programs that help the poor, and the savage attacks against immigrants, many of whom are either legal or already citizens; yet all of them—whether Latin American or Middle Eastern—cast as either “criminals, thugs, rapists” or “threats to national security”, and subjected to imprisonment and deportation.
A distinct goal of the current protests, however, as noted by Tehran Times , is the urgent emphasis on voting in the upcoming midterm elections, since the average voter turnout in midterm elections is only 48%, despite a rise to 52% in 2022. Midterm elections occur halfway through a presidential term, and determine the composition of both chambers of Congress, Representatives and Senators. This November’s election is particularly crucial, for if Trump loses his Republican majority in Congress, Democrats plan to launch investigations into his blatantly corrupt family businesses, the Epstein files, immigration enforcement, and corporate profiteering. And if Trump also loses control of the Senate, Democrats can block Trump’s nominees for Cabinet positions, paralyze his appointment of federal judges and nominees to the Supreme Court, give Democrats subpoena power that would enhance their power to investigate the administration, and might possibly lead to impeachment proceedings.
While Trump and his base—both the “uneducated” he claims to love and the oligarchs he pampers—fear such an outcome, the rest of the country dreads that the administration may steal the election, as he attempted to do in 2020, and which Trump continues to hallucinate having won.
For more astute protesters, deeper dimensions lie beyond their immediate private afflictions and political tactics: the current regime is the malignant harvest of a systemic sociopolitical disease, an incremental process that has achieved only its most virulent embodiment in Trump. Decades of lavish tax breaks for the ultra-rich have impoverished and depleted life for the ordinary citizen, accomplished by the long assault on Labor Unions and the obscene rise in Corporate Profits. The struggle is against a system devoted to perpetual war and militarism, the rise of a surveillance state behind a shabby façade of “democracy” whose flimsy mask conceals the true face of a merciless plutocracy.
The entire society has been commodified: humanity, personhood, culture, art, law, and indeed the Earth itself are subordinated to the calculation of profit for the oligarchs. As one corporate executive affirmed, “We have to save capitalism from democracy.” [Quoted in Nancy MacLean’s masterful Democracy in Chains (2017)]. But this catastrophe did not begin with Trump, whose flagrant vulgarity, malice, ignorance and blatant corruption have reduced every ideal to a “deal”, every principle to “profit”, every fact to “fake news.” Nonetheless, Trump has crossed a threshold, representing an apotheosis of the Neoliberal ideology that has reigned since Reagan and Thatcher. Not to be confused with “Liberal” social values, Neoliberalism is not merely an economic theory but a Worldview that envisions the absolute supremacy of the spurious “Free Market”: privatization of all public space, the erasure of any regulations and responsibilities that protect workers, the public and the environment. The social fabric is devastated: citizens are reduced to mere consumers; elections succumb to legal bribery; the indivual will is divinized, while community and compassion are mocked as “Communist.”
At its root, Neoliberalism is an assault on all transcendent values, which are reduced to mere transactions: the evisceration of the Goodness, Truth and Beauty that form the very basis and deep fraternity of authentic principles that might unite the threefold Abrahamic Traditions and bridge the distance between East and West. But for the plutocracy, nothing is sacred: all life is merely “collateral damage” in the cult of money and power. Meanwhile, a perverse, heretical “Christian fascism” mirrors the Zionist desecration of Judaism and mutilates our shared dialectical heritage into a weapon of conquest.
On leaving office in January, 1961 President Eisenhower warned against the Military Industrial Complex (MIC), which over the last six decades has metastasized into the Military-Industrial-Media-Academic Complex (MIMAC), whereby Corporate Media serves as flagrant propaganda, and corporatized University Administrations silence and expel voices dedicated to the practice of critical thinking, professors who bravely stand for global justice, peace and accountability, while war crimes and genocide are upheld with lies, prevarication and impunity.
Trump has waged an assault on the very foundations of American society: the Constitution, a crucial element of which is the “separation of powers” between the Executive, Legislative and Judiciary branches, designed to avert the rise of tyranny. While Trump has attacked judges appointed by former presidents of both parties, he has fantasized that Article II of the Constitution gives him the right to do “whatever I want.”
The Will to Power and Addiction to Avarice reign supreme. In 2018, Trump unilaterally abrogated Obama’s JCPOA—the accord (in conjunction with China, France, Germany, Russia, and the United Kingdom) limiting Iran’s nuclear development in exchange for sanctions relief—despite Iran’s compliance, as verified by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). That fateful decision resulted from pressure exerted by his billionaire donors, amid the long-established aims of the CIA in conjunction with Mossad.
What many Iranians as well as Americans grasp is that we are facing an administration of the most deeply cynical character, whose abysmal inhumanity was crystallized in the heartless retort of Matt Schlapp (chairman of the American Conservative Union), on a Piers Morgan broadcast in March: dismissing Peter Beinart’s compassionate lament that if the U.S. and Israel had not attacked Iran on February 28, the schoolgirls killed at the Shajareh Tayyibeh elementary school in Minab “would be alive”, Schlapp quipped: “They’d be alive in a burqa… in a barbaric, unequal society… with no ability to make career choices.” By Schlapp’s cavalier reckoning, the illegal, unprovoked war of aggression launched against Iran was blameless, the humanity of both the dead and living girls, their teachers and parents obliterated, along with the lives of the 73 boys whose massacre was omitted in nearly all US media reports.
Be it noted that Schlapp has faced multiple sexual harassment charges involving other men.
