The bombing of Minab was no mere “accident”, given that Pete Hegseth, Trump’s Secretary of War (formerly “Defense”) openly implemented a doctrine of “More lethality and less accountability”, publicly spurning what he called “stupid rules of engagement.” Not mere bravado: he dissolved the policy to limit civilian casualties established by the Department of Defense, known as the Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response (CHMR, pronounced “Chimmer”), and fired the senior advisor at the Pentagon’s Civilian Protection Center of Excellence, Air Force combat veteran Wes J. Bryant. “We’re departing from the rules and norms that we’ve tried to establish as a global community since at least World War II,” Bryant said. “There’s zero accountability.”
As the eminent former Ambassador Chas Freeman has declared, “diplomacy… begins with empathy.” The tragic reality of US foreign policy, he laments, is quite the opposite: “We don’t do diplomacy anymore. [In] the ‘rules-based order,’ … we make the rules and decide who they apply to and who is exempt from them.”
Freeman’s grim insights are amply confirmed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s shameless scorn of “so-called International Law”, as the administration engages in attacking and dismantling every mechanism designed to promote and ensure human rights and global accountability, from the UN to the ICC, which Trump himself has called “an evil group of people”. For the US soars above the law, which it makes and breaks, supports or sabotages at will, in accordance with its capricious, often incoherent and myopic “interests” bereft of values, blind to principles, contemptuous of truth.
Like a lobotomized version of Netanyahu, Trump exemplifies what Marc Owen Jones has called alethocide: the killing of truth, in brash defiance of Hannah Arendt’s warning: “The ideal subject of totalitarian rule is not the convinced Nazi or the convinced Communist, but people for whom the distinction between fact and fiction (i.e., the reality of experience) and the distinction between the true and the false (i.e., the standards of thought) no longer exist.” [The Origins of Totalitarianism. Part 3, Ch. 13, §3., p. 474. (1979 ed.)].
Yet lest we be comforted by the hope that a Democratic majority would make the needful turn to empathy and diplomacy, we have only to regard the dismal Biden policy toward Palestine to sober such wishes, from its refusal to condemn the brutal evictions of Palestinian families in East Jerusalem (2021), to its audacious denials of Israeli apartheid—documented and declared from 2020-2022 not only by the UN, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International, but by Israeli human rights organizations B’Tselem and Yesh Din—to its brazen lies and duplicity in the face of war crimes and genocide, as Biden’s minions violated US domestic law by providing Israel a flood of weapons, and “willfully enabled atrocities” in Gaza, as meticulously detailed in the recent book Crossing the Red Line by Akbar Shahid Ahmed.
As demonstrated since the Clinton presidency, the key difference between the two US parties rests in rhetoric and comportment, not in substance: while Trump spews vulgarity, racism, misogyny, megalomania and toxic fables; threatens Iran that “a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again”; declares Climate Change a “hoax” and sneers at the global scientific consensus regarding the ecocide we continue to commit—Democrats deplore his barbarity and ignorance, while urbanely praising human rights but ignoring their implementation, raise insipid procedural objections against the war, and prudently pose and gesture toward crucial shifts to renewable energy—yet only two candidates even mention “climate” on their current campaign websites.
After Gaza, the Democrats’ notoriety as “the lesser of two evils” is more woefully suspect than ever. Both parties serve the corporate and financial elite, even as they seduce and betray their constituents, far too many of whom remain complacent in the face of the fascist tide, distracted by celebrity worship, sports events, casinos, and barbecues, while vainly imagining themselves immune to the lure of “bread and circuses” and the lust for dominion and military might that leads to the suicide of empires. Trump is merely, as Chris Hedges avows, “the naked, stripped-down expression of this suicidal pact.”
The thirst for hope must not erase our nation’s long history of depredation, too rarely taught in our schools: throughout the twentieth century US support for Latin American dictators reached its peak during the Reagan administration, but the Empire emerged long before: the Mexican-American War (1846-8) was provoked by the US in order to justify stealing the territories and riches of California and Texas; Hawaii was overthrown in 1893; and the Spanish-American War of 1898—purportedly to “liberate Cuba from the domination of Spain (the erstwhile analogue of our era’s ennemis du jour, whether “Communist” or “Islamist”), but in truth to ensure US domination of the Caribbean sugar market—extended to the Philippine War (1899-1902) to annex and subjugate the archipelago under the guise of independence, freedom, and “Christian” values.
The dynamic satirized in Mark Twain’s scathing essay of 1901, “To the Person Sitting in Darkness” exposed the seething Imperialism and avarice beneath the dazzling veil of rhetorical hypocrisy in its lethal quest to “enlighten” the “savage”, “heathen”, “uncivilized” peoples and lands whose sovereignty and dignity were despoiled in our grotesque triumph.
A modicum of change will doubtless come with time, but the imperative transformation of consciousness may well arrive only with the bitter gift of regret: the inevitable collapse of our hegemonic Heart of Darkness.

articles.title: Congressmen urge Trump, Musk to give Ukraine ability to destroy missile launchers in Russia – media
articles.body:
American congressmen, including 16 members of the Democratic Party and seven members of the Republican Party, have signed a letter urging U.S President Donald Trump and SpaceX founder Elon Musk to grant Ukraine access to Starlink satellite systems to detect missile launchers on the territory of Russia.
"We are writing to urge you to ask Elon Musk to let Ukraine use the Starlink satellite internet system to hunt for missile launchers inside Russia. With one phone call, you could both save lives and give Vladimir Putin greater incentives to negotiate," reads the text of the letter sent on Wednesday, as cited by The Hill.
Among the Republicans who signed the letter are Joe Wilson (South Carolina), Brian Fitzpatrick (Pennsylvania), Don Bacon (Nebraska), Carlos Gimenez (Florida), Jeff Hurd (Colorado), Andy Harris (Maryland), and Max Miller (Ohio).
"Mr. President, we all share the goal of ending the war in Ukraine and the devastating loss of life it has caused... If Ukraine cannot reliably intercept Russian arrows, it must be able to strike the archer. The Starlink system, operated by Mr. Musk's SpaceX, could help with this," the letter states, with the congressmen noting that Vladimir Putin "currently has no intention of stopping the bloodshed."
As reported, Ukraine began using StarShield in 2024. Standard StarLink (Starlink Mini), installed on drones, has a limited speed of up to 160 km/h, which is insufficient to perform certain missions. To make an aircraft fly faster, it is necessary to gain access specifically to the military version of StarLink – StarShield.
SpaceX, without warning the Ukrainian Defense Forces on the night of October 14, unilaterally restricted the operation of StarShield terminals; this complicated the work of UAV missions, in particular interceptors and middle strikes. By the end of that same day, the operation of terminals at speeds of 160 km/h resumed, but Ukraine received confirmation that the 160 km/h restriction applies only within its territory.
On the same day, Musk stated that decisions regarding restrictions on the operation of military StarShield systems are made by the U.S military and the president, and commercial StarLink cannot be used for offensive military actions. However, Trump later stated that Washington was not involved in slowing down StarShield for Ukraine, and U.S Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that StarShield was allegedly unavailable to Ukraine and the White House had nothing to do with disruptions in StarLink's operation. U.S Secretary of War Pete Hegseth reported that his department refrained from issuing any directives regarding restricting StarShield's operation. Later, the British newspaper The Telegraph, citing its own sources, reported that Musk personally appealed to Trump with a proposal to limit StarLink's operating speed for the Ukrainian military.
Following this, a number of senators and congressmen stated the unacceptability of such actions, Musk's influence on the course of the war in Ukraine and U.S security, and that they would demand an investigation into the restrictions on the operation of StarShield systems in Ukraine and hold those responsible accountable.
On October 20, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that the American side had restored the operation of Ukraine's early warning system for Russian ballistic missile launches and announced a conversation with Rubio, while Rubio himself stated that he had nothing to do with decisions made by Musk and SpaceX regarding the operation of StarLink and StarShield.
The European Commission stated that SpaceX's restrictions on StarLink services for Ukraine contradict agreements, and the company must ensure full access for Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine exchange strikes as US envoy leaves after talks
articles.body:
Russia pounds Kyiv, Ukraine launches drones, despite talk of renewing negotiations
KYIV/MOSCOW, Oct 22 - Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow overnight as the warring sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest US push to end the conflict.
Russia said on Wednesday it was ready to resume US-mediated talks with Ukraine next month, after President Vladimir Putin hosted US envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in St Petersburg.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he hoped negotiations, which would be the first since February, would take place early in November.
Ukraine said Russia fired at least 21 ballistic missiles in three waves. Russia said Ukraine launched 630 drones towards the capital Moscow during the night.
The two sides held an exchange of war dead, with Moscow handing over 252 bodies and Ukraine handing over 25, according to the Belta state news agency in neighbouring Belarus. Such exchanges have accompanied moves towards talks in the past.
But while Witkoff spoke of "some degree of momentum" after meeting Zelenskiy and European and NATO officials in Oslo earlier in the week, the Kremlin expressed doubts.
"The Americans sensed some new nuances (in Oslo) and told us about this. But these nuances, so to speak, do not entirely satisfy us," Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said.
A senior Russian official, briefed on the results of the Putin-Witkoff talks, said they were relatively short and not substantive. The American brought a set of proposals drafted in Oslo and handed them to Putin for review, the person said.
Another source close to the Kremlin said the US proposals included a scenario where Ukraine would cede all of its Donbas region to Russia in return for receiving a guarantee of its future security from NATO.
Russia says it launched the war, the deadliest in Europe since World War Two, in part to prevent Ukraine from joining NATO. It has repeatedly said it would not end fighting unless Ukraine cedes more land, limits the size of its forces and is permanently barred from forming alliances.
Ukraine, which says the invasion was an unprovoked war of conquest, has long dismissed Russia's conditions as a demand for capitulation that would leave it defenceless against future Russian attacks.
US PRAISE FOR 'HUMANITARIAN' PUTIN GOES DOWN BADLY WITH KYIV
Zelenskiy's meeting with Witkoff was aimed in part at smoothing over a deterioration in relations with Washington this month, after President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and lifted sanctions on Moscow.
Kyiv says Washington failed to provide early-warning data on Russian missile launches, throttled the SpaceX satellite system used to guide Ukrainian drones, and withheld missile defence systems bought on its behalf by Europeans. Washington denies any shift in policy to intentionally hamper Ukraine's forces.
Trump has repeatedly rebuked Ukraine for attacking Russian oil refineries while saying little about far deadlier Russian attacks on Ukraine. He called for Zelenskiy to be replaced and said Russia's actions in Ukraine have been "fine".
Zelenskiy, who long avoided any criticism of the Trump administration, has increasingly pushed back against what he describes as a shift towards sympathy with Moscow.
On Thursday Zelenskiy snapped back at Witkoff for saluting Putin as a "humanitarian" during his visit to Russia, when the US envoy thanked Putin for releasing a 74-year-old American captured by Russian forces in Ukraine.
"Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian 'humanitarians' since yesterday evening," Zelenskiy posted on X. "They used 21 missiles. Unfortunately, numerous sites across the city have been hit and damaged."
He said 2 people were killed and 34 injured, including five children, in attacks on a dozen Ukrainian regions.
Russia said it carried out a "massive strike" overnight on port infrastructure in Ukraine's Odesa region, as well as on vessels used by the Ukrainian military.
In Russia, two people were wounded near Moscow by drones launched towards the capital during the night, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram. Most of the drones were downed at long range, he added.
In the Russian border region of Belgorod, one man was killed and another wounded by Ukrainian drones, local officials said.
With the frontlines of the war largely static, both sides have escalated long-range air strikes this year. Russia has particularly targeted the Ukrainian power grid, while Ukraine has aimed at Russian oil refineries. Both have struck data centres, commercial warehouses and Black Sea shipping.
The war has ground on for more than 4-1/2 years, defying Trump's pledge during his 2024 election campaign that he could end it in a day. No breakthrough emerged from three short meetings in Istanbul last year and three rounds of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi and Geneva at the start of this year. REUTERS

articles.title: Putin agrees to resume three-way peace talks with Ukraine and US
articles.body:
Putin agrees to resume talks on Ukraine war with Kyiv and Washington, Kremlin says
In short:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month.
The Russian leader has met with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg.
What's next?
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he supports the proposal, and is hopeful the three-way talks will take place in early November.
The Kremlin says Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume three-way negotiations next month with Washington and Kyiv aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.
The Russian leader met US envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg.
Mr Putin's foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said the focus would be on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends".
The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran.
Mr Witkoff's talks with Mr Putin about Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine took place as US President Donald Trump pushed Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has insisted that only a leaders' summit can break the impasse.
Latest proposals have little of value, Kremlin says
The Kremlin said the discussion in St Petersburg lasted about three hours and came a day after Mr Witkoff met Mr Zelenskyy and some European leaders in Norway's capital, Oslo.
Mr Ushakov said the proposals from the Oslo meeting "contained little of real value in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis".
However, he later told Russian state TV that while Moscow was not "fully satisfied" with the Oslo proposals, they were a step in the right direction.
Mr Zelenskyy said he supported the proposal for three-way talks.
"We have received feedback that … Russia supports a trilateral meeting at the level of our [negotiating] teams," he said.
"The American side has proposed holding it as soon as possible and we support that …The Ukrainian side has been in contact with its American partners. They will do everything to ensure that the meeting takes place as early as possible, in November. I think no later than early November."
Mr Zelenskyy said that Kyiv supported "any proposals for a ceasefire, an end to the war, an energy ceasefire as well as humanitarian initiatives".
Witkoff sees 'some degree of momentum' in peace efforts
Mr Witkoff and Mr Putin met at St Petersburg's Constantine Palace, with Mr Ushakov and Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev also at the table.
Mr Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the discussion via a video link.
Before the meeting, Mr Witkoff said that there was "some degree of momentum" in talks.
In televised opening remarks, Mr Witkoff thanked Mr Putin for agreeing to send diesel to the US after Mr Trump lifted a ban despite anger from some US lawmakers, adding that the fuel would help reduce prices for American farmers and truckers.
Mr Putin said he was ready to consider restoring US-Russia economic ties and was prepared to discuss the US-led conflict with Iran.
He said Moscow stands ready to use its relationship with Tehran to help bring peace.
Mr Ushakov said that "large-scale joint economic projects that offer significant prospects for cooperation" between Russia and the US were discussed in detail with Mr Witkoff.
"Some of these are, in fact, nearing the implementation stage," he said.
Russia resumes attacks on Ukraine
Just as Russia indicated its readiness to join the trilateral peace talks, officials in Ukraine reported the capital Kyiv had been attacked with ballistic missiles on Wednesday evening, local time.
Homes, a petrol station and transport equipment were damaged and six people were injured.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram there were strikes in two districts on the east side of the Dnipro River bisecting the city, and posted on social media:
"Explosions in the capital. Kyiv is under ballistic attack.
"Stay in shelters!"
The city remained under a drone warning for more than two hours after the initial alert was declared.
Russian authorities also said they downed most of the 630 drones heading towards Moscow overnight.
Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram that two people were injured in the attack outside of the city.
AP/Reuters

articles.title: Ukraine’s military admits it fails to intercept any single Russian ballistic missile again
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. Ukrainian air defenses failed to intercept a single Russian ballistic or cruise missile last night, as follows from the data of the country’s General Staff analyzed by TASS.
This is not the first time that Ukrainian air defenses have failed to intercept a single Russian missile overnight launched at military facilities and sites used by Ukraine’s military.
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky has regularly called on the West to supply new interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems. Kiev has repeatedly complained that weapons deliveries from partner countries have declined amid the US-Israeli war against Iran. Zelensky argues that Ukraine must receive interceptor missiles individually from countries willing to supply them.
Russia’s Defense Ministry reported on the morning of October 22 that Russian forces had launched a massive overnight strike against Ukraine’s military-industrial sector involved in the production and storage of cruise missiles, long-and medium-range unmanned aerial vehicles, transport infrastructure in Kiev, port infrastructure in the Odessa Region, and vessels at sea supporting the Ukrainian army’s operations.

articles.title: A ‘pipe dream of EU hawks’: What’s in Brussels’ new Arctic Strategy?
articles.body:
A ‘pipe dream of EU hawks’: What’s in Brussels’ new Arctic Strategy?
The EU has updated its Arctic strategy, and militarism has replaced climate activism as Brussels’ new preoccupation in the frozen north. Despite what the new strategy claims, however, the Arctic is not “the EU’s Northern Neighborhood.”
Unveiled on Tuesday by the European Commission, the ‘Strategy for the Arctic’ describes the region as a “critical” zone for trade, investment, and conservation, and a flashpoint for military confrontation with Russia.
Today, we adopt our new 🇪🇺 Arctic Strategy. The Arctic is where the tectonic plates of geopolitics collide head-on. It requires us to change our strategic posture. And work with like-minded partners that share our values ↓ https://t.co/B6GvgUOCQk
— Ursula von der Leyen (@vonderleyen) October 20, 2026
“With Russia and China increasing their footprint and ambition, the Arctic has become a front line of global power competition,” top EU diplomat Kaja Kallas said in a statement. “Our revamped Strategy reflects this new reality and puts security firmly at its core.”
To understand just how dramatic this new focus on security is, it’s necessary to turn back the clock to 2021, when the commission released its previous Arctic strategy.
The EU’s green past
Published on October 13, 2021, the strategy opened by describing climate change as “the most comprehensive threat the Arctic is facing.” Russia’s refurbishment of Soviet-era military bases along its Arctic coastline was presented primarily as something that could “further aggravate the consequences of climate change,” and the EU pledged to work with Moscow “to improve environmental and health security,” and to leave military relations with Russia up to NATO and individual member states.
Four months later, Brussels severed relations with Moscow and entered the Russia-Ukraine conflict on Kiev’s side. The title of the 2021 strategy – ‘A stronger EU engagement for a peaceful, sustainable and prosperous Arctic’ – needed an update that reflected the EU’s new militarism.
Brussels claims the Arctic
“Russia’s unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression against Ukraine has reshaped the security of the Arctic and the EU as a whole,” the new document opens, going on to assert that “the Arctic is not someone else’s frontier. It is Europe’s Northern Neighbourhood and the European Union is part of the Arctic.”
Geography is not exactly on Brussels’ side here. The 27-member union has no coastline on the Arctic Ocean, and only two of its members – Finland and Sweden – have territory inside the Arctic Circle (although a Danish dependency, Greenland left the EU in 1985). Russia accounts for 53% of the Arctic Ocean’s coastline, and 45% of all land inside the Arctic Circle.
To compensate for this, the new strategy proposes that all waters north of 60 degrees latitude be considered ‘Arctic’. The commission argues that this would allow its environmental regulations to “cover the actual footprint of Arctic shipping.” It would also dramatically expand the EU’s ‘Arctic’ territory and population by bringing almost all of Finland and Sweden into the new region, including Finland’s entire 1,340 kilometer border with Russia. It is on this frontier that the EU is preparing for conflict.
War preparations
The strategy sets out a lengthy list of military objectives, with the commission promising to:
- “Deepen engagement with NATO” and hold military exercises focused on moving troops and equipment into the Arctic
- Develop military logistics corridors from central Europe to the Arctic
- Upgrade ports and airports for military use
- Expand icebreaker capacity
- Expand satellite surveillance of the region and tracking of Russian oil tankers
- Develop polar-capable undersea drones
- Establish a “Maritime Security Hub” and increase data-sharing with NATO
- Deepen military ties with Canada, Iceland, Norway, the UK, and US
The strategy is short on some specifics, and almost all of these goals are presented without an accompanying price tag. The only actual figures listed are €260 million for ten existing European Defence Fund projects, €107 million toward the construction of an undersea internet cable to Greenland, and the €200 million Greenland ‘Partnership Package’, which was announced last month. Although the commission says that this investment package will “support resilience, security and peace in the Arctic,” none of the €200 million in funding is earmarked for explicitly military projects.
Even though these objectives make up more of a wishlist than a set of concrete commitments, one in particular has the potential to push tensions with Russia to the breaking point. The strategy states that the EU will use its ‘Copernicus’ satellite network to track Russian “shadow fleet vessels,” thus making it easier for EU states to interdict and seize them. Belgium, Estonia, Finland, France, and Sweden have detained 12 of these vessels since December 2024, a number that would likely increase with the aid of satellite surveillance.
‘Shadow fleet’ is an EU euphemism for tankers carrying Russian oil in international waters. Russian oil exporters do not abide by EU sanctions, nor do importers outside the EU. Nevertheless, EU member states have abrogated the authority to seize them, in what the Kremlin considers “flagrant violation of international law” and “outright piracy and robbery.”
Should the seizures continue, Russian President Vladimir Putin has threatened to respond in kind.
The ‘hybrid war’ deception
The EU’s militarization of the Arctic is justified, the document states, as Russia is “pursuing hybrid strategies against its neighbours… from drone incursions and Global Navigation Satellite System jamming to the sabotage of undersea cables.” In the absence of real, verifiable military action by Russia against Europe, EU and NATO leaders have taken to accusing Moscow of waging “hybrid war,” describing drone sightings, fires, and accidents at weapons factories, protests, and even natural disasters as Kremlin-orchestrated plots to destabilize the West.
A wave of “drone incursions” across northern Europe and Scandinavia last year turned out to be a hoax, with Belgium’s defense minister attempting to pass off a photograph of a police helicopter as a ‘Russian drone’. Around the same time, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s PR team lied about Russia “interfering” with her jet’s navigation systems over Bulgaria. Western spy chiefs have since admitted there is no evidence that Russia has sabotaged undersea power and internet cables.
Nevertheless, claims of ‘hybrid war’ have persisted in European politics and media, to the point where some analysts view the claims themselves as a form of “hybrid warfare” against the European public, used to justify military spending hikes and welfare cutbacks.
“When you are sure it is the Russians, or almost sure it is the Russians, attribute it to the Russians,” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte advised the bloc’s political leaders and intelligence chiefs earlier this month.
Russia has been holding military exercises in the Arctic for decades, and the refurbishment of its Soviet-era bases in the region has been underway since before the EU published its 2021 Arctic strategy. However, the newly militarized EU is no longer content to handle this matter through old mechanisms – namely the Arctic Council – and insists that countering Russia in the north is its responsibility as well as NATO’s.
The Europeans dictate their terms
The EU’s new strategy calls on Russia to “ensure that freedom of navigation is preserved” along the Northern Sea Route (NSR), a formerly impassable navigation corridor that can now be traversed year-round, thanks to receding polar ice caps and the assistance of Russia’s vast icebreaker fleet. The NSR cuts transit time from China to northern Europe in half, and in August, the first Chinese container ship arrived at the port of Murmansk via this route.
The NSR skims along more than 24,000 km of Russian coastline, and through internationally recognized Russian territorial waters. Russia is the only state capable of rendering assistance to any ships passing through the route, and vessels wishing to pass in winter must pay to be escorted by Russian icebreakers. Moscow retains the right to deny any ships access to the NSR.
Nevertheless, the EU insists that it has a say over Russian maritime policy, even as it vows to “continue to sanction the shadow fleet entering from the Northern Sea Route” and place Russian shipping under satellite surveillance. The latest Arctic strategy states that the EU will “actively engage” with other nations to ensure freedom of navigation in the Arctic, but omits any possibility of engagement with Russia. Only “like-minded partners,” a term mentioned nearly two dozen times in the document, will be consulted.
Diplomatic and economic disputes in the Arctic were previously handled at the Arctic Council. However, seven of the council’s eight members – every one except Russia – stopped participating in high-level Council meetings in March 2022. That same month, the EU joined Finland, Denmark, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden in suspending any activities involving Russia within the separate Barents Euro-Arctic Council.
The EU’s Arctic delusion
The central fallacy of the EU’s Arctic strategy is that it presumes Brussels can regulate, with laws or with arms, what Russia does in its own back yard. It presumes that the bloc, which has no Arctic coastline, can ignore long-established forums for cooperation and directly dictate terms to a superpower that controls half of the Arctic’s land and sea area; and that by repeating the mantra “the Arctic is the EU’s northern neighborhood,” it can overcome geographic reality and the massive power differential between Russia and everyone else in the region.
In a message released by its embassy in the Netherlands on Tuesday, the Russian Foreign Ministry described the document as “another pipe dream of EU hawks.”
“A quick reality check: Russia operates a fleet of 40+ icebreakers. How many does the EU have in total?” the ministry asked. “The Arctic should be a place of cooperation, not confrontation. Maybe it’s time to stop the provocations?”

articles.title: Inside the institution where Ukraine races to counter Russia's evolving drones
articles.body:
Inside the institution where Ukraine races to counter Russia's evolving drones
From a Canon camera to a magnetometer, wreckage reveals how Russian weapons keep advancing and why Ukraine’s countermeasures struggle to keep pace.
The aftermath of a Russian Geran-5-type jet-powered drone strike on a Ukrnafta petrol station is seen in the Holosiivskyi district of Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sept. 15, 2026. (Kostiantyn Liberov / Libkos / Getty Images)
In a government office, researchers of drones and electronic warfare gather around a small metal device recovered from a Russian Geran drone. Its purpose — to measure the Earth’s magnetic field for navigation.
"This is the most recent component we found, about a week or two ago," said one of the researchers.
Outside, a Russian drone’s jet engine roared — a sound that has become almost constant in Kyiv in recent months as advances in drone technology allow Russia to strike farther, more often and with greater precision. The small metal sensor on the table could make that threat even more vicious.
If it works as the researchers suspect, it could keep drones on course even when their satellite navigation is jammed, making the prospect of a winter under near-constant Russian attack even grimmer.
The researchers work at an institution under Ukraine’s Defense Ministry, and its work is rarely seen by outsiders. Here, specialists dismantle Russian weapons recovered from the battlefield or attacks to identify vulnerabilities, help develop countermeasures, and anticipate what Russian engineers might try next. The Kyiv Independent was given rare access on the condition that neither the institution nor the people inside be identified.
Their work is a race against time. The researchers estimate that developing an effective countermeasure usually takes four to six months, while Russia can introduce further modifications after two or three.
Regarding the sensor they found — in technical terms called a magnetometer — the researchers said they were still investigating its purpose and whether Russia might deploy it at scale.
But finding a new component is not the same as understanding it, and understanding it is not the same as having a way to counter it. And the Russian engineers who put the magnetometer in the drone face a similar gap. Fitting it to a handful of drones is not the same as being able to deploy it at scale.
What Russia’s drone wreckage reveals about the threats ahead
Inside the institution, the fluorescent-lit hallways were filled with pieces of missiles, drones, fuzes, and motherboards, all neatly organized and labeled. People move in and out, some in camouflage, others in jeans and plain shirts, some carrying paperwork, others pieces of military hardware.
There is the nose of a North Korean missile, taller than a grown man, and a large section of a Russian Oreshnik missile, its cylindrical body roughly as wide as a passenger car. On the other side of the hallway were several Russian Geran drones, their triangular bodies resembling black paper airplanes enlarged to more than three meters long (9.8 feet), with wings spanning roughly three meters.
Outwardly, the Russian Gerans still resemble the Iranian drones Russia began using to terrorize Ukrainian cities in the fall of 2022. Inside, however, successive modifications had made them markedly different from those early aircraft, and even from the first Russian-made Gerans that appeared by the summer of 2023.
To trace the drones' evolution, the researchers work backward from the ones they recover. They begin by identifying and documenting each drone’s basic features, then dismantle it to map its internal systems, trace its components to their manufacturers, and reconstruct how each part contributes to the aircraft’s operation.
The researchers explained that changes inside the drones often reflected the success of Ukraine’s defenses. A navigation system that had once guided an aircraft to its target could become vulnerable to jamming, prompting Russia to try something else.
"When the Russians see that the effectiveness is decreasing, they introduce other technologies," one researcher said.
But the two sides don't take turns. Russia can introduce another modification while Ukraine is still working out how to defeat the previous one.
On one of the tables lies a Canon camera recovered from one of the first iterations of Russian drones from late 2022 used for attacks on Ukrainian cities. Still in its original casing, it looked much as it would in a shop, except that its settings had been glued in place against the vibrations of flight.
read also
The next example they recovered a few months later, a Sony, had been stripped of its casing, leaving its lens and colorful wiring exposed. "You can already see that it’s quite a development compared to the first sample," a researcher said.
Such details helped the specialists judge how far an adaptation had progressed. You can tell a lot from the workmanship and the way it’s put together, one researcher explained. Specialists look for whether a part was improvised and attached to a drone or whether the drone was built to carry it — a sign that an experiment might be entering regular production.
Sometimes the clue is simpler. Sometimes there are letters "E" or "EE" on a drone’s tail fins, which the researchers believe stands for "experiment."
Other clues had been deliberately erased. The researchers showed antennae chips with their identifying markings scratched off, an effort, they said, to hide the supply chains bringing American and European electronics into Russian weapons despite sanctions.
"Removing markings does not make identification impossible," one researcher said. But it can turn what might have been a glance at a label into an investigation requiring specialized equipment and scarce time.
Reconstructing Russian technology can take months or even years, hampered by a lack of specialized equipment, resources, and expertise in Ukraine, and even with help from foreign partners, some electronic components remain nearly impossible to decipher without access to manufacturers’ proprietary information, which they are often unwilling to share.
A threat long in the making
Hanging in the stairwell was a completely intact Geran-3 that had reached the institution in 2025, well before this autumn’s urgent calls to accelerate production of interceptors capable of catching jet-powered drones. It had run out of fuel and landed in sand without detonating.
At its rear was a silver jet engine, roughly the size of a large melon, replacing the propeller-driven engine that gave earlier iterations of these drones their familiar moped sound. Faster flight and higher operating altitudes made jet-powered variants harder for mobile teams armed with machine guns to engage.
A message written on the black body of the drone in white marker read "greetings to Serhii from the engineers." The researchers believed it was addressed to Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky on defense technology. One researcher found a small consolation: the Russians had misspelled "engineers."
The same recovered aircraft had carried another indication of what was coming this summer beyond the jets: a camera and a mesh modem. "(That meant it was) able to send back video footage and receive control signals," a researcher said.
The researchers have a collection of the palm-sized mesh modems in their office, which they identify as Chinese-made. Mesh modems allow drones to relay video and control signals through one another, extending communications beyond an individual aircraft’s direct connection to its operator.
One researcher compared the technology to repeaters used to extend Wi-Fi coverage through a house. Here, the repeaters are other drones. This allows operators to change targets during flight and pursue even moving targets, such as trains, rather than simply sending a drone toward fixed coordinates, the researchers said.
The video feed allows the Russian operator to watch a civilian building draw closer while continuing to steer the drone toward it. He is far from the people inside but can see who he is targeting.
"If it is a civilian site, he knows what he is hitting and how," one researcher said.
read also
The next unknown
The institution has possessed evidence of Russian attempts to implement jet engines and mesh relays since last year. But what a single recovered aircraft could not establish last fall was how soon or whether at all the same hardware would appear in large numbers.
Half a year later, it did. Since this summer, jet-powered drones have targeted Ukraine, particularly Kyiv, on a daily, constant basis, with the sound of explosions a regular occurrence in the capital throughout the day.
The researchers described the interval before an effective response to a modification became available as a "window of opportunity" for Russia. Once a change proved useful, Russia could concentrate resources on producing and deploying it while Ukraine was still developing a countermeasure.
"They don’t wait for us to come up with a countermeasure," one of the researchers said. The engineers attribute this problem mostly to scale. Russia likely has institutions similar to theirs, just several times larger with more resources.
The magnetometer the researchers recently recovered was still at an earlier stage of their investigation. "We can’t say for sure what it is, until we’ve completed all the necessary research," one said.
It might prove a modest refinement rather than a breakthrough. To become a widespread threat, its integration would need to be refined and its production scaled up.
But even a slight edge could be enough, helping more aircraft stay on course and tilting the balance of the war further in Russia's favor.

articles.title: Drones reportedly hit a Russian weapons plant near Moscow that Washington and Kyiv sanctioned
articles.body:
An explosion hit the 75th Arsenal, a Russian army plant in Serpukhov south of Moscow, overnight on 22 October, Russian Telegram channel Astra reported. Russian officials also claimed drone attacks on the Moscow region, Tula, and Lipetsk that night.
As Russia presses its full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s long-range drones and missiles keep hitting military plants and refineries deep inside Russia. Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi says this plant specializes in repairing Buk and S-300 air defense systems. Astra describes it more broadly, as making weapons and ammunition and repairing military equipment. If Militarnyi is right, the blast hit a site that fixes Russian air defenses. It came the night Moscow’s mayor credited air defenses with stopping hundreds of drones.
Blast at the arsenal
An Astra OSINT analyst placed the explosion inside the site from a video, the channel said. Residents claimed in local chats that blasts followed passing drones, then at least three missiles. Astra did not confirm the missile count. Serpukhov lies about 99 km south of Moscow. Ukraine has sanctioned the plant, and the US Treasury has listed it too. As of the morning of 22 October, no Russian official had confirmed the blast.
630 drones, by Moscow’s count
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed that 630 drones flew toward the Moscow region from 20:30 on 21 October to 04:00 on 22 October. He claimed most were destroyed far out and 163 were neutralized on approach to Moscow. Two people were injured in Voronovo, in New Moscow, he stated.
Tula Oblast Governor Dmitry Milyaev claimed air defenses downed 70 Ukrainian drones over his region. Private homes were damaged in Tula and the Zaoksky district, he stated.
Lipetsk governor claims homes and a clinic damaged
Earlier in the night, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ posted footage of commotion in Lipetsk after explosions. Lipetsk Oblast Governor Igor Artamonov claimed a drone strike damaged homes, apartment blocks, and a closed polyclinic. A man born in 2001 was injured and hospitalized, Artamonov claimed.
In May, Ukrainian intelligence said Russia was deploying more regiments against strike drones. In September, Ukrainian units hit more Russian air defense systems and radars than in any month since 2024, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said. Analyst Oleksandr Kovalenko counted 76 destroyed in September with days of the month still to go and argued Russia cannot replace such losses. If Militarnyi’s description holds, losing repair capacity would deepen that gap.
Read also
- Ukrainian units hit record number of Russian air defense systems and radars in September, one of them 552 kilometers away
- Ukraine destroys record 76 Russian air-defense systems this month, losses analyst says Russia “will never be able to restore”
- Russia reportedly rushes four regiments and 162 batteries to defend Moscow from Ukrainian drones

articles.title: Greece’s alliances with UAE and Israel fail eastern Libya–Turkey test
articles.body:
Greece’s alliances with UAE and Israel fail eastern Libya–Turkey test
In the days before Libya’s eastern parliament approved a contentious maritime agreement with Turkey, Greece was trying to assemble its allies - Egypt, Israel and the UAE - to prevent the deal, multiple officials in the region told Middle East Eye.
But on Tuesday, the Libyan House of Representatives in Benghazi ratified the agreement, showing that a fractured Libya, at the very least, could come to a consensus in acknowledging Turkey’s sweeping maritime claims over the Eastern Mediterranean.
“Turkey has cemented itself in Libya. It’s almost impossible now for a Libyan leader in the future to sign a deal with Greece because there is a Libyan consensus,” Constantinos Filis, director of the Institute of Global Affairs in Athens, told Middle East Eye.
But the deal is more than a setback for Greece or a diplomatic notch in the belt for the Mediterranean. It underscores how the Middle East is rearranging itself in the wake of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and simmering conflicts across the region.
In sum, the partnerships that Greece depended on to counter Turkey in the Mediterranean failed to deliver because the Middle East is undergoing a geopolitical reordering of priorities.
Egypt and Turkey have mended fences after a deep rift, while Persian Gulf states like the UAE are looking for new security partners, with the Iran war on the verge of flaring up again. The irony for Greece is that the actions of its closest partner, Israel, have contributed to these shifts.
The maritime rivalry between Greece and Turkey in the Eastern Mediterranean long predates the fracturing of Libya into rival governments following the 2011 removal of Muammar Gaddafi. The two neighbors came close to war in 1996 over an uninhabited island.
Traditionally, Greece and Turkey could push the envelope in their tensions, knowing that the U.S. would intervene to prevent its NATO allies from crossing the line into direct conflict. But that dynamic has changed.
The U.S. is now less engaged in the Middle East and is at loggerheads with NATO on several fronts, like the war in Ukraine. Greece is a big spender in NATO, but Turkey has developed a domestic weapons industry of its own.
Turkey’s regional power is increasing, with an ally now governing Syria and Persian Gulf Arab states looking to it as a security partner as the U.S. steps away.
Tom Barrack, the American ambassador to Turkey and envoy to Syria and Iraq, said on Tuesday that the United States’ “grand bargain” of oil for security with the Persian Gulf was “transitioning”.
A Libyan source familiar with the matter told Middle East Eye that eastern Libya’s ratification of the maritime deal is one step in a wider plan to unite Libya under one government that the Trump administration has agreed to with Turkey.
The source said the United States wants Turkey to broker a deal between rival governments in Benghazi and Tripoli. Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin visited the latter on Tuesday.
Greece has sought new Middle Eastern allies as the U.S. retreats from its security role, and Turkey flexes its muscles in the region. The maritime deal Ankara has with Libya disregards Greek claims to maritime zones not just in uninhabited islands, but large ones like Crete, home to 600,000 Greeks.
Greece's search for allies to fill the US gap
Athens has doubled down on its relatively warm, historic ties to Egypt. When Turkey first signed the maritime demarcation deal with Libya’s Tripoli-based government, Athens responded by signing a deal with Egypt to counter it.
Greece has also moved closer to the UAE. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis was one of the first foreign leaders to visit the Persian Gulf state at the height of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. In 2020, when tensions between Greece and Turkey soared, the UAE sent warplanes to Crete.
But most controversially, Greece has forged a close alliance with Israel, which is clashing with Turkey for power in hotspots like Syria and even the Horn of Africa. In August, Greece even agreed to purchase a $3.5bn air defence system from Israel - the largest arms deal in Israel’s history.
Eastern Libya’s ratification of the Turkish maritime deal stings especially hard for Greece because Israel, Egypt and the UAE are the main backers of Khalifa Haftar, the military commander who controls eastern Libya and has traditionally been a rival to Libya’s Tripoli-based government.
Greece has leaned on these relationships to try to counter Turkey in Libya.
Last year, Greece sought Egyptian support to forestall Benghazi’s ratification of the maritime deal. An Egyptian delegation visited Athens just five days ago to confer with Greece on Libya.
Khalifa Haftar’s son, Saddam Haftar, is increasingly seen as the next ruler of eastern Libya. Although Turkey intervened in Libya’s civil war to prevent his father from capturing Tripoli, Saddam has moved closer to Ankara. This summer, with some nudging from the UAE, Saddam was convinced to visit Athens despite his rapprochement with Turkey, MEE understands.
“It’s not up to Egypt or the UAE to support us in Libya. They have other interests. It was unwise for Greece to expect that they would support Greece at the sake of their own interests,” Filis told MEE.
Turkey and Egypt's rapprochement
Until a few years ago, both Egypt and the UAE were at loggerheads with Turkey. Cairo and Abu Dhabi supported the Haftars in Libya’s civil war, while Turkey backed the government in Tripoli. But since then, these countries have taken steps to restore ties.
Egyptian officials have stressed multiple times to MEE that Cairo’s rapprochement is not aimed at Greece. Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held a call with his Greek counterpart on Tuesday, reaffirming their shared interests.
Egypt does not want to see the Eastern Mediterranean turned into a Turkish lake, Arab officials tell MEE, but Egypt and Turkey now converge in more hotspots than they compete.
Both countries are wary of Israeli expansionism in the wake of the October 7 attacks. Israel has carried out a genocide in Gaza and occupies swathes of Syria and Lebanon.
Egypt and Turkey are also aligned in the Red Sea. Both states support Somalia and oppose Israel’s recognition of a breakaway Somaliland republic. They also support Sudan’s armed forces against the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary, which is friendly to Israel, by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s own admission.
In Libya, there is also room for cooperation. Egypt wants to build a $1bn oil pipeline from Tobruk to the port of Alexandria.
While the UAE and Turkey are on opposite sides of these regional hotspots like Sudan, they have since moved to manage their differences. For example, in 2022, the UAE purchased Turkish-made TB2 drones.
Then there is Israel.
Notably, Eastern Libya’s recognition of Turkey’s maritime claims came the week that Netanyahu shared a map that showed the territory as “friendly” to Israel, the UAE and Greece.
Saddam Haftar even met in September with Netanyahu in the UAE, a Libyan source told MEE, confirming previous reporting. But Israel might see a wider Turkish claim to the Eastern Mediterranean pushing Greece closer into its orbit, one European official told MEE.
The fact that Greece’s partners did not mobilize to prevent Eastern Libya’s ratification of the maritime deal shows just how much the Middle East is changing.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine exchange overnight strikes, one killed in Kiev
articles.body:
Russia and Ukraine reported overnight drone and missile attacks on Thursday, with Ukrainian authorities saying one person was killed and 22 were injured in Kiev, while Moscow said air defences had intercepted 630 drones approaching the Russian capital.
Russian forces launched ballistic missile strikes on six districts of Kiev overnight, causing fires and destruction, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said in a statement.
"Kiev: one person was killed and 22 injured, including four children, as a result of Russian shelling," it said.
Meanwhile, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said the Russian capital and the surrounding region were also under attack overnight, with 630 drones having flown towards the Moscow region.
Most of the drones were intercepted by air defences at long range, while 163 were destroyed on approach to Moscow, Sobyanin added.
In a separate statement, the Russian defence ministry said its forces had carried out a large-scale overnight strike using precision-guided ground-launched weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles.
According to the ministry, the strikes targeted Ukrainian military-industrial enterprises involved in the production and storage of cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones, as well as transport infrastructure in Kiev and port infrastructure in the Odessa region.
The ministry also said vessels used in the interests of the Ukrainian armed forces had been targeted.
The claims by both sides could not been independently verified.

articles.title: Committee questions whether attack submarines put to sea
articles.body:
Evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines raises serious questions about whether Britain can meet its High North commitments before new capabilities enter service, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, records reporting that all five of the Astute class nuclear attack submarines then in service had recently been tied up in dockyards at the same time, with none deployed.
Dhesi said: “The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the High North. Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and the UK, including the nuclear deterrent. Despite this, the Ministry of Defence has accepted a serious anti-submarine warfare gap. Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments in the High North.”
Professor David Blagden of the University of Exeter told the committee: “[i]t was reported in the media quite recently that a French SSN [attack submarine] had been seen in Faslane around the time that one of [our] SSBNs sailed on its patrol… [i]s this the French now doing ‘delousing’ for a UK nuclear deterrent submarine going on patrol? Is that great alliance solidarity or is it, ‘Oh my god, we can’t get one of our own SSNs to sea to do one of the highest missions?'”
Delousing is the activity in which an attack submarine sanitises the waters around a ballistic missile submarine to ensure it is not being tracked or tailed by an adversary as it leaves on or returns from a deterrent patrol.
The Rt Hon the Lord Case, chair of Team Barrow, told the committee in November 2025 that the government is saying to the defence industry “[p]lease, how quickly can you build our nuclear submarines for us? We are having to make up for decades of neglect.”
Retired Rear Admiral Philip Mathias, a former Director of Nuclear Policy at the Ministry of Defence, said in December 2025 that one consequence of a lack of investment in the submarine fleet was that the duration of patrols for Vanguard class crews, which were seventy days during the Cold War, were now more than two hundred days, and that there was a shockingly low availability of submarines to counter the Russian threat in the High North.
The committee’s conclusion states: “The Royal Marines’ Arctic expertise is a significant national strength, but it cannot compensate for shortfalls in the naval platforms needed to deploy, protect and sustain operations in the region. The UK’s ability to deter and respond to threats in the High North depends not only on future programmes, but also on the readiness of the Royal Navy’s existing ships, submarines and specialist forces. Russian submarine and seabed warfare capabilities based in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic, UK waters and the nuclear deterrent. Evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines therefore raises serious questions about whether the UK can meet its High North commitments before new capabilities enter service.”
The committee asks the government to provide a plan setting out how the department will improve the availability of the Royal Navy’s frigates, destroyers and attack submarines before 2030, noting that the update might be presented at a classified level but that it expects a version to be made publicly available.
Ministers have consistently declined to disclose submarine availability, and Luke Pollard MP told Parliament this week that it is British policy not to disclose the operational availability or deployment details of submarines, as doing so would be likely to prejudice the capability, effectiveness or security of the armed forces.

articles.title: U.S. Reportedly Considering Major Strikes on Iran After Midterms
articles.body:
The U.S. and Israel are reportedly developing plans for major strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections in November.
Citing people familiar with the deliberations, the New York Times reported on Wednesday that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed the possibility of renewed strikes on Iran with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel this week. Possible targets of the strikes reportedly include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
U.S. officials have repeatedly asserted that the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps are teetering on the edge of collapse but are deliberately prolonging the war in an effort to meddle with Republican prospects in the midterm elections. Once the elections are over, President Donald Trump promised last month, the Iranian regime would quickly capitulate.
“I think the war is going to end immediately after the election,” Trump said. “They can’t hold out any longer.”
Renewed strikes could complicate that outlook.
Some officials have reportedly argued that resuming attacks for an intense but limited campaign would hasten Iran’s economic collapse, especially as the country has been squeezed by an ongoing U.S. blockade on Iranian ports and economic sanctions campaign. The officials hope the blow will make Iran more amenable to negotiations.
Trump has at times shared that view.
Last week, Trump told Newsmax he was considering additional military action in Iran, including a possible strike on Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a nuclear facility deep underground. His comments came amid reports that he was weighing deploying a 22,000 GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, also known as the “mother of all bombs.”
The President added the war would end soon, be it through negotiation or escalation.
“Do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he said in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly last month.
“But I believe we’ll make a deal,” he added, “right after the election.”
Will the U.S. renew strikes on Iran?
Intensified fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels and the Saudi and Yemeni governments has threatened to create a broader regional crisis that could be harder to disengage from. The State Department on Wednesday ordered nonemergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia amid escalating attacks by the Houthis on Saudi infrastructure.
Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and Aramco facilities, as well as their attempts to disrupt shipping through Bab El-Mandeb, which has become an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz for energy trade, could prompt direct U.S. strikes in support of Saudi Arabia, analysts have said. Trump said earlier this month that the U.S. “may” join Saudi strikes on the Houthis, although that has yet to transpire.
Israel’s Oct. 27 election could also raise the stakes of additional military action. Netanyahu, whom Trump has endorsed, would remain in office until a new government is formed, even if his bloc loses the election, and his government would retain the authority to order strikes during that transition. But renewed strikes before the election, or after an electoral defeat, could invite scrutiny. “One ordered in the last weeks of a deadlocked campaign would be judged in Israel as politics as well as strategy,” Gregg Roman, executive director of the Middle East Forum, wrote in a September analysis.
Nevertheless, the forum assessed that a large-scale Israeli strike on Iranian territory, with or without U.S. participation, was probable before the end of the year. Analysts told the Times Netanyahu could use the prospect of joint strikes to form a unity government that could allow him to stay in power.
“The larger constraint,” Roman argued, “is Washington.”
Trump has not yet approved the proposed strikes, the Times reported.
Trump has also called off plans to renew attacks on Iran before. He reportedly blocked an Israeli plan for a multi-day offensive against Iran earlier this month, and rejected five proposals for major operations against Iran or the Houthis in recent months.
The U.S. and Iran have not exchanged major fighting in recent weeks. The last reported U.S. strikes on Iran were on Sept. 8, even as Iranian attacks on commercial shipping have continued. Earlier this month, Trump ruled out attacking Iran before the midterms.
How might Iran respond to new strikes?
Tehran’s reluctance to make concessions to the U.S. appears to have strengthened, rather than weakened, over the course of the war. Iranian leaders reiterated this week that they will not directly negotiate with the U.S. unless Washington accedes to certain demands, which include ending its naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian funds.
The initial U.S. and Israeli bombing campaign on Iran that began the war on Feb. 28, as well as June 2025 attacks during an earlier round of U.S.-Iran nuclear diplomacy, also hardened the Iranian view that the U.S. is not serious about negotiating. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in March that the previous disruptions of negotiating rounds had increased distrust in Washington.
Last month, the IRGC published an open letter appealing to American voters to “wrest control” from their government. In the letter, the IRGC said: “Despite all the hardships that our enemies impose on us, we will continue fighting, as we have done for the past 47 years.”
Both the U.S. and Iran appear to believe they hold enough leverage to achieve their goals, and those “dueling perceptions” have impeded progress towards a deal, according to an Oct. 1 analysis by the New York-based nonpartisan research organization The Soufan Center.
Iran’s key point of leverage is its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway vital to global energy trade. Iran’s militarization of the strait has disrupted global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, leading to soaring energy prices and inflation.
Analysts previously told TIME that the higher prices are politically costly for Trump. In recent weeks, a growing number of Republicans have broken with Trump on Iran. The President has also seen his lowest approval ratings of his second term.
Iran’s ability to choke off regional oil exports, however, appears to be waning. Middle East oil exports topped prewar levels last week as shipping companies use alternative routes to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. HSBC Group Chief Executive Georges Elhedery also projected that Hormuz could be “redundant” in five years thanks to investment in alternative logistics routes.
Iranian officials told the Times that they are aware of the U.S. and Israel’s war planning and are developing their own tactics.
Earlier this week, IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi told the Tehran Times that “even a limited” attack from Washington would provoke a “serious energy crisis” for the world. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said that an attack on Pickaxe Mountain would be met with a response “just as hard,” if not “stronger.”
And earlier this month, Iranian officials said Iran had prepared potential retaliatory operations that would depart from the U.S. and Israel’s assumptions. Security Chief Mohsen Rezaei told Press TV that Iran could respond to renewed attacks by targeting new targets, including U.S.-linked data centers and AI facilities in the Gulf, as well as subsea communications cables. Last month, Iran threatened to retaliate against any further U.S. attacks by targeting U.S. oil and gas assets in the Gulf.
In a post on Telegram on Sunday, Mahdi Mohammadi, a senior adviser to Iran’s negotiator Gen. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said, if the U.S. and Israel attack, “they may want to keep it short, but we will not allow it.”
He added on Wednesday: “The war will continue longer and across a wider geography than the enemy calculates.”

articles.title: Witkoff calls Putin a 'humanitarian' at Russia peace talks without Ukraine
articles.body:
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff called Russian President Vladimir Putin a "humanitarian" on Wednesday, at talks in St. Petersburg about ending the war in Ukraine.
In a video posted to social media, Witkoff thanked Putin for describing President Donald Trump as a "humanitarian" and added: "You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again."
The talks began a day after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy insisted that any negotiations over his country's future must include Kyiv.
Speaking alongside the leaders of Finland and Norway in Oslo late Tuesday, Zelenskyy said discussions with U.S. officials had been constructive and that Washington had reaffirmed its commitment to providing Ukraine with security guarantees.
But he stressed that any agreement concerning Ukraine's future would be acceptable only if Kyiv had a seat at the negotiating table.
"It can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations," he said, adding that he had discussed the reported proposal of a trilateral meeting between the U.S., China, and Russia to negotiate an end to the nearly five-year full-scale war. "Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine," he said.
At the start of talks in St. Petersburg, Russia announced it would release an American man, retired teacher Stephen Hubbard, who had been "wrongfully detained," according to the State Department, on charges that he was a Ukrainian mercenary. Witkoff thanked Putin for the release.
Vice President JD Vance told reporters Wednesday morning that he agreed with Witkoff giving praise to Putin for Hubbard's release. He added that it doesn't matter to him whether people agree with the sentiment.
"I care much less about what Steve said and about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family," Vance said. "We should all be celebrating that."
On Tuesday, Zelenskyy said the Oslo meeting had included discussions on NATO's Article 5 — which says that an armed attack against one member constitutes an attack on all — and "different kinds of security guarantees," which Witkoff will share with the Russians. "We will hear his feedback in one day," Zelenskyy said Tuesday.
The developments come amid heightened tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine as Trump and Zelenskyy have traded public criticism. Trump has accused the Ukrainian president of not wanting peace, while Zelenskyy has argued that Washington's easing of sanctions on Russia, including a deal on diesel, risks prolonging the conflict.
Overnight, Russia struck energy and civilian targets across Ukraine, resulting in at least one casualty, according to local media reports. It follows Trump's Oct. 11 claim that he had brokered an "energy ceasefire," whereby the countries would refrain from striking each other's energy infrastructure amid high diesel prices.
Ukraine paused such attacks for three days before resuming them, citing continuing Russian attacks.
On Tuesday, Zelenskyy confirmed that U.S. intelligence had resumed sharing early warnings of Russian attacks, while discussions continued over SpaceX's Starlink connectivity and Patriot air defense systems.
— Irit Skulnik contributed to this report.

articles.title: What a Russian Satellite Stalking a Commercial Spacecraft Means for the Space Force
articles.body:
Over a two-week period beginning in late September and culminating in mid-October, a Russian satellite maneuvered dangerously close to a commercial Finnish satellite currently providing intelligence to the Ukrainian military.
The apparent provocation has experts wondering why Russia made the move—testing new capabilities, collecting intelligence, or trying to intimidate the Finnish company—and what, if anything, the U.S. Space Force could or should do about these types of events in the future.
While the incident did not involve a U.S. asset, the Russian action highlights the growing importance of commercial space assets to military operations and how those relatively defenseless assets could be vulnerable in or before a conflict.
Between Oct. 15-19, a Russian satellite dubbed COSMOS 2612 performed deliberate, fuel-intensive maneuvers to close in on the Finnish ICEYE-X36 satellite, according to a report by LeoLabs, which the company shared with Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Instead of a somewhat standard flyby, COSMOS matched, shadowed, and orbited around the ICEYE satellite, coming as close as 500 meters to it, according to the report.
The Russian satellite spent months adjusting its orbit, then rapidly closed the distance with the ICEYE satellite, continuously maneuvering around it before COSMOS abruptly ended its movements and distanced itself Oct. 18-19.
The LeoLabs report characterizes the event as a “red” on “blue” engagement in orbit and calls it a planned, highly coordinated rendezvous and proximity operation, which required precise navigation and onboard sensing.
An ICEYE spokesperson declined to provide a detailed response to a query from Air & Space Forces Magazine about the incident.
“We are aware of the situation and tracking it closely. Our constellation architecture is designed for continuity and resilience,” the spokesperson said in an email.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies held an online event Oct. 21 to discuss the incident and its implications for the U.S..
Neither of the two experts at the CSIS event claimed to understand Russia’s goals with the stunt, but Greg Gillinger, senior vice president of strategy and development at Integrity ISR, called it unusual and said it indicated Russia’s intent to send a message to the Finnish company.
“I still scratch my head about what the Russian endgame is with this,” Gillinger said.
Clayton Swope, deputy director of the CSIS Aerospace Security Project, said the event certainly was not “benign.”
“I don’t think we have enough information right now to know whether or not Russia achieved the objectives it wanted to achieve here,” Swope said.
The COSMOS/ICEYE incident comes about a month after Space Force leadership publicly announced that the force has on-orbit offensive space weapons at its disposal and under Guardians’ control.
“Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenge of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink said during the opening keynote at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference on Sept. 14. “This is why the Space Force now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”
The timing of the satellite maneuvers, following Meink’s comments, could be a Russian signal, threat, or influence campaign meant to deter outside, commercial support for Ukraine—or even a bluff, retired Air Force Col. Jennifer Reeves, the senior resident fellow for Space Studies at the Mitchell Institute, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
What USSF Can Do
In 2025, USSF’s Rapid Capabilities Office kicked off a project to field threat-awareness sensors that communicate close hazards to space asset operators. Such sensors would presumably alert operators if a Russian satellite came as close as it did to the ICEYE bird.
Beyond sensing and communicating, though, an April report from the Secure World Foundation noted that more nations are starting to fund “bodyguard” capabilities for their space assets, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported at the time. Germany, India, France, and Japan are all either building or planning to acquire such space-based bodyguards, which could protect and counterattack any space-based incursions.
Swope, speaking on the COSMOS/ICEYE incident, said spacefaring nations need clearer expectations for behavior in space, and predicted events like the recent incident would likely happen again.
“I just feel like it’s not a question of if; it is a question of when we see these satellites do something that we’re going to say is hostile again,” Swope said.
He also said any use of bodyguard satellites needed to include a clearer explanation of what they will accomplish in orbit.
Reeves likewise said the Space Force needs to be prepared to both understand and respond to future incidents like this one. While the service has been building its space domain awareness capabilities in recent years, that’s only one piece of the larger puzzle, she said.
“There’s a big difference between knowing where something is and understanding what it’s doing,” she said.
The force has made “tremendous progress” in tracking orbits and objects with a sophisticated sensor network and other tools, she said. But the Pentagon must put more “rigor” into protecting both military and commercial assets in space, Reeves said.
“The Space Force needs to be running through these scenarios on the regular, and hopefully they are,” Reeves said. “I’m going to trust that they are in their wargames and exercises.”
Those exercises need to include both allies and commercial partners, Reeves added.
“We’ve got to determine how quickly we can determine what happened,” she said. “Can we distinguish an accident from something deliberate? How confident are we in attribution?”
Both Reeves and Swope separately noted that any counterattacks or deterrence to space-based provocations don’t have to involve space-based retaliation or actions.
Reeves pointed to the U.S. ability to strike ground-based facilities to sever links to satellites. Swope noted increased pressure on Russia’s oil “shadow fleet,” a network of an estimated hundreds of old tankers used to export oil while evading sanctions, could be a lever to nudge Russia away from space tomfoolery.
Necessary Guidance
Ultimately, while the Space Force will be the entity dealing with satellite harassment or attacks, the force’s role needs clearer definitions on what constitutes aggression and merits a response, especially given the long-term consequences of space debris and other factors involved in kinetic actions in orbit, Reeves said.
“I don’t think it’s necessarily the Space Force itself that should be determining that,” Reeves said. “I think it should be our national leadership that’s coming up with that. … Because at this point in time, we don’t have that coming from the national-level leadership.”
That lack of guidance has placed the burden on military leadership to decide what the U.S. believes hostile actions in space look like and how the military should respond.
“We don’t want to be doing this thought work when we’re living it in real time,” Reeves said. “There are dire consequences in space if the wrong action is taken or a hostile action is taken.”

articles.title: Pentagon extends Raytheon deal for missile defense radars
articles.body:
- The Missile Defense Agency extended Raytheon’s AN/TPY-2 radar sustainment contract by two years, raising its ceiling from $2.6 billion to nearly $3 billion.
- The ordering period now runs to Oct. 31, 2028, with $112.3 million obligated at award.
The Missile Defense Agency has extended Raytheon’s contract to operate and maintain the U.S. military’s AN/TPY-2 missile defense radars for two more years, adding $394 million to the deal and lifting its ceiling to nearly $3 billion, the Department of War announced.
The sole-source modification raises the maximum value of the contract from about $2.6 billion to $2.999 billion and keeps the ordering period open until Oct. 31, 2028, with $112.3 million in fiscal 2027 operations and maintenance, research and development, and procurement funds obligated at the time of award.
The AN/TPY-2 is a transportable X-band radar that sits at the heart of the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense system, better known as THAAD, and also serves as a standalone early warning sensor for U.S. ballistic missile defense. The radar can work in two ways: deployed far forward to spot ballistic missiles shortly after launch and pass tracking data to other defenses, or as part of a THAAD battery to track an incoming warhead and guide interceptors to hit it as it descends.
Under the extension, Raytheon will continue to run and support the radars from its facility in Woburn, Massachusetts, and at radar sites in the United States and overseas, where the company’s field teams help keep the sensors operating around the clock. The work combines cost-plus-incentive-fee, cost-plus-fixed-fee and firm-fixed-price contract items, and the Missile Defense Agency at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, is also extending the task orders that fund individual radar sites.
The U.S. Army fields eight THAAD batteries, each with one AN/TPY-2 radar, including units at Fort Bliss, Texas, in South Korea and on Guam, while forward-based radars have been stationed at sites including the Shariki area in Japan, Türkiye, Israel and Qatar. The radar is also sold abroad, and in 2020 the Missile Defense Agency awarded Raytheon a production contract worth up to $2.3 billion for seven AN/TPY-2 radars for Saudi Arabia, built with gallium nitride components that extend the radar’s range and sensitivity.
The radars have come under direct fire during the war with Iran this year, and satellite images analyzed by CNN showed that a THAAD radar at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan was apparently destroyed by an Iranian strike in early March, along with damage at radar sites near Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and in the United Arab Emirates. Each AN/TPY-2 costs hundreds of millions of dollars and takes years to build, which makes keeping the existing fleet working a priority for the Missile Defense Agency while new radars are produced.
The original contract was awarded to Raytheon on a sole-source basis in 2018 as the radar’s designer and builder, and the extension was likewise issued without competition. The new ordering period gives the Missile Defense Agency two more years to keep the current support arrangement in place before it decides how to handle long-term sustainment of the AN/TPY-2 fleet beyond October 2028.

articles.title: Vigilance coupled with avoidance of provocative actions
articles.body:
Vigilance coupled with avoidance of provocative actions
Sazandegi examined the distinction between a preemptive strike during an active military confrontation and military action undertaken during a relative pause in hostilities. Quoting Mohammad Atrianfar, a member of the central council of the Servants of Construction Party (Sazandegi), the article stated that a preemptive attack may be considered within the logic of military operations during an active conflict.
However, this differs fundamentally from situations in which both sides are observing a temporary ceasefire or experiencing a relative suspension of hostilities. In such circumstances, launching a preemptive attack would not necessarily resolve existing issues and could instead intensify tensions and broaden the scope of conflict.
