articles.title: Expert sees creation of ‘nuclear belt’ as next step in militarization of the Arctic
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. The next stage of Arctic militarization will likely involve the expansion of nuclear military infrastructure across the region and the emergence of a nuclear belt along Russia’s northern borders, encompassing Northern Europe and Greenland, Alexander Stepanov, a military expert at the RANEPA Institute of Law and National Security, told TASS.
He was commenting on the European Commission’s new Arctic strategy, which, for the first time in more than 30 years, places primary emphasis on military development.
According to Stepanov, the EU’s formal adoption of a militarization agenda, driven in part by efforts to exploit the Arctic’s natural resources, will entail a strengthening of NATO’s northern flank. This trend aligns with the strategic priorities of Northern Europe’s military-industrial complexes, Finland and Sweden’s accession to NATO, and the designation of the Baltic and North seas as priority areas for Europe’s geo-economic and military presence.
"The next step will most likely be the ‘nuclearization’ of the Arctic, specifically through the expansion of nuclear military infrastructure into the region. I envisage a ‘nuclear arc’ stretching from the Baltic Sea to the northern seas. A nuclear belt is taking shape in the areas adjacent to the Arctic along Russia’s borders, encompassing Northern Europe and Greenland, which has recently de facto legalized an expanded US military presence. This will likely involve the deployment of nuclear-capable assets, including US strategic bombers and nuclear-powered submarines," Stepanov said.
He noted that the necessary legal frameworks are already being prepared in several countries. In Finland, steps are being taken to remove restrictions on the potential deployment of nuclear weapons, effectively reversing a policy that had been in place since 1987. A similar trend is evident in Sweden, where the country’s leadership has signaled a possible willingness to host nuclear weapons. Lithuania, meanwhile, has removed restrictions at the constitutional level, effectively opening the way for the deployment of nuclear arsenals.
"The Arctic is becoming a key area of interest not only for the United States but also for the European Union, which urgently needs access to hydrocarbons and rare-earth metals. This creates additional threats to the peaceful development of the Arctic and to the maritime trade routes that are vital to Russia," Stepanov concluded.

articles.title: Macron targets Trump over French riots
articles.body:
Macron targets Trump over French riots
French President Emmanuel Macron has slammed as “stupid” and “unacceptable” remarks by foreign leaders about the unrest gripping France, in an apparent swipe at US President Donald Trump, who blamed the violence on Paris’ lax border policies.
France has been rocked by some of its worst riots in years, sparked last month by teacher shortages and crumbling schools before escalating into nationwide protests over inequality, soaring living costs and public service cuts.
Hundreds of thousands took to the streets over the weekend as demonstrations descended into clashes with police, arson and looting. Nearly 2,400 people were arrested, around 1,000 officers injured, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched, with damage estimated at “hundreds of millions of euros.”
Trump pours fuel on the fire
Trump claimed that “migrants, jihadists, and communists” had “conquered, looted, and burned” France, accusing Macron of failing to secure its borders. He urged European leaders to “close their borders,” before seizing on the unrest to rally Republicans ahead of the November 3 midterms, warning that scenes of “burning steeples and raging fires” were “what the Radical Dumocrats want to do to AMERICA” with their own migration agenda.
Macron isn’t amused
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Macron accused outside actors of manipulating information about the events to their gain.
“There was foreign manipulation of information, which gave rise to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders,” he said. “We have had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false… These people annoy me.”
Asked whether he was referring to Trump, Macron replied: “Among others.”
President Emmanuel Macron said Wednesday that foreign leaders — including those “on the other side of the Atlantic” — were seeking to exploit France’s tense social climate for political gain following a weekend of street violence and looting.
Protests over soaring living costs… pic.twitter.com/XlitrzVoK6
— The Associated Press (@AP) October 21, 2026
While there is no clear evidence that migrants have played a disproportionate role in the unrest, multiple videos posted online have shown protesters waving Palestinian flags alongside French ones.
They said the riots and destruction in France were about the cost of living and schools.
Then explain the Palestinian flags and keffiyehs.
Allowing mass third-world migration is why France is done. pic.twitter.com/jDr733vcOx
— TaraBull (@TaraBull) October 19, 2026
French authorities have largely blamed the violence on radical far-left groups and opportunistic criminals, without linking its organization to immigrants. Meanwhile, politicians across France’s political spectrum blamed Macron and his government for the unrest, accusing the administration of undermining public services and failing to maintain order.
Macron leaves the building
Macron made his remarks during a Middle East trip that he refused to postpone despite the turmoil at home, leaving his government to deal with the fallout. He tried to defend his decision, insisting that changing his plans would have signaled “nervousness” and that he had given his government a “sufficient roadmap.” Yet with just six months until France’s presidential election and his approval rating at a record-low 15%, the trip has only fueled perceptions of a lame-duck presidency as Macron quite literally left the scene as Paris and other cities burned.
His absence drew criticism of an “absent president” and left rivals Marine Le Pen, who leads first-round polling for April 2027 with 32-36% support, and Jean-Luc Melenchon, to dominate the debate at home.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has ordered curfews ahead of fresh protests, with gatherings banned near Paris landmarks including the Louvre and Champs-Elysees for three days. France also plans to deploy 1,000 counterterrorism troops to reinforce police on Saturday, October 24. Lecornu is due to meet mayors of riot-hit cities on Thursday to coordinate efforts to prevent further violence.
Russia, the usual suspect
In his remarks, Macron also dismissed suggestions of foreign interference in the unrest itself, citing a lack of evidence. His remarks followed a flurry of Western media speculation seeking to blame the riots, which spread from France to Belgium, Italy, Portugal and Albania, on outside meddling – with Russia once again cast as the usual suspect.
Outlets such as The Financial Times and the Telegraph, citing “anonymous” sources, reported that several EU governments had asked intelligence agencies to investigate possible Russian involvement. The FT expanded the suspect list to Iran and Algeria, claiming some officials had even demanded a formal EU probe.
European officials also joined the finger-pointing. Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto suggested the riots were part of a “hybrid war” waged through social media by an unidentified actor. Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama went further, accusing Russian and Iranian intelligence services outright.
Yet the allegations have apparently failed to convince even Brussels. According to Euronews, the European Commission has declined to launch an investigation, citing insufficient evidence.
The speculation follows a familiar pattern of EU officials invoking “hybrid warfare” and the alleged “Russian threat” amid domestic turmoil. Just this week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen accused Moscow and Minsk of “weaponizing migration,” linking them to the summer crisis in Spain’s Ceuta, where an estimated 70,000 migrants crossed from Morocco, sparking a border emergency and political fallout over EU migration policies. However, yet again, she presented no evidence connecting either country to the crisis.
Moscow says look closer to home
Moscow routinely dismisses allegations of interference and claims of a Russian threat as “absurd” fabrications, accusing EU leaders of using the narrative to deflect blame for their own policy failures and distract from mounting domestic crises.
Responding to Rama’s accusations, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told him to look closer to home.
“These are citizens of your own country who took to the streets to protest. Don’t shift your responsibility onto others. Deal with your own domestic problems,” she said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, meanwhile, described the unrest sweeping the EU as evidence of “a major crisis… bordering on chaos.”

articles.title: Russia and Ukraine trade major attacks as Trump touts progress
articles.body:
Russia and Ukraine trade major attacks as Trump touts progress
Zelensky said the strikes, which came hours after US envoy Witkoff met Putin, showed ‘no change’ in Moscow’s position
Moscow firing ballistic missiles at Ukraine shortly after talks between US envoy Steve Witkoff and Russia’s Vladimir Putin showed the Kremlin’s position on the war had not changed, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday.
The Kremlin had said it was willing to restart trilateral talks with Kyiv and Washington next month, though dismissed new ideas brought by Witkoff – developed with European countries and Ukraine – as lacking substance.
Russia hit a dozen Ukrainian regions overnight, including Kyiv, killing at least two people and wounding 34, Zelensky said, adding that children were among those hurt.
Residential houses, energy sites, a shopping centre and a monastery had been damaged in Kyiv, where Russia has significantly intensified its strikes ahead of winter.

articles.title: Russia ready to resume trilateral Ukraine talks in November: Kremlin
articles.body:
Russia has said it is ready to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine in November, with discussions potentially taking place in Abu Dhabi.
President Vladimir Putin conveyed Moscow’s position to US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff during three hours of talks in St Petersburg on Wednesday, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told reporters on Wednesday.
“Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, prepared to resume the aforementioned trilateral negotiations around the 10th of November,” Ushakov said.
The meeting was Putin and Witkoff’s ninth in-person encounter.
Ushakov said the situation in Ukraine was a central topic, with Moscow’s readiness to resume negotiations particularly concerning the creation of a post-war “security system” for Moscow and Kiev.
Putin praised Washington’s mediation efforts, Ushakov said. The Vesti news outlet also quoted the Kremlin aide as saying the talks could take place in the Emirati capital, Abu Dhabi.
Moscow and Kiev held three rounds of US-mediated negotiations earlier this year, on January 23–24, February 4–5 and February 17–18. Abu Dhabi hosted the first two rounds, while the third took place in Geneva.
Diplomacy on Iran
Ushakov said Putin also confirmed Russia’s willingness to help find political and diplomatic solutions concerning Iran.
“Vladimir Putin emphasised that diplomatic opportunities are far from exhausted. And that it is possible and necessary to reach an agreement with Tehran, our strategic partner,” he said.
He also said Witkoff briefed Putin on the substance of talks he took part in on Tuesday in Oslo, which included Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and leaders of Finland and Norway, and that the US sensed "some new nuances in the behaviour of the European leaders."
“They mentioned this to us, but, truth be told, these nuances do not entirely satisfy us,” he said.
The discussions also covered the implementation of agreements on Russian diesel supplies to the US and global markets following a phone call between Putin and US President Donald Trump earlier this month.
“The parties also held a detailed discussion on other large-scale joint economic projects, which offer significant prospects for cooperation between the two nations. Some of these initiatives are now nearing the implementation stage,” Ushakov said.
American prisoner released
During the meeting at Constantine Palace, Witkoff announced that Russia had released 73-year-old American Stephen Hubbard.
Hubbard was sentenced by the Moscow City Court on October 7, 2024, to six years and 10 months in a penal colony after being convicted of fighting alongside Ukrainian forces.
Ushakov said Russian officials handed Hubbard over to Witkoff at St Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport for his return to the US.
The envoy thanked Putin on Trump’s behalf for the “gesture of goodwill”, saying the release would be appreciated by the US president and the American public, Ushakov added.

articles.title: Pentagon pledges to buy 850 F-35 jets under 10-year deal with Lockheed Martin
articles.body:
Berk Kutay Gokmen
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The Pentagon has moved to purchase at total of 850 F-35 fighter jets from Lockheed Martin over the next 10 years, marking the longest commitment among recent Trump administration efforts to prepare suppliers for wartime production.
The new framework agreement, announced on Thursday, includes 850 F-35 Lightning II aircraft for the US military, hundreds more for international customers, as well as spare parts and other equipment.
The deal would secure the defense contractor’s plan to produce 156 jets each year in the coming years.
The Defense Department said Lockheed Martin had agreed to fund $7 billion in investments from its own resources to support the long-term production plan.
The agreement announced on Thursday is a step toward a final contract, which would require tens of billions of dollars in congressional funding to be finalized.
The stealth fighter program has already been described as the world’s most expensive weapons program, with projected lifetime costs of $2 trillion for purchasing, operating, and maintaining the aircraft.
Pentagon officials have said that firm, multiyear purchase commitments help make weapons procurement more efficient. Suppliers involved in military programs often complain that inconsistent congressional funding makes long-term planning difficult.
“This multiyear framework strengthens the way we can plan and invest in the F-35 enterprise,” said Lockheed Martin CEO Jim Taiclet.

articles.title: What's behind Hamas's threat, and can it strike Israel? ‘The capabilities are there’
articles.body:
What is behind Hamas's latest threat to carry out another October 7-style attack against Israel, and does the terrorist organization still have the military capabilities to follow through? According to senior Israeli officials, the capabilities exist, although Hamas is no longer believed to be capable of launching an assault on the scale of the 2023 massacre. It could, however, attack military outposts, abduct soldiers or attempt to infiltrate Israeli communities.
The assessment follows ynet's revelation earlier Thursday that senior Hamas officials had delivered an unusually direct warning to Israel through U.N. humanitarian coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov, threatening renewed attacks inside Israel, in the West Bank and abroad. The warning has intensified concerns within Israel's security establishment that Hamas is preparing for another confrontation rather than merely seeking to exert political pressure.
According to assessments recently presented to the security cabinet, Hamas has stepped up preparations for renewed fighting, accumulating weapons and personnel and transferring military equipment into civilian areas. Israeli officials believe the organization assumes that Israel's ability to undertake major military operations is constrained by the October 27 Israeli election and the November 3 U.S. midterms, giving Hamas an opportunity to strengthen its position.
At a cabinet meeting earlier this month, Military Intelligence chief Maj. Gen. Shlomi Binder addressed the thousands of attackers who crossed into Israel on October 7, 2023. "Of the 6,000 who crossed the fence on October 7, 4,000 have been eliminated. Two thousand remain. We will get every last one of them," he said, according to the account of the meeting.
Senior officials say Hamas is deliberately buying time to manufacture additional weapons and recruit new fighters, while recognizing that its opportunity to do so may be narrowing. Against that backdrop, Israeli intelligence has identified several significant changes in the organization's behavior.
Weapons, visible gunmen and arms distributed to civilians
One of the most noticeable developments is Hamas's increasingly open presence above ground. Whereas its members previously tended to remain concealed or move around in civilian clothing, they are now more frequently seen wearing uniforms and openly exercising authority over Gaza's population.
Israeli officials also report that Hamas is transferring weapons from underground tunnels into civilian facilities, including hospitals and schools. According to the military, similar practices were identified during earlier stages of the war, when Israeli troops regularly discovered weapons in civilian buildings and populated areas.
Another change concerns Hamas's public statements. Since the Gaza agreement was announced, the organization had at times suggested that it would surrender its weapons and respect its obligations. That language has increasingly been replaced by more confrontational rhetoric, culminating in the threat reported Thursday.
Israeli officials say they have not encountered a warning of comparable force, boldness and directness from Hamas since the October 7 massacre.
There are also reports that Hamas has begun distributing weapons to civilians. Israeli officials suspect the move is intended to preserve part of the organization's arsenal ahead of any disarmament process, allowing it to hide weapons while claiming to have surrendered those in its possession.
The developments have reinforced an Israeli assessment that Hamas no longer believes the current agreement has a realistic chance of succeeding and is preparing for a possible return to fighting.
Officials also believe Hamas may not wait for Israel to initiate hostilities. Instead, once it concludes that Israel is about to receive a green light for renewed military operations, the organization could attempt to strike first.
Hamas stops playing along
Israeli officials also point to a widening gap between the international perception of Hamas and the picture emerging from Israeli intelligence assessments.
Since the Gaza agreement was announced, Hamas has benefited from the impression that it is prepared to relinquish its weapons and surrender political control of the territory. Israel, meanwhile, has increasingly been portrayed as the party obstructing implementation of President Donald Trump's Gaza plan.
Israeli officials believe Hamas has exploited its apparent willingness to cooperate with the American initiative to buy time and preserve its remaining military and political power.
The significance of the latest threat, they argue, is that Hamas may now be signaling that it is no longer prepared to maintain that appearance.
According to assessments by the IDF and Shin Bet, the central condition for advancing the Gaza plan, Hamas's disarmament, is not being fulfilled. Israeli officials say the organization continues to violate the understandings and has shown no genuine willingness to surrender its weapons.
Officials familiar with the intelligence acknowledge that there is no known date for renewed hostilities and no information about a finalized operational plan for an attack. However, they describe the assessment that Hamas will not voluntarily disarm as unequivocal.
That assessment has also been presented to Israel's political leadership. The military's position is that Israeli ground forces will eventually have to return to areas deep inside Gaza to dismantle Hamas's remaining military infrastructure, a task officials believe cannot be accomplished by an international force.
Israeli officials also anticipate that Hamas would attempt to manipulate any disarmament process. They believe the organization could surrender weapons that are defective or already known to Israeli intelligence, claim to have fulfilled its obligations and conceal a substantial portion of its remaining arsenal and personnel.
What Hamas has lost, and what it can still do
Despite the extensive damage inflicted on its military infrastructure, Hamas retains considerable manpower. Israeli estimates place the organization's armed wing at tens of thousands of members, with some assessments suggesting approximately 30,000, not dramatically different from its estimated strength before October 7.
An additional estimated 50,000 employees work in government ministries controlled by Hamas. The organization continues to dominate civilian administration in Gaza and has prevented the proposed technocratic government from beginning its work.
Recruitment also remains relatively easy. Israeli officials attribute this partly to years of indoctrination among young Gazans and partly to Hamas's ability to offer salaries higher than those available through most other employment opportunities in the territory.
The organization also retains members of its elite Nukhba force, which played a central role in the October 7 attack.
Nevertheless, cabinet ministers say Hamas's current fighters are generally less skilled and less thoroughly trained than their predecessors, while the weapons available to them are often of lower quality.
Much of their training is now theoretical because conducting practical exercises in open areas would expose them to Israeli strikes.
Hamas's command-and-control capabilities have suffered particularly severe damage. According to senior Israeli officials, some key positions have changed hands six or seven times since October 7, with each replacement generally possessing less experience and training than the person who preceded him.
Targeted Israeli strikes against Hamas commanders and fighters have continued during the ceasefire, further disrupting the organization's leadership structure.
Its rocket arsenal has also been severely degraded. Israeli assessments indicate that hundreds of rockets remain in Gaza, although many are not capable of reaching distant targets.
Officials believe Hamas has almost no ability to rebuild this capability and that its capacity to cause significant damage inside Israel through rocket fire is now extremely limited, if it exists at all.
There are, however, gaps in Israeli intelligence. The IDF has not identified every rocket-launching shaft or position remaining in the territory.
Another concern involves areas of Gaza where Israeli ground forces have not operated extensively. These include the humanitarian zone in Al-Mawasi, the central Gaza refugee camps of Al-Bureij, Al-Maghazi and Nuseirat, and parts of Gaza City.
Israeli officials believe Hamas retains weapons depots, manufacturing workshops and underground tunnels in those areas. The IDF also assesses that the organization has restored a substantial portion of its tunnel network in territory outside Israeli control.
Targeting these facilities presents additional difficulties because they are situated in densely populated areas where military operations could result in extensive civilian casualties.
In the West Bank, Hamas retains the capability to attempt terrorist attacks, although Israeli officials assess that the security situation is more tightly controlled because of intensive IDF and Shin Bet operations and continued security coordination with the Palestinian Authority.
Nevertheless, attempts to organize attacks cannot be ruled out.
The organization has also threatened to operate abroad, partly because carrying out attacks inside Gaza has become more difficult.
Israeli officials believe that, with no Israeli hostages remaining in Gaza, Hamas has lost a major bargaining chip. This may help explain the organization's renewed references to abducting soldiers.
According to the Israeli assessment, any Hamas attack, whether inside Israel or overseas, would also provide Israel with considerably greater freedom to launch military operations against the organization.
Beyond its military capabilities, Hamas's financial position is another important factor in assessing whether it can sustain a renewed confrontation.
Israeli security officials believe the organization's finances have improved in recent months through money transferred from outside Gaza and its control over humanitarian aid entering the territory.
Security sources identify Iran and Turkey as Hamas's principal sources of funding. According to those officials, much of the money arrives through digital currencies, which Hamas subsequently converts into cash to pay members of its military wing and civilian administrative structures.
Hamas also remains the dominant governing force in Gaza, according to Israeli assessments, with no significant local rival currently capable of challenging its authority.
That assessment persists despite the presence of armed clans and militias supported by Israel as potential alternatives to Hamas rule.
Israeli officials believe those groups have lost much of their influence as larger quantities of aid have entered areas controlled by Hamas, reinforcing doubts about whether a viable alternative government can be established through local Palestinian factions.
Meanwhile, meaningful reconstruction of Gaza has yet to begin because of insufficient funding. Neither the proposed technocratic administrative committee nor the international stabilization force is operating inside the territory.
COGAT's dilemma: Supplying Gaza without financing Hamas
As winter approaches, Israel is preparing to gradually restore coordination for commercial goods entering Gaza, following reports from Palestinian merchants that Hamas has canceled substantial payment demands previously imposed on traders.
The development prompted requests from merchants to resume the import coordination process, but Israeli officials remain concerned that Hamas could continue exploiting commercial activity to generate revenue and preserve its grip on the territory.
According to Israel's Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), merchants reported that Hamas had withdrawn demands for approximately 10,000 shekels per truck entering Gaza, alongside requirements that goods be sold for cash and that the organization receive 30% of each truck's cargo value.
At a rate of approximately 600 trucks entering Gaza each day, a charge of 10,000 shekels per truck would theoretically generate 180 million shekels a month. That calculation illustrates the potential value of the mechanism rather than establishing how much Hamas actually collected.
COGAT has stressed that the merchants' reports do not independently confirm that Hamas has stopped collecting taxes or demanding payments.
The Israeli authority therefore intends to restore coordination gradually, giving priority to essential supplies ahead of winter while increasing oversight of the traders involved.
Under the arrangements, merchants will be required to make and receive payments exclusively through documented bank transfers. Any trader found to have transferred money to Hamas will lose authorization to operate under the import mechanism.
COGAT says the purpose is to prevent the organization from using commercial imports to strengthen its military and economic capabilities.
The financial stakes are substantial. Previous ynet reporting, based on Israeli security assessments, estimated that approximately 30,000 Hamas personnel across a range of military and administrative roles receive salaries averaging 3,000 shekels a month, creating an estimated monthly payroll of 90 million shekels.
Israeli officials believe Hamas imposed substantial taxes on Gaza merchants, including those receiving goods from outside the territory, partly to finance these payments and prevent the organization from disintegrating.
The question now is whether the reported cancellation of the organization's tax demands is genuine or whether Hamas has simply changed how it collects money from commercial activity.
The dispute over truck payments and cash transactions reflects a broader Israeli concern that Hamas can continue operating extensive financial and administrative networks even as Israel seeks to weaken its military and political control over Gaza.
As winter approaches, Israeli authorities face a dual challenge: allowing essential supplies to reach Gaza's civilian population while preventing Hamas from using the same commercial channels to generate revenue and rebuild its capabilities.
COGAT has emphasized that restoring coordination does not constitute confirmation that Hamas has stopped collecting payments. Officials say the tighter banking requirements and transaction monitoring are intended to reduce the possibility of the organization benefiting financially from incoming goods.
Another component of the Gaza reconstruction effort is also stalled. A company expected to begin clearing areas as part of a pilot project in Rafah has so far completed only a survey and mapping of the territory, with no further progress reported.
The unresolved question is how Israel can ensure that goods and resources entering Gaza reach their intended civilian recipients rather than reinforcing Hamas's control over the territory.
For Israeli security officials, that economic challenge is inseparable from the military threat. Their assessment is that Hamas has lost much of its conventional strength but retains substantial manpower, underground infrastructure, financial resources and the ability to organize smaller attacks.
The central concern is therefore not that Hamas can reproduce the October 7 massacre on the same scale. Israeli officials believe it cannot. It is that the organization, convinced the diplomatic process is approaching failure, may attempt to use the capabilities it still possesses before Israel moves to dismantle them.

articles.title: Son of Stephen Hubbard, American freed from Russian jail, speaks out
articles.body:
Son says Stephen Hubbard was experiencing "extreme tiredness with life" before release from Russian jail
Washington — Fr. Joseph Coleman feared he would never again see his father, Stephen Hubbard, when they had a brief phone conversation last year while Hubbard was in a Russian prison.
"He was expressing a very extreme tiredness with life, the life that he was experiencing at that time. I don't want to say suicidal thoughts, but the conversation hinted it leaned in that direction," Coleman, a Greek Orthodox priest, told CBS News on Wednesday in his first television interview since his father's release.
Hubbard's release was announced earlier Wednesday during a meeting between U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Hubbard, a U.S. citizen, was imprisoned in Russia for more than four years after being accused of fighting for Ukraine. The U.S. government had deemed Hubbard wrongfully detained.
Hubbard touched down back in the U.S. Wednesday night, President Trump said while returning from a rally in South Carolina. He said Hubbard would visit the White House "in the next day or so."
Mr. Trump said Putin had agreed to release Hubbard at his request, with "no 'swap' necessary," though he also said that his decision to waive new sanctions against Russia played a role in Hubbard's release.
In a one-minute phone call with his father before Hubbard took off from St. Petersburg, Coleman said he sounded better than he had during their last conversation in May 2025. Witkoff was also present, leaving little opportunity for a private exchange.
"I want to embrace him as a son embraces his father. I want to personally assess his health to make sure he's well," Coleman said. He said he would also give his dad space to adjust to freedom and expected to see Hubbard later that evening.
Coleman, who lives in Cyprus, did not grow up in the same home as Hubbard, who was divorced from Coleman's mother. He said the family had lost track of Hubbard entirely for roughly three years after his detention.
Martin De Luca, Hubbard's U.S.-based attorney, told CBS News that when his legal team took on the case in February 2025, neither the family nor the U.S. Embassy knew precisely where Hubbard was being held.
Lawyers in Russia eventually located him and arranged for legal visits, money for food and basic necessities, and the brief phone call with his son.
De Luca said the isolation had taken an enormous toll.
"It's just being isolated from everybody you've ever known and just from the outside world," he said.
After Putin granted Hubbard's release, Witkoff praised the Russian president as a "humanitarian," prompting swift backlash from Republican and Democratic lawmakers. Putin is wanted by the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes involving the deportation of Ukrainian children, and Russian forces have been accused of widespread abuses during the war.
Asked about Witkoff's description of Putin, Coleman called his father's release "a small step toward peace in this greater conflict" and thanked Putin for signing off on the deal.
He described the decision as an act of "compassion and even mercy."
Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired schoolteacher, was captured in Ukraine shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022 and accused of manning a checkpoint for mercenaries. He was later sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony following a closed-door trial.
His family has consistently disputed the charges.
De Luca said his legal team conducted its own investigation, interviewing people who knew Hubbard and examining his circumstances before the invasion. He said they found no evidence that Hubbard had served in the Ukrainian military or was physically capable of doing so at roughly 70 years old.
"We have not seen any evidence to support those allegations," De Luca said. He added that the Russian case file was largely sealed and that his team had repeatedly sought evidence substantiating the charges.
De Luca and Coleman both credited the Trump administration's diplomatic engagement with Moscow for securing Hubbard's freedom.
Asked whether recent U.S. decisions benefiting Russia — including sanctions relief and purchases of Russian diesel — were connected to Hubbard's release, De Luca said he did not believe there was a direct link, though he acknowledged that bilateral relationships involve multiple overlapping interests.
Mr. Trump, however, has explicitly said that allowing new sanctions to take effect would have prevented Hubbard's release.
And despite Hubbard's release, as many as 20 Americans remain imprisoned in Russia, including some whose families dispute the charges against them. The State Department continues to warn Americans against traveling to Russia because of the risk of wrongful detention.
De Luca said he was not concerned that the administration's engagement with Moscow would encourage further detentions, arguing that diplomatic dialogue had helped secure several Americans' freedom.
But Russia has not been designated a state sponsor of wrongful detention under a new Trump administration policy, despite its history of imprisoning Americans on questionable charges. Iran and Afghanistan have both received the designation.
Coleman stopped short of blaming his father for his circumstances but acknowledged he might have made a mistake by remaining in Ukraine as Russian forces advanced.
"The Russian forces told foreign nationals to leave and he did not," Coleman said. "I do not like what happened to my father. I am ecstatic that he is free. But he was living in an area that was a war zone."
"I'm not saying his detainment was justifiable. I'm not saying that," he said. "But these things happen in war."

articles.title: Europe cannot count on American rescue, inquiry told
articles.body:
Europe cannot count on the United States returning to the European Arctic as the security partner and ally that Britain and Europe previously relied on, and NATO’s Article 5 is functionally moribund in the American sense, according to evidence published by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, examined the implications of American policy for High North security as part of its inquiry.
Dhesi said: “Our report calls for the government to reassess the JEF’s role and consider whether it should focus more on countering threats in the High North, particularly if the UK has to plan for uncertainty over US support for NATO. The UK’s presence in the Baltics, particularly in Estonia, may need to be bolstered to offset the effects of any greater JEF focus on the High North.”
Professor David Blagden of the University of Exeter told the committee: “[w]e can talk about the formal aspects of withdrawal or not but, functionally, you would probably say Article 5 in the American sense is pretty much moribund at the moment now anyway. No one really believes that the Americans are riding to the rescue if there were some situation in the Baltic states.”
The report sets out that the American 2026 National Defense Strategy outlined four lines of effort to achieve its America First strategic approach, covering defence of the United States homeland, deterring China in the Indo-Pacific through strength, increasing burden-sharing with allies and partners, and supercharging the American defence industrial base. The committee states that none of these suggest a return to greater engagement in Europe’s defence over the medium term, including the High North, and that where the Arctic is mentioned in the strategy it is in relation to American homeland defence.
The committee was told that “[e]ven if the next US President was a dyed in the wool Atlanticist—Eisenhower 2.0 or something—the US would not have the capacity to pivot back to playing the role it did in Europe and the High North”, largely because the United States perceives the maximum likelihood of conflict in East Asia as between 2027 and 2035.
On troop numbers, the report records a reported plan to cut between 25,000 and 40,000 American troops from the roughly 80,000 currently stationed in Europe, despite congressional provisions in the FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act restricting reductions below 76,000 personnel, and notes that significant future reductions in fighter jets, strategic bombers, destroyers, submarines, tanker aircraft and armed drones could also follow.
The Kiel Institute calculated that replacing American military capabilities with European weapons would cost an extra €50 billion each year over the next decade.
Professor Blagden also told the committee: “[t]he caveat, though, to all that glass-half-full stuff is that the UK, for years and years, has been generating SDSR-type documents in which we talk about how far we lean on allies. It has ultimately reached the point where the greatest of those allies has suddenly become unreliable… [w]e cannot just say, ‘We lean on an ally for this. We lean on an ally for that.’ When it comes to the High North, the UK is the major power now. The American cavalry is not about to ride over the horizon and save our fecklessness.”
Ministry of Defence witnesses drew a distinction between American capabilities and American commitments. On capabilities, the department said the United States is making it known to the rest of NATO that “[h]ere are the capabilities we [America] intend not to offer in the future. That is what we think a more European NATO looks like…” On commitments, Brigadier Jeremy Lamb, Head of Euro-Atlantic Security at the department, told the committee that “[w]hat they are talking about, is basing; it is not necessarily what they will make available to the SACEUR (Supreme Allied Commander Europe) in a crisis.”

articles.title: Denmark guarantees 750 million kroner loan for Ukrainian rocket fuel factory in Vojens
articles.body:
Denmark will guarantee a loan worth 750 million kroner ($110 million) for a Danish subsidiary of Ukrainian defense company Fire Point to establish a rocket fuel factory in southern Jutland.
The Ministry of Industry, Business and Financial Affairs announced the state-backed guarantee in a press release, saying the support was necessary because the war in Ukraine makes it difficult for Fire Point to secure financing through conventional Danish lending arrangements.
The factory will be built in Vojens, near Skrydstrup Air Base. Production is now expected to begin in late 2027, a year later than originally planned.
Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh announced the delay in August, citing slower-than-expected construction.
Business Minister Martin Lidegaard said the project would strengthen Ukraine’s defense capabilities while supporting Denmark’s defense industry and European security.
Denmark invited Fire Point to establish production in the country in September 2025, becoming the first NATO member to welcome Ukrainian weapons manufacturing on its territory.
That same month, the Danish Parliament passed legislation allowing the defense minister to waive certain regulations for military projects considered nationally important.
Under the legislation, Fire Point can temporarily bypass more than 20 laws and regulations, including rules covering environmental protection, planning and nature conservation.
The company must eventually comply with the standard regulations governing such facilities.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said manufacturing military equipment outside Ukraine would help protect supply chains from Russian attacks.
He added that access to secure production facilities and critical defense technology was essential to Ukraine’s ability to defend itself.

articles.title: U.S. Midterms Loom Over a Deadlock Between Trump and Tehran
articles.body:
Iran may have found a weapon in the American electoral calendar. With the midterm elections two weeks away, Tehran is intensifying attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, calculating that higher energy prices will deepen President Donald Trump’s political troubles and make another U.S. military campaign too costly to contemplate.
The wager is seductive: an American president anxious about diesel prices and his party’s prospects in the midterms, Iran seems to believe, will have little appetite for another major war.
Trump’s declaration that he will refrain from striking Iran before the Nov. 3 vote appears to vindicate this view, even as he periodically threatens to use force again. Having survived two rounds of war and absorbed punishing economic losses, Iran’s leaders believe they can endure a little longer. By disrupting Gulf commerce, they gain leverage their conventional forces cannot provide. They also hope to make that leverage permanent and compel Washington to accept Tehran’s authority over passage through the world’s most important energy chokepoint.
Yet the past nine months of war against Iran have made it clear that renewed military conflict before the midterms or after the elections is unlikely to resolve the disputes between the U.S. and Iran. The two countries will eventually have to sit across the negotiating table to resolve their long-running disputes.
Miscalculations in Tehran and Washington
Tehran may be misreading how political peril shapes an adversary’s decisions. Trump could decide that appearing powerless as Iranian attacks push up prices is more damaging than another round of military strikes. Reports that his administration has considered fresh strikes suggest the military option remains in play. A serious attack on American forces could turn Trump’s promise of restraint into a political liability overnight.
The political situation in Israel adds a combustible variable. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces an Oct. 27 election with his bloc struggling to secure a majority. He has staked his political reputation on the claim that only he can neutralize the Iranian threat.
With Tehran rebuilding its missile and drone capabilities and uncertainty surrounding its nuclear program, Netanyahu may see renewed strikes as both a strategic opportunity and a means of restoring his standing at home. Such a gamble could deepen Israel’s insecurity, but electoral desperation seldom improves anyone’s judgment.
The convergence of these calculations makes the coming weeks particularly perilous. Iran thinks Trump’s electoral weakness will constrain him. Trump and Netanyahu might each conclude that a show of force could rescue their political fortunes. Each side imagines it can calibrate the violence and manage the aftermath. The experience of this year’s conflict, in which successive rounds of fighting outran diplomatic efforts to contain them, offers little reason for that confidence.
Even if October passes without another conflagration, November brings its own hazards. After the midterm elections, the political constraints Trump has publicly imposed on himself will disappear. With substantial American forces already positioned in the region, Washington may be tempted to break the deadlock through another round of attacks. Tehran, fearing another surprise attack, might choose to strike Israel or U.S. military assets in the region first. What might seem like prudent preparation in Washington or Tehran could help bring about the war it is meant to deter.
The underlying impasse is as stubborn as ever. Washington wants a nuclear agreement and believes its blockade will ultimately compel Iran to negotiate. Tehran insists on upfront economic relief and an end to the war before substantive talks on the nuclear issue can begin.
America can point to tankers still transiting Hormuz, but shipping that depends on costly military protection and remains under threat is a poor substitute for normal trade. Iran can inflict considerable damage on the oil exports of its Gulf neighbors, but it has so far failed to turn that leverage into meaningful American concessions.
Dangers of a wider war
Another surge in hostilities would widen this gulf rather than bridge it. American and Israeli aircraft can destroy missile launchers, production facilities, and infrastructure, but Iran has repeatedly demonstrated that it can retaliate and survive. Iran’s response could extend further to target Gulf energy infrastructure, maritime commerce, data centers, and other critical networks.
The Houthi confrontation with Saudi Arabia already offers a grim illustration of how quickly the costs can spread. The war in Yemen has been reignited with devastating consequences, including deadly attacks on civilian airports and a spiraling cycle of retaliation. The fighting now threatens to draw in Turkey and Pakistan to support Saudi Arabia, as the three countries recently signed a mutual security pact known as the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.
A new campaign could leave Iran poorer, Israel more exposed, and the U.S. burdened with an even more expensive regional commitment, while markets around the world absorb another shock.
The outlines of a diplomatic bargain have been visible for months: reciprocal steps to reopen Hormuz, calibrated sanctions relief, and a resumption of nuclear negotiations. The difficulty lies in sequencing and trust. Tehran fears that surrendering its maritime leverage first would invite fresh demands; Washington worries that easing pressure would reward coercion without securing lasting constraints on Iran’s nuclear program. Addressing those fears will require reciprocal steps and credible verification. More bombing won’t help.
Leaders contemplating an October surprise or an offensive after the midterms must remember that uncomfortable truth. Military force may alter the balance of pain without resolving the disputes each side will eventually have to confront across the negotiating table.
After another round of death and destruction, they could find themselves negotiating over the same issues, with less trust, greater bitterness, and far fewer resources to rebuild what they have broken. Their choices will be no easier then; the cost of reaching an agreement will be far greater.

articles.title: Britain still plans new nuclear sub every eighteen months
articles.body:
Ministers have confirmed that the intention remains to procure up to twelve SSN-AUKUS submarines, and that the investments needed to establish industrial capacity for a submarine every eighteen months from the mid-2030s have been made, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Andrew Rosindell, the Reform UK member for Romford, asked the Secretary of State for Defence whether he would make it his department’s policy to increase total hull numbers in the submarine service.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “As set out in the Defence Investment Plan (DIP), the Ministry of Defence intends to procure up to 12 SSN AUKUS submarines.
“The programme is currently midway through the Detailed Design and Long Lead (D2L2) phase and we anticipate that the number of submarines will be confirmed before the end of this phase in 2028.
“Through the DIP, the Government has made the investments necessary to establish the industrial capacity required to ultimately deliver a submarine every 18 months from the mid-2030s to ensure we can deliver an expanded SSN force.”
Britain currently operates seven Astute class attack submarines, and this publication reported the government’s commitment to build twelve new nuclear attack submarines when the plan appeared. A drumbeat of one boat every eighteen months would be the fastest sustained British submarine production rate since the Cold War, and the figure follows from the capacity being built at Barrow.
Barrow has been expanding through the Barrow Infrastructure Programme, with new build halls, a reconfigured yard and a recruitment effort that has taken the BAE Systems workforce there past twelve thousand. Rolls-Royce Submarines in Derby has doubled its site to produce reactors for both Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS, and the Sheffield Forgemasters work on large forgings feeds the same chain.
Confirmation of the final number before the end of the detailed design phase in 2028 ties the fleet size to what the yard can actually sustain. Senior officials told the Commons Defence Committee earlier this year that submarine fleet size was conditional on Barrow output, and a decision due in 2028 falls inside this Parliament.
Australia will build its own SSN-AUKUS boats at Osborne in South Australia to a common design, and the two production lines are intended to share a supply chain, which is part of the case for the industrial investment on the British side. Dreadnought holds priority at Barrow through the late 2020s, so attack submarine production builds up behind the ballistic missile boats.
Pollard confirmed in a separate answer the same day that steel will be cut on the first British SSN-AUKUS next year, and that the Preliminary Design Review for the class concluded on the first of July. Twelve boats remains an upper bound until the design phase closes.

articles.title: Moscow and Beijing could seal major gas pipeline deal by year-end – Russian deputy PM
articles.body:
Moscow and Beijing could seal major gas pipeline deal by year-end – Russian deputy PM
Russia and China could finalize agreements on a major new gas pipeline by the end of the year, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak said on Wednesday, in a potential breakthrough that would significantly expand Moscow’s energy exports to Asia.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of talks between Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and his Chinese counterpart Li Qiang in St. Petersburg, Novak said the planned Power of Baikal pipeline was among the issues discussed.
“Our companies – Gazprom and China National Petroleum Corporation – are negotiating a second route for gas supplies from Russia to the People’s Republic of China,” he said. “We are waiting for our companies to complete commercial negotiations and hope they will reach the relevant agreements by the end of the year.”
Li arrived in St. Petersburg on Tuesday for the regular meeting of the Russian and Chinese heads of government.
Russia already supplies gas to China through the Power of Siberia, a more than 3,000-kilometer pipeline launched in 2019. It carries gas from the Chayandinskoye field in Yakutia and the Kovyktinskoye field in Irkutsk Region through Russia’s Far East and across the border near Blagoveshchensk, connecting to a Chinese network extending toward Shanghai. Its annual export capacity is 38 billion cubic meters (bcm), with deliveries reaching 38.8 bcm in 2025.
The planned Power of Baikal, previously known as Power of Siberia 2, would open a major new energy corridor. The roughly 2,600-kilometer pipeline is designed to deliver up to 50 bcm annually from Russia’s Arctic gas fields on the Yamal Peninsula to China via Mongolia, including the Soyuz Vostok transit pipeline.
Unlike Power of Siberia, which draws gas from eastern Siberia, the new route would tap western Siberian reserves that previously supplied Europe, giving Moscow a major new outlet for gas following the collapse of much of its European market. Novak said the project was renamed Power of Baikal to distinguish it from the existing pipeline and reflect its planned route along the southern shore of Lake Baikal. The precise route remains subject to final commercial agreements.
Together, the two pipelines would give Russia a combined nominal export capacity of around 88 bcm annually to China – roughly 80% of the 110 bcm combined capacity of Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2, built to supply Russian gas to Europe via the Baltic Sea.
Gazprom and CNPC signed a legally binding memorandum on the project in September 2025, envisaging deliveries of 50 bcm annually over 30 years. A final supply contract, however, was not signed. Pricing is a key sticking point, with media reports suggesting Beijing is seeking rates close to Russia’s domestic prices, while Moscow has pushed for more commercially favorable terms. President Vladimir Putin said last year that pricing would follow a market-based formula similar to that used for European supplies, stressing that there would be “no charity” on either side.
The expansion comes as Russia accelerates its energy pivot toward Asia in light of Western sanctions and EU efforts to phase out Russian supplies. Before the Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022, Europe was Russia’s largest pipeline gas market, with Gazprom providing around 40-45% of the bloc’s total gas imports. Deliveries subsequently plunged as Brussels pursued alternative suppliers and imposed successive sanctions on Russia.
Meanwhile, China has emerged as Russia’s largest pipeline gas customer, with Power of Siberia reaching its full contracted capacity and further export routes under development.
Unlike oil, which can be redirected by tanker, pipeline gas requires extensive infrastructure, making Power of Baikal a key project in Moscow’s efforts to replace lost European demand. Moscow has repeatedly accused Western governments of undermining European energy security through their sanctions policies.
The shift also follows the September 2022 sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines that previously brought Russian gas to Germany beneath the Baltic Sea. Novak said on Wednesday that Moscow remains ready to resume deliveries through the one Nord Stream pipeline string out of the four that remained undamaged.
“We have one of the four strings in working condition. If European consumers and politicians want it, supplies can, of course, be delivered through that line,” he said. The decision rests primarily with European countries, particularly Germany, where the pipeline terminates, Novak added. He said the three damaged strings could also be restored if demand and economic conditions justified repairs, suggesting it would not take long to bring them back to working order.
Russia has repeatedly offered to resume energy supplies to Europe, particularly in light of the disruptions to global markets caused by the Middle East crisis, but says its proposals have received no response from European governments.

articles.title: Driver at Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant killed in drone attacks, managers say
articles.body:
Driver at Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant killed in drone attacks, managers say
Oct 21 - Management at the Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in southeastern Ukraine said a driver at the station had been killed on Wednesday after two days of Ukrainian drone attacks.
Russian forces seized the station, Europe's largest with six reactors, in the first weeks of the February 2022 invasion. Each side has since repeatedly accused the other of military activity liable to jeopardise nuclear safety.
The plant's managers in a post on Telegram said buses carrying staff to and from the plant had come under attack for two days in a row.
"The second straight day of attacks on the station's transport shows that these strikes are deliberate," the statement said.
It said the attacks "pose a direct threat" to staff who ensured operations at the plant.
Russia has in recent months accused Ukraine of attacking sites and services associated with the plant, including transport.
Rosatom, Russia's state nuclear corporation, said a Ukrainian drone attack on a service car in July killed the plant's chief engineer and the vehicle's driver.
The city of Enerhodar, where most of the nuclear station's staff live, has also been a frequent target.
Rosatom last week said a truce agreement, mediated by the UN's nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency, was in place to allow repairs at a thermal power station supplying power to the nuclear plant. REUTERS

articles.title: Russia returns bodies of 252 Ukrainian soldiers
articles.body:
Russia returns bodies of 252 Ukrainian soldiers
Russia has handed over the remains of 252 Ukrainian soldiers killed in the conflict and received the bodies of 25 Russian troops in return, according to multiple reports.
The transfer reportedly took place on Thursday in Belarus near the Novaya Guta border crossing with Ukraine. Officials and media outlets in all three countries confirmed the details of the repatriations.
Footage from the scene shows monitors from the International Committee of the Red Cross overseeing the transfer.
The disparity in the number of bodies returned is typical, unlike prisoner-of-war swaps, which are generally conducted on an equal basis.
Pro-Kiev commentators have long argued that the imbalance does not reflect the actual ratio of battlefield casualties, as advancing Russian forces are better positioned to recover the bodies of fallen Ukrainian soldiers. However, the latest round, which followed Kiev’s claims of a major offensive near the city of Liman, showed no significant change in the proportion.
Neither Russia nor Ukraine officially publishes comprehensive figures for its military casualties. Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky has cited death tolls that even pro-Kiev commentators consider implausibly low. In July, he claimed that “about 50,000” Ukrainian troops had been killed, down from the 55,000 deaths he reported in February.
Many Ukrainian battlefield casualties are classified as missing in action, which allows the cash-strapped government to defer compensation to the families of the fallen soldiers.
In summer 2025, Russian officials accused their Ukrainian counterparts of refusing to take hundreds of remains. The Ukrainians rejected the allegations, which the Russians said could be explained by a shortage of bodies in Kiev’s reserves and its concerns over the bad optics of a one-sided repatriation.
On three separate days in mid-June 2025, Russia unilaterally returned 1,200 bodies to Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia has chance to help resolve US-Iran conflict — expert
articles.body:
TEHRAN, October 21. /TASS/. Russia’s continued partnership with Iran puts Moscow in a strong position to advance its own peace initiative aimed at resolving the conflict between Tehran and Washington and preventing a resumption of hostilities, Oleg Akulinichev, an expert on Iran and Middle Eastern affairs, told TASS.
On October 8, US President Donald Trump said Washington did not intend to launch strikes against Iran before the US midterm congressional elections scheduled for November 3.
"This is clearly a continuation of a hybrid war in which military pressure, a blockade and cyber operations all serve a single purpose: to force Tehran to capitulate. The threat of renewed missile strikes, both before and after November 3, remains," Akulinichev said, commenting on Trump’s recent statements.
Against this backdrop, Moscow’s continued diplomatic engagement with Tehran gives Russia an opportunity to advance a peace initiative, the expert said. One possible step, he suggested, would be to convene an international conference to develop a new, inclusive security architecture for the region.
Akulinichev noted that questions remain over the sincerity of Trump’s pledge to refrain from strikes at least until November 3, particularly amid the US military buildup in the Persian Gulf and increasingly frequent contacts between American and Israeli officials.
The success of Russia’s initiative, he concluded, will depend on "how quickly Moscow can convert the current level of trust with Iran into a concrete negotiating formula, before the US military machine is set in motion."
On October 19, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived in Tehran for a working visit. During his stay, he met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council.
