articles.title: EU member to relaunch talks with Moscow
articles.body:
EU member to relaunch talks with Moscow
Slovakia will discuss economic cooperation with Russia, including energy supplies, in Moscow next week, the Slovak Foreign Ministry has said.
The landlocked EU nation has remained a buyer of Russian oil and gas despite the deterioration of the ties between Moscow and the EU in the wake of the escalation of the Ukraine conflict. The country is supposed to phase out Russian energy by late 2027 under the bloc’s plan to replace Russian oil and gas supplies from elsewhere.
The Russian-Slovak intergovernmental commission for economic, scientific, and technical cooperation has been inactive since November 2021 but is now set to meet next Monday, the Slovak Foreign Ministry announced late on Tuesday. The commission will discuss a broad range of topics, including farming, environment, sports, and culture, and focus on energy supply, including nuclear energy, according to the ministry.
“The fundamental topic will be energy and the possibility to cooperate in securing supplies of strategic resources. The Slovak side is also interested in discussing gas supplies and the continuation of oil supplies,” it said in a statement.
Bratislava continues “to base its approach on its European Union and North Atlantic Alliance membership and keeping commitments of this membership” but wants to create room for dialogue, the ministry said.
Slovakia dissented on the EU’s course to dismantle ties with Moscow and prop up Kiev in the conflict after Robert Fico retook the prime minister’s office in October 2023, for the fourth time in his long political career. Under Fico, Slovakia has remained skeptical of assisting Ukraine and of Kiev’s push to join NATO, while halting government weapons shipments and calling for peace. The stance has resulted in repeated public spats between Bratislava and Kiev, as well as criticism from Brussels.
Last month, Fico warned that Europe was moving dangerously close to a direct clash between NATO and Russia, accusing the West of seeking a “pretext” for a major conflict. He accused EU nations of engaging in increasingly bellicose rhetoric and described the Ukraine conflict as “out of control.”
“The situation has never been as serious and tense regarding the possibility of a pan-European war conflict as it is now,” he said.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis claim missile strike on military target near Aden airport
articles.body:
ADEN, Yemen, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Wednesday it had launched a ballistic missile at a military target near Aden International Airport in the southern port city of Aden, where a powerful explosion shook surrounding neighborhoods, with no casualties immediately reported.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said in a statement posted on social media platform X that the missile targeted what he described as a "Saudi military operations room" at Badr military base in Aden, claiming the strike was "direct and precise."
A local security official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed to Xinhua that a ballistic missile had struck the vicinity of Aden International Airport, but said the exact target and extent of any damage remained unclear.
The explosion rocked parts of Aden, the temporary seat of Yemen's internationally recognized government, while smoke was seen rising from an area near the airport, according to a Xinhua reporter on the ground and local residents.
The blast caused panic among residents around the airport in the city's populated Khormaksar district that houses Aden International Airport and Badr military base, a key military facility used by the government forces backed by the Saudi Arabia-led coalition.
Wednesday's strike came five days after two Houthi ballistic missiles landed inside the grounds of Aden International Airport on Oct. 16, while a third struck a military base near the headquarters of the Saudi-led coalition forces in Al Buraiqa district in western Aden.
A day earlier, on Oct. 15, missiles struck the Al-Ma'ashiq Presidential Palace compound in Aden, killing five people and wounding 16 others, according to the Yemeni government. The Houthi group later claimed responsibility for the attack, saying they had targeted a Saudi military operations headquarters inside the compound.
The latest attack comes amid intensified fighting between the Houthi group and government forces supported by the Saudi-led coalition, alongside an escalating exchange of missile, drone and air strikes between the Houthi group and Saudi Arabia.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

articles.title: Exclusive: Ben-Gvir’s Plan to Push Netanyahu Right
articles.body:
In a small office in the industrial district of Lod, a city outside Tel Aviv where Israeli forces expelled thousands of Palestinians during the 1948 war, sits the campaign headquarters of Otzma Yehudit, or “Jewish Power.” The ultra-nationalist party is led by Itamar Ben-Gvir, a far-right firebrand once deemed too extreme to serve in Israel’s military. He now sits in Benjamin Netanyahu’s cabinet as national security minister, overseeing the country’s police and prison services.
If Ben-Gvir has his way, the Oct. 27 election will give his party more seats in parliament and himself greater leverage over another right-wing government led by Netanyahu. His ambition is not to replace the prime minister but to make him even more dependent on the hardline parties pushing for Palestinians to leave Gaza and the West Bank—and for Israel to extend sovereignty over the territories.
“I want Netanyahu to be prime minister. He’s a leader. I prefer him a million times over Eisenkot,” Ben-Gvir tells me in a rare interview on Oct. 19, referring to Netanyahu’s chief rival, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Pounding his chest, he adds: “What will really help Netanyahu be right wing is if I, Ben-Gvir, will be a senior minister and it’s a full right-wing government.”
The post he covets is defense minister, which would give him command over Israel’s armed forces and greater authority to pursue his vision for Gaza and the West Bank: fewer constraints on military operations, the “voluntary emigration” of Palestinians from both territories, and the expansion of Israeli control over lands he believes belong to the Jewish people. Netanyahu has resisted giving Ben-Gvir the portfolio. But Ben-Gvir and his allies hope to win enough seats to force Netanyahu to accommodate their demands or risk losing power. He may benefit from the rightward shift of Israeli politics, particularly among younger voters drawn to his confrontational style and uncompromising vision of Jewish sovereignty. In a Channel 12 survey of first-time Jewish voters, nearly three-quarters identified as right-wing or center-right.
Polls suggest a tight contest, with Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party edging ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud in several recent surveys, but neither the prime minister’s right-wing bloc nor the opposition appears close to the 61 Knesset seats needed to govern. An average of four recent polls puts the two camps at roughly 50 and 53 seats, respectively, leaving Arab parties and smaller factions potentially pivotal. The result could be another fragile coalition; an unlikely unity government between Netanyahu and Eisenkot; or a prolonged deadlock that sends Israelis back to the polls.
Ben-Gvir, dressed in a white shirt and white kippah, speaks halting English. Under his leadership, Israel’s prison service has drawn allegations of abuse for its treatment of Palestinian detainees. But he wants a more direct role in determining Israel’s future in Gaza and the West Bank.
“If Israel wants to continue to live and not be destroyed, we have to capture all of Gaza,” he says. “We have to promote voluntary emigration. Gaza could be a Riviera. It’s a beautiful place. But we can’t have one Hamas member there.” His proposal would have Palestinians leave Gaza for countries willing to receive them, and then allow Israelis to establish settlements in the coastal enclave. It would reverse a defining decision of an earlier right-wing prime minister, Ariel Sharon, who in 2005 withdrew Israeli forces and evacuated more than 8,000 Jewish settlers from Gaza.
Ben-Gvir offers no clear explanation of which countries would accept large numbers of Palestinians, or how their departure could be considered voluntary under the conditions he proposes. “Gaza was always ours,” he says. “Israel is a tiny country. We have to be wider, broader. Hamas are terrorists who don’t just want to destroy Israel. They want to destroy the whole world.”
When I suggest that removing Palestinians from Gaza and resettling it would deepen Israel’s international isolation, he dismisses the concern. “I think that the stronger we are, we won’t be isolated,” he says. “Israel is isolated when it’s weak. If we help the population leave Gaza, we can be very strong.”
Ben-Gvir’s rhetoric and policy designs have drawn widespread condemnation at home and abroad, with critics across the political spectrum accusing him of inciting war crimes and eroding the foundations of Israeli democracy. “He’s a source of immense trouble,” Efraim Halevy, a former head of the Mossad, tells me.
His ambitions in the West Bank are no less sweeping. Ben-Gvir wants Israel to annex the territory, which he, like most Israelis, calls by its biblical names, Judea and Samaria. It is home to 3.3 million Palestinians and governed by the Palestinian Authority (PA), created by the 1993 Oslo Accords that envisioned a Palestinian state. Controlled by the Fatah party, the PA has a lightly armed security force that is trained by the U.S. military and historically works with Israel to suppress terror attacks. But Ben-Gvir wants Israeli security control over the area Palestinians envisage as the heartland of a future state. “We need to take away the weapons for the Palestinian Authority,” he says. “As of now, they are training in Jericho. They’re not training to direct traffic, are they? They want to do another Oct. 7.” A spokesperson for the PA did not respond to a request for comment.
The vision goes beyond annexation. Ben-Gvir says he would encourage millions of Palestinians who have lived in the West Bank for generations to pack up and go. “We want sovereignty in Judea and Samaria, where we also want voluntary emigration,” he says. “Just so we understand, we want voluntary emigration—not kicking anyone out. People will choose the option to leave.”
Whether Ben-Gvir can translate those ambitions into official Israeli policy will depend in part on the leverage his party wins on Oct. 27. He is counting on voters to strengthen his hand. “I hope the nation sends its message,” he says.
Ben-Gvir, 50, was born into a relatively secular Jewish family of Iraqi and Kurdish descent in Mevaseret Zion, a suburb of Jerusalem. His mother had belonged to the Irgun, the Jewish underground that fought British rule before Israel’s founding, but his parents were, by all accounts, not ideological zealots. Ben-Gvir took a different path. He became religious at 12 and, amid the violence of the first Palestinian intifada, gravitated toward the teachings of Meir Kahane, the American-born rabbi who advocated expelling Arabs from Israel and the occupied territories. By his teens, he was an activist in Kahane’s movement, which Israel eventually outlawed as a terrorist organization. Ben-Gvir was considered so extreme that the Israeli military barred him from compulsory service.
Today, Ben-Gvir continues to revere Kahane, even as he disavows some of his mentor’s most fanatical positions. “I went to his yeshiva. He did a lot of good things. He protected Jews. He was murdered sanctifying God’s name,” he tells me. “Not everything that he did do I fully agree with. In the past, I thought we should kick out all the Arabs from the land of Israel. Now I think there can be some. I accept that there are some Arabs who live here. And I have no problem with part of them. Those who recognize the State of Israel as the Jewish state. Those who are loyal to the Jewish State.”
As a young adult, Ben-Gvir moved to Kiryat Arba, a Jewish settlement overlooking the Palestinian city of Hebron, where Kahane’s legacy runs particularly deep. According to published accounts, he and his future wife, Ayala, visited the grave of Baruch Goldstein on their first date. Goldstein, an American-born physician and Kahane admirer, had massacred 29 Palestinian Muslims at prayer in Hebron in 1994 before being beaten to death by survivors. For years, Ben-Gvir displayed Goldstein’s portrait in his living room. He became an attorney for Jewish settlers and activists accused of extremist violence. He also acquired a criminal record, including convictions for incitement to racism and supporting a terrorist organization.
For years, Ben-Gvir remained on the fringes of Israeli politics, a familiar presence at settler demonstrations but an unlikely candidate for national office. Over time, he softened some of his rhetoric, publicly distanced himself from Kahane’s demand to remove all Arabs, and cultivated a more approachable persona without abandoning his annexationist aspirations.
His political breakthrough came under Netanyahu. Ahead of the 2022 election, the prime minister helped broker an alliance between Ben-Gvir’s party and Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism, giving Netanyahu enough seats to assemble a government. Netanyahu’s decision to bring two Jewish supremacists into government became emblematic of Israel’s rightward turn—and one of the factors in its growing international isolation.
As national security minister, Ben-Gvir has pursued a hardline agenda: expanding civilian gun ownership, imposing an increasingly draconian regime on Palestinian prisoners, and pressing for tougher policing of anti-government protests. He wore a noose-shaped pin as he championed legislation imposing the death penalty on Palestinians convicted of deadly terrorist attacks, and released an AI-generated video depicting Palestinian prisoners emerging from Israeli jails emaciated and weeping, a grotesque statement about the conditions of their confinement.
Ben-Gvir also encouraged Jewish prayer at the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, challenging a decades-old arrangement governing the disputed religious site, which has traditionally permitted Jews to visit but reserved the right to worship there for Muslims. Under Ben-Gvir, Israeli police have increasingly allowed Jews to pray at the site, a deliberate provocation to the Arab world, drawing condemnation from Palestinian and Jordanian authorities. “It used to be an apartheid up there and Jews could not pray,” he tells me. “That could not happen in any normal country. I returned justice to the Temple Mount.”
Ben-Gvir has also become one of the leading voices on the Israeli right seeking to shift responsibility for Oct. 7 away from Netanyahu and onto Israel’s military and intelligence establishment. Among the claims he repeats is that security officials failed to wake the prime minister as the attack unfolded—which is disputed by former security officials.
“Even if he’s not perfect, and even if he made mistakes, and he indeed made mistakes, what screwed him up on Oct. 7 was our intelligence,” Ben-Gvir says of Netanyahu. “The army, the intelligence, the Shin Bet. They are all to blame,” he adds. “Netanyahu is not clear of blame, but there are many people who are more at fault than him.”
Ben-Gvir’s relationship with the prime minister is not exactly warm. “I’m not backing him; I’m not his crony on everything. I think he’s much better than Eisenkot,” Ben-Gvir says. “I want to be next to him. I want him to be very strong. I want to pull him to the right.”
He tells me he would not join a unity government between Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a possibility if neither can assemble a governing coalition. “Governments like that are never good,” he says. “It's dancing in two weddings.” Besides, he adds, “It won’t fulfill my dreams.”
What Ben-Gvir wants from another Netanyahu government would place him at odds with the diplomatic framework advanced by the Trump Administration and its partners in Europe and the Arab world. The American-led Board of Peace envisions Gaza’s reconstruction under Palestinian leadership, the withdrawal of Israeli forces, and a possible path toward Palestinian statehood.
Ben-Gvir, on the other hand, wants Israeli sovereignty and the departure of much of Gaza’s Palestinian population. He cites polling that he says shows 52% of Gazans want to leave the territory, devastated by years of war and Hamas rule. If Israel helps that majority leave, he reasons, those who remain will eventually want to follow. “They will see it is successful for them, they’ll see there’s a future, there’s a life,” he says. “There’s good places in the world. Pretty places.” He offers no evidence that the remaining population would choose to relocate, or how such a migration could be arranged without coercion.
For Ben-Gvir and his allies, the coming election offers a chance to advance a far-reaching transformation of Israeli politics and society—to move the country toward a maximalist vision of a Jewish state, one with expanded territorial ambitions, fewer judicial constraints, and a government less inclined to heed international objections. Ben-Gvir dismisses concerns that such policies would cement Israel’s status as a pariah state. In his telling, the military campaigns against Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran demonstrate the value of uncompromising power. “We made Israel stronger,” he says. “When Israel is stronger, the world respects that.”
– With reporting by Liam Forberg

articles.title: Tanker with 21 Indian sailors struck in Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
21 Indian sailors stranded on Hormuz tanker
A Kuwait-flagged tanker carrying 21 Indian seafarers was struck by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, the second time the ship was attacked in less than two months. All crew members were reported to be safe following the attack.
The oil-products tanker MT Al Dasma was hit about 11 nautical miles west of Bukha, Oman, sparking a fire that was later extinguished. The vessel remained stationary following the strike, according to maritime security reports.
India is monitoring the situation and remains in contact with the ship’s management company to ensure the crew’s safety, Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said on Wednesday.
“All 21 of our Indian crew members, along with the rest of the crew are completely safe,” Sonowal posted on X.
⚠️ IMPORTANT UPDATE ⚠️ On Oct 21, Kuwait-flagged oil product tanker M/T AL DASMA, carrying 21 Indian seafarers, was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz. All 21 of our Indian crew members, along with the rest of the crew are completely safe. We are continuously monitoring the situation and remain in close contact with the ship management company to ensure the ongoing security and wellbeing of our seafarers.
— Sarbananda Sonowal (@sarbanandsonwal) October 21, 2026
The tanker was previously attacked on September 7, southeast of the Strait of Hormuz, according to the International Maritime Organization (IMO). The vessel was damaged in both incidents, with no pollution reported.
Indian crews have been caught in several recent attacks on commercial ships in the Middle East. On October 16, the tanker MT ST 3, carrying 15 Indian seafarers, was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz. All crew members were reported safe.
Five days earlier, two Indian sailors were reported missing after the tanker MT Petro Dolphin was struck near Oman. Another tanker, MT Valthera, was hit the same day, but all 11 Indian seafarers aboard were unharmed.
The Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao also sank near the strait on October 14, weeks after an attack killed an Indian seafarer.
The IMO had recorded 119 confirmed maritime incidents and 24 seafarer deaths across the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East as of October 21.
Meanwhile, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said Thursday that four vessels allegedly involved in illegal oil transfers were struck and caught fire in the northern Persian Gulf on Wednesday.
Three more vessels struck mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, the IRGC claimed, warning that continued US military provocations could trigger a wider response against American bases in the region, Reuters reported. The Iranian statement did not identify Al Dasma or establish a connection to its attack.
New Delhi previously condemned the recurring attacks on commercial shipping and called for immediate de-escalation through dialogue and diplomacy.
“Attacks on commercial vessels, seafarers and civilian infrastructure must cease,” India’s Foreign Ministry said on October 11, stressing the need to protect freedom of navigation and the uninterrupted flow of maritime commerce.

articles.title: Poland fumes as Ukrainian city celebrates ‘architect of genocide’
articles.body:
Poland fumes as Ukrainian city celebrates ‘architect of genocide’
Poland has accused Kiev of making unacceptable “suicidal” moves after the Ukrainian city of Lviv dedicated 2027 to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and its leader, Nazi collaborator Roman Shukhevich.
To celebrate the 120th anniversary of Shukhevich’s birth and mark 85 years since the creation of the militant group that perpetrated mass killings of ethnic Poles, Jews, and Russians, the Lviv Regional Council decided on Tuesday to organize “cultural, memorial, scientific, and mass media events,” as well as exhibitions and national-patriotic rallies.
The announcement was met with widespread condemnation in Poland, which regards the UPA as perpetrators of genocide against Poles in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia and its leader, Shukhevich, as a key ‘architect’ of the massacres. From 1943 to 1945, Ukrainian nationalist militants murdered an estimated 100,000 ethnic Poles in the regions, which are now largely part of modern Ukraine.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the move a “suicidal tactic,” and Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz called it “unacceptable.” Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski condemned the announcement, calling for the resolution’s key sponsor, Lviv regional lawmaker Svyatoslav Sheremet, to be placed on Poland’s travel ban list.
The Ukrainian Foreign Ministry attempted to downplay the incident, blaming the Lviv regional authorities for making the “harmful decision.” The ministry also said the regional council did not consult any central authorities regarding “the consequences of their actions for bilateral relations with Poland.”
The resolution ultimately vanished from the Lviv council’s website without any explanation. Speaking to Polish media on Wednesday, Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki said Warsaw received assurances from Kiev that the resolution would not be implemented.
“We take on faith the words of the administration of Vladimir Zelensky that this catastrophic decision will not be implemented,” Bosacki stated, calling the disappearance of the resolution from the council’s website a “good sign,” but cautioning against interpreting it as an official cancellation of the celebrations.
Ukraine’s increasingly open honoring of WWII-era nationalists and Nazi collaborators has drawn criticism from Warsaw, which remains one of Ukraine’s key backers in the conflict with Russia.
Poland regards the UPA and the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), which collaborated with Nazi Germany during the early stages of its 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union, as perpetrators of genocide, while modern Ukraine cherishes them as freedom fighters and national heroes.
Earlier this year, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky named a military unit after the ‘Heroes of the UPA’ and established a ‘pantheon of outstanding Ukrainians’ at Kiev’s main military cemetery, where OUN leader and Nazi collaborator Andrey Melnik was reinterred with state honors in May.

articles.title: British drone downs attack drones with guided rockets
articles.body:
A modified version of the Malloy Aeronautics T-150 uncrewed air system has intercepted multiple one-way attack drones during an American experiment in Florida, firing laser-guided rockets from a three-pod launcher and engaging several targets in succession without landing or reloading, according to BAE Systems.
The trials ran from 21 to 25 September at Eglin Air Force Base during the United States Office of the Under Secretary for Research and Engineering’s Mission Capabilities Joint Readiness Experimentation exercise. BAE Systems conducted them alongside SURVICE Engineering, its Maryland-based partner, using BAE’s own APKWS laser-guided rockets.
Thomas Lancashire, Head of UAS Business Development at BAE Systems’ FalconWorks, said: “Our customers are facing drone threats right now, so we’ve worked at pace with our partners to move from concept to a proven system, which can engage multiple targets in a single mission.
“Military technology is evolving faster than ever and it’s vital that effective capabilities reach those who protect us as quickly as possible. In today’s environment, the speed at which we deliver equipment can be just as important as the system itself.”
Gregory Thompson, President of SURVICE, said: “Supporting the warfighter has been at the core of SURVICE’s mission since its founding over 45 years ago. Bringing the TRV-150 to the US warfighter and now adding APKWS as a proven, precise, and cost-effective capability to our TRV-150 UAS platform is exactly the type of innovation SURVICE was designed to deliver.”
The aircraft is a heavy-lift electric multirotor built by Malloy Aeronautics at Maidenhead in Berkshire, a company BAE Systems took a stake in during 2019 and acquired outright in 2024. The version flown in Florida, designated TRV-150, was adapted to United States Army requirements by SURVICE Engineering, and the APKWS modification kit was developed and integrated by BAE Systems FalconWorks.
APKWS is a laser guidance kit that converts the seventy millimetre Hydra rocket into a precision weapon, built by BAE Systems in New Hampshire. United States Navy and Air Force fighters used it against Houthi drones over the Red Sea in 2024 and 2025, at a unit cost well below that of an air-to-air missile.
BAE Systems said the September trials build on the first firing of a precision munition from an adapted T-150 in July last year, which was a single shot, and that the launcher used in Florida is a production-ready three-pod system.
The T-150 has already served with Britain’s forces in the logistics role. The Royal Navy cleared the Malloy T-150 for front line use and conducted its first drone supply run between warships, and the type carried stores between ships throughout the Prince of Wales carrier strike group’s eight-month Indo-Pacific deployment last year, which this publication covered when drones launched from the British carrier in the Pacific.
Malloy also builds the larger T-650, developed with Royal Navy and Defence Equipment and Support involvement as a heavy-lift aircraft able to carry loads including torpedoes.
BAE Systems said the team will now look to extend the T-150’s use in this role to the maritime environment. The company noted that the imagery released with the announcement comes from an earlier trial.

articles.title: As Russia penalises European firms over Ukraine, US rivals largely spared
articles.body:
As Russia penalises European firms over Ukraine, US rivals largely spared
MOSCOW, Oct 21 - Russia has deepened a crackdown on European companies in response to Europe's support for Ukraine, while largely sparing US firms as Moscow courts business ties with Washington, Russian officials and US business people said.
Of 20 foreign-owned firms that Russian President Vladimir Putin has placed under temporary administration since Donald Trump's inauguration as US president in January 2025, only three were linked to the US, with the remainder controlled by European companies, a Reuters analysis of official data shows.
A person close to Russian financial regulators said that while business negotiations were underway with Washington, it was not in Moscow's interest to take as tough a line on US firms as the Kremlin was adopting towards those from Europe.
US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday for talks aimed at resolving the war in Ukraine. Russian news agencies reported Putin told Witkoff he was interested in restoring economic ties with the United States.
Ukraine and its allies have voiced concerns that the US is backing away from Kyiv, and Trump has criticized Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries even as European leaders have lined up behind Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy.
Russia, citing Europe's wartime support for Ukraine and involvement in "direct battlefield hostilities", has since last month taken control of local units of Swiss food group Nestle and retailers Auchan and Metro.
Last week it seized control of the local assets of four smaller companies from France, Germany, Sweden and Belgium.
"Their country of origin was one of the factors taken into account in making the decision," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, adding that these countries were involved in "illegal expropriations of Russian property".
Nestle, which said in September it would take steps to protect its rights in Russia, declined to comment further. The other companies did not respond to requests for comment.
A spokesperson for Switzerland's State Secretariat for Economic Affairs said that the available information supported the perception that more European than US firms were being hit.
The Kremlin declined to comment on how it was treating US and European companies in Russia, while the White House did not respond to a request for comment.
'WE HAVE TRUMP'
Russia's relations with the Trump administration, meanwhile, have warmed. The US announced a deal this month to buy Russian diesel and other deals, including on gas, have been discussed at meetings in recent months. Trump signed an executive order on Saturday waiving key sanctions and tariffs on Russian goods.
Russian negotiator Kirill Dmitriev, a US-educated investment banker who heads the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) and has pushed in talks for the return and expansion of US firms, hailed the move as a "historic moment".
Trump's envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner have used the prospect of multibillion-dollar deals with Russia as an incentive to push Putin toward a peaceful settlement since the start of talks in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, in February 2025.
Dmitriev said last week Russia and the US would soon announce new joint initiatives that could move ahead before the war ends. The US has previously signalled that deals are unlikely while the conflict continues.
One person familiar with the situation said that some Russian officials who do not support peace efforts could yet push for the Kremlin's actions to include more US companies.
The RDIF's only current partnership with a US company is a joint investment with New York-listed Titan International in a tyre factory in Volgograd.
Another person familiar with the situation said Dmitriev has in private highlighted this as an example of a thriving US business in Russia.
Titan did not respond to a request for comment.
Trump's commitment to economic cooperation with Russia and ongoing talks have helped to protect the interests of US companies, two US business people in Moscow said.
American Chamber of Commerce Russia President Robert Agee said in December last year that European firms in Russia were less optimistic than American ones, citing European policy. The chamber estimates there are some 300 US firms left in Russia.
"We have Trump and they don't, and our hopes are linked to him," Agee told Russian media last year. Agee and the chamber declined to comment further for this story.
Russia did target some mid-sized US firms during its property redistribution drive after the start of the war. One report estimated Moscow seized more than $50 billion worth of private property from both Russian and foreign owners.
The European Commission in Brussels declined to comment on the number of EU firms being targeted relative to US ones, but said the recent asset seizures were without due process and amounted to "forced expropriation in all but name".
"This follows a clear pattern of economic retaliation," a Commission spokesperson told Reuters, adding that the moves showed that "Russia is not a safe environment for business".
"The EU has measures in place to respond. We can sanction those profiting from forced expropriations," they added. REUTERS

articles.title: Who are the Americans detained in Russia?
articles.body:
Who are the Americans detained in Russia?
Oct 22 - Russia freed Stephen Hubbard, a retired US schoolteacher, from prison on Wednesday, as Moscow and Washington held a new round of talks about settling the war in Ukraine.
At least nine publicly identified Americans are believed to remain imprisoned in Russia, although the full number may be higher.
While Hubbard was in prison, the US State Department formally designated him as wrongfully detained, a status that placed his case under a dedicated US government process for securing his release. Other imprisoned Americans lack that designation, potentially reducing the scope for efforts to free them.
Here are details on some of the cases:
ALEKSANDR ANTONOV
A US-Russian-Ukrainian citizen, Antonov was detained at passport control in Russia in spring 2025 after travelling to attend to business in Russian-controlled Crimea and family in Ukraine.
He was later sentenced to six years in a prison colony on charges of inciting terrorism and extremism, based on pro-Ukrainian comments posted online. He pleaded guilty.
CHUCK ZIMMERMAN
Zimmerman, a US Navy veteran, was intercepted in June 2025 by the Russian Navy as he sailed on the Black Sea during a round-the-world sailing trip, according to his family. He was charged with arms smuggling after a rifle was found on board his boat.
He was sentenced in late 2025 to five years in prison, according to a verdict published in January.
GORDON BLACK
An active duty US Army staff sergeant formerly based in South Korea, Black was detained in May 2024 in Russia's Far East on suspicion of stealing money from his Russian girlfriend.
A court found Black guilty of stealing 10,000 roubles ($123) from the woman and threatening to kill her, sentencing him to three years and nine months in prison. The sentence was reduced by seven months in 2025, following an appeal.
US officials have said the Army has stopped paying Black's wages and may prosecute him for violating its rules if he returns to the US.
DANIEL JOSEPH SCHNEIDER
A court in Kaliningrad region sentenced Schneider to six years in prison in September 2024 for kidnapping his own son, after he tried to leave Russia with the 4-year-old without permission from the boy's mother.
Schneider was detained near Poland by Russia's border service while trying to cross the border in a forest swamp, the court said.
MICHAEL TRAVIS LEAKE
A musician and former US serviceman, Leake was sentenced to 13 years in prison in July 2024 on drug-related charges.
Leake pleaded not guilty following his arrest in June 2023.
ROBERT ROMANOV WOODLAND
A US citizen adopted from Russia as a child, Woodland had moved back to Russia and was working as an English teacher when he was arrested on charges of attempting to sell drugs.
He was sentenced in July 2024 to 12 years and six months in prison. His lawyer said Woodland had partially admitted guilt. In 2025, a court reduced his sentence to nine years and six months.
EUGENE SPECTOR
A Russian-born US citizen and former pharmaceutical executive, Spector was convicted of espionage in a closed trial and sentenced in late 2024 to 15 years in a penal colony. He was first arrested in 2020 on bribery charges.
Before his arrest, Spector served as chairman of the board of Medpolymerprom Group, a company specialising in cancer drugs, state media said. He had pleaded guilty to helping bribe an assistant to a former Russian deputy prime minister. It was not clear how he pleaded to the espionage charge.
DAVID BARNES
Barnes was sentenced by a Russian court in February 2024 to 21 years on charges of abusing his two sons in the United States. Barnes, who had been involved in a custody dispute with his Russian ex-wife, denied all the charges.
The allegations had previously been investigated in Texas, where authorities found no grounds to charge him. In 2025, a court increased his sentence by six months.
ANDRE KHACHATOORIAN
An Armenian-American from Los Angeles, Khachatoorian was sentenced to eight years in prison in 2023 for arms smuggling. He was arrested in 2021, while travelling from California to Armenia via Moscow, after a firearm was found in his luggage.
Khachatoorian said that his firearm was legally owned in the US, and that he was tricked into applying for a Russian visa at the airport, and removed from the transit zone, where he could be arrested under Russian law. REUTERS

articles.title: Putin, Xi and Trump could hold ‘historic summit’ – Kremlin
articles.body:
Putin, Xi and Trump could hold ‘historic summit’ – Kremlin
Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump could hold a “historic” three-way meeting at the APEC summit in China, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov has said.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit is scheduled to take place in Shenzhen, China, on November 18-19.
Speaking to the Russian outlet Vesti on Wednesday, Ushakov said Beijing had already begun preparations for the potential talks. 
“Everyone is ready for this, but much, if not everything, depends on the Chinese hosts of the summit,” he said.
The possibility of three-way talks was also discussed during Putin’s meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, according to the Kremlin.
Ushakov described the proposed gathering as potentially “historic,” noting that it would be the first meeting of the three leaders in this format.
Putin and Trump last met in person at a summit in Anchorage, Alaska, in August 2025, and have remained in contact by phone, most recently on October 9.
Putin and Xi have also held regular talks, including on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek in August. The two previously met in Beijing in May during Putin’s state visit.
Trump and Xi have met twice so far this year, first in Beijing in May and then at the White House last month.
Trump has previously expressed openness to three-way talks, suggesting that nuclear disarmament could be among the issues discussed.
Asked whether the talks could also contribute to peace efforts in the Ukraine conflict, Ushakov said a single meeting would not be enough. “Even if the meeting lasts one, two or five hours, it still won’t be possible to resolve all the problems,” he said.
Commenting on whether the summit could amount to a “new Yalta,” Ushakov said: “I think that if the meeting takes place, there will be a storm of comments and assessments.”
The 1945 Yalta Conference brought together Soviet leader Joseph Stalin, US President Franklin D. Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill to discuss the final stages of World War II and the postwar international order.

articles.title: S. Korea urges DPRK to return to dialogue
articles.body:
SEOUL, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's defense ministry on Thursday urged the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) to return to the dialogue table to prevent accidental border clashes.
"To bridge the gap in perception and prevent accidental military clashes, North Korea (DPRK) must step forward to the dialogue table, and these actions must come to a halt," Defense Ministry spokesperson Chung Binna told a press briefing.
Chung emphasized that the current reliance on public statements between the two Koreas indicated that all official inter-Korean military hotlines were completely severed.
The call came as tensions flared over cross-border psychological warfare.
Kim Yo Jong, department director of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea of the DPRK, said in a statement Wednesday that her country will use loudspeakers for psychological warfare against South Korea along the border this month.
Kim accused Seoul of committing "provocative warning loudspeaker blaring and shots again in at least two spots" on Wednesday. ■

articles.title: Putin and Witkoff discuss resumption of trilateral talks on Ukraine — Kremlin aide
articles.body:
ST. PETERSBURG, October 21. /TASS/. During the meeting, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff have specifically discussed a plan for a possible resumption of talks with the participation of Russia, the United States and Ukraine, Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov said.
"It is important to note that the scheme of a possible resumption of trilateral negotiations with the participation of representatives of Russia, the United States and Ukraine was specifically discussed," Ushakov told reporters.
"It is important to note that the scheme of a possible resumption of trilateral negotiations with the participation of representatives of Russia, the United States and Ukraine was specifically discussed," Ushakov said.
"Their planned resumption immediately after the State Duma elections, as is known, was disrupted by the Ukrainian regime, having inflicted super-massive strikes on the main day of voting on Moscow, other cities, polling stations and directly on the election commission employees, some of whom died."

articles.title: Germany arrests Ukrainian national under suspicion of spying for Russia
articles.body:
A Ukrainian national was arrested in the German state of Brandenburg on suspicion of spying for Russia, a statement by federal public prosecutors said on Thursday.
Prosecutors said the person, identified as Vadym Y., had been in contact with a Russian secret service via an intermediary since July 2025 at the latest.
The person was gathering military intelligence, including information on the production of armored vehicles, ammunition and explosives, as well as personnel and military installations at locations designed to secure NATO’s eastern flank, they said.
While some of the information was publicly available, other details were solicited from individuals in the European defense industry, they said.
Accused to appear before judge on Friday
According to the statement, the accused will appear before the investigating judge at the Federal Court of Justice tomorrow, who will serve him with the arrest warrant and decide on the enforcement of pre-trial detention.
German media first reported the news.

articles.title: Britain near bottom of NATO rearmament table
articles.body:
Britain stands thirty-first out of thirty-two NATO countries on an internal alliance measure of how effectively members are meeting their rearmament promises, with only Iceland lower, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, sets the figure against the government’s Defence Investment Plan and the warning that Russia could attack NATO as soon as 2030.
Dhesi said: “And if the UK government means what it says – that Russia could attack NATO as soon as 2030 – then work to rectify these vulnerabilities cannot start soon enough.”
The report states: “However, the current reality could hardly be bleaker. According to an internal document apparently drawn up by NATO to measure how effectively members are meeting their rearmament promises, the UK is number 31 out of 32 Alliance countries. Only Iceland, a country with no military capability, is lower on the table.”
Ed Arnold, senior research fellow for European security at the Royal United Services Institute, told the committee: “[s]o that’s a pretty poor position to be in… [a]nd the only way that you can increase that really is through cash because it’s all about fleet availability, it’s all about readiness to be out of the door as soon as possible and as soon as needed.”
The Defence Investment Plan published in June splits funding into two parts, investing £298 billion in the four years to 2029-30 to reach 2.7 per cent of national income spent on defence, and a period running to 2035 by which all NATO allies including Britain have committed to spending 3.5 per cent of national income on defence.
Sir Keir Starmer, then Prime Minister, said in June this year that it was the British intelligence assessment, and the assessment of other NATO countries, that there could be an attack by Russia on NATO as soon as 2030.
The committee concludes that the near £300 billion investment over the next four years represents the bedrock on which any British contribution to deterring or defeating Russian hostility against NATO from 2030 rests, and that the Ministry of Defence needs to enhance the readiness of existing military assets as well as investing in new capabilities.
A separate conclusion states: “Government is already investing in the Hybrid Navy and Atlantic Bastion concepts to deter and, if necessary, defeat those threats in the High North. However, Royal Navy equipment readiness and platform numbers in particular are currently far worse than the government’s stated requirements. With 2030 identified as a key date by which to be ready to deter or defeat any Russian threat, dramatic progress is required before the end of the decade to improve the availability and capabilities of the UK’s Armed Forces for operations in the High North.”
In evidence to the inquiry the Ministry of Defence said capabilities are held at varying levels of readiness, that every platform goes through a cycle of deployment, maintenance, training and preparation, and that equipment is held at different readiness depending on the capability it is required to meet for NATO.

articles.title: Base security boosted after Fairford and Molesworth breaches
articles.body:
An additional £470 million over four years will go into protecting defence sites, with security strengthened across the estate following the incidents at RAF Fairford and RAF Molesworth and work under way to extend restricted airspace protections around military bases, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Andrew Rosindell, the Reform UK member for Romford, asked what steps the Secretary of State has taken to ensure the security of military bases.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “We remain highly vigilant to threats against Defence sites and have strengthened security across the estate following the incidents at RAF Fairford and RAF Molesworth. Recent arrests demonstrate that those who seek to compromise the security of Defence sites can expect a robust security and police response. Where criminal offences are suspected, we won’t hesitate to use the full range of powers available, including the National Security Act.
“The Defence Investment Plan provides an additional £470 million over four years to enhance site protection and reduce legacy underspending. Defence has invested in surveillance and counter-drone capabilities and is working to extend Restricted Airspace protections around Defence sites.”
Counter terrorism police arrested two Latvian nationals inside the perimeter at RAF Molesworth earlier this month, at a site in Cambridgeshire that houses American and NATO intelligence functions, and the pair were later bailed. The Fairford incident involved the Gloucestershire base that hosts United States Air Force bomber deployments to Europe and has been used for B-2 and B-52 rotations.
Perimeter fencing, lighting, access control and surveillance across hundreds of sites have competed for funding against front line equipment for years, and the new money corrects an underspend that built up over that period. Spread across four years and the whole estate, £470 million is modest.

articles.title: DARPA wants smart nuclear reactor for space and bases
articles.body:
- DARPA awarded SpaceNukes an agreement to ground-test a Kilopower nuclear reactor with active, autonomous control rods under its Fat Cat program.
- The team behind the 2018 KRUSTY reactor test will run the new test with Los Alamos National Laboratory.
The Pentagon’s top research agency wants a nuclear reactor that can run itself, and it has hired the team that built America’s last space reactor to prove it can be done. DARPA has awarded Space Nuclear Power Corporation, a small Los Alamos, New Mexico, company known as SpaceNukes, an agreement to build a Kilopower reactor with self-adjusting control rods and switch it on in a full nuclear ground test, the company announced on Oct. 21.
DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, was created in 1958 after the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, with a mandate to make sure the United States would never again be caught off guard by a rival’s technology. The agency does not build weapons itself; it funds high-risk ideas that the military services and industry consider too uncertain to pay for, and its bets have included the ARPANET network that grew into the internet and early stealth aircraft research. The new work falls under a DARPA program called Fast Capacitance, or Fat Cat, run by program manager Tabitha Dodson in the agency’s Defense Sciences Office, which is looking for ways to let reactors operate on their own for national security missions.
The reactor at the center of the project has already worked once. Between November 2017 and March 2018, engineers from Los Alamos National Laboratory and NASA ran a test called KRUSTY, short for Kilopower Reactor Using Stirling Technology, at the Nevada National Security Site, powering up a reactor built around a solid cast uranium-235 core about the size of a paper towel roll. Sodium heat pipes carried heat from the core to Stirling engines that turned it into electricity, and the reactor ran at full power for about 28 hours while engineers deliberately cut power, shut down engines and disabled heat pipes to see whether it would keep going, which it did.
That test used a passive design, in which the reactor’s own physics kept it stable without moving parts adjusting the reaction. The new version will add active control rods that move to raise or lower the reactor’s output, giving it the ability to change power on demand and respond quickly to shifting needs, which SpaceNukes says opens the technology to a much wider range of missions. A reactor that manages itself matters most in places where no operator can reach it quickly, such as a spacecraft, a base on the Moon or a remote military outpost, where power needs can change suddenly and a human may be minutes or hours away.
“There is no substitute for demonstrated technology when American national security objectives are at stake,” said Andy Phelps, CEO of SpaceNukes. “This award lets us advance the work begun in the KRUSTY program and bring another tested capability forward for the nation.”
SpaceNukes is essentially the KRUSTY team reassembled as a company. Chief technology officer David Poston and chief operating officer Patrick McClure led the reactor work at Los Alamos, chief engineer Marc Gibson ran the program at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, and the company holds a license from Los Alamos for the Kilopower design. Gibson will lead integration of the new test hardware at the company’s workshop in Medina, Ohio, and the program will move through design, procurement and integration stages before the reactor goes critical in a joint test with Los Alamos.
“This award recognizes the maturity and continuity of the team that designed, built, and tested KRUSTY in 2018,” said Patrick McClure, chief operating officer of SpaceNukes.
The project lands as Washington is pushing hard to get reactors into space and onto military bases. A White House policy memo in April directed the Pentagon and NASA to compete designs for space reactors, with an orbital demonstration targeted as early as 2028 and a reactor on the Moon as early as 2030, while on the ground the U.S. Army has committed up to $2.2 billion to build nuclear microreactors at five military bases. The KRUSTY reactor was designed to deliver between 1 and 10 kilowatts of electricity continuously for at least a decade, and the DARPA test will produce flight-relevant hardware that has actually been run on nuclear power, along with the engineering basis for reactors that can control themselves.

articles.title: British forces board German warship by air and sea
articles.body:
Royal Marines boarded the German support ship FGS Berlin by air and by sea during Exercise Strike Warrior, fast-roping from a Merlin helicopter while a second team climbed from a rigid inflatable boat, according to Defence Operations.
The post said the commandos were “making an entrance the commando way” and had boarded the vessel “sharpening their skills alongside NATO allies”, adding: “Training together to defend together.”
⚓ Making an entrance the commando way@RoyalMarines boarded German warship FGS Berlin by air and sea during Exercise Strike Warrior, sharpening their skills alongside @NATO allies.
🛡️Training together to defend together.#ExStrikeWarrior #SW26 pic.twitter.com/F2D1ya5Mhf
— Defence Operations 🇬🇧 (@DefenceOps) October 21, 2026
FGS Berlin is the lead ship of the German Navy’s Berlin class replenishment vessels and was serving as flagship of Standing NATO Maritime Group One, the alliance’s permanent naval force in northern European waters, which is currently under French command.
The boarding was carried out by personnel from K Company, 42 Commando, the Royal Marines unit that specialises in maritime interdiction. One team went up the ship’s side from a rigid inflatable boat using caving ladders, a physically demanding method in strong winds but one that preserves surprise, while another fast-roped onto the deck from a Merlin of 824 Naval Air Squadron, which is quicker but noisier.
Once aboard, the teams cleared the ship compartment by compartment carrying short-barrelled L119A1 rifles, prioritising the bridge and control rooms. A simulated casualty allowed commando and Royal Navy personnel to rehearse evacuating a wounded man from inside a ship.
Exercise Strike Warrior ran from 28 September to 9 October and involved more than two thousand personnel, eight warships and nineteen aircraft across Cape Wrath, the Western Isles, the North-West Approaches, Galloway, the Borders and the North Sea. The Royal Navy describes it as the largest test of the United Kingdom Commando Force in fifteen years, and the first time since the war in Afghanistan that all of its specialist elements have trained together.
The exercise rehearses allied crisis-response operations in the High North and the North Atlantic. Alongside Britain it drew in forces from the Netherlands, Canada, Germany, Norway and the United States, with the Portuguese frigate NRP Dom Francisco de Almeida, the Dutch frigate HNLMS Van Amstel and the Royal Canadian Navy frigate HMCS St John’s taking part.
Elsewhere in the exercise, soldiers of 148 (Meiktila) Commando Forward Observation Battery were carried to the Scottish coast aboard the German submarine U36, a Type 212A boat, before going ashore near Cape Wrath to direct naval gunfire from Portuguese, Dutch and Canadian warships onto simulated targets.
This publication reported when NATO warships arrived in Glasgow ahead of Strike Warrior and when Merlin helicopters headed to Scotland to protect the submarine force.

articles.title: U.S. Air Force tests shipping military cargo by rocket
articles.body:
- The Air Force Research Laboratory flew cargo pods aboard a SpaceX Starfall capsule on Oct. 20 to test rocket delivery of military supplies.
- The pods carried survival gear, medical equipment and trackers, with sensors measuring heat, shock and vibration during launch and reentry.
The U.S. Air Force has sent military-style cargo into space and back aboard a SpaceX Starfall capsule as it tests whether rockets could one day deliver supplies to troops anywhere on Earth within hours.
The Air Force Research Laboratory flew its own cargo pods inside the capsule on a commercial rideshare launch from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Oct. 20, packing them with satellite trackers, batteries, survival gear, a water desalinator and emergency medical equipment to see how they would hold up through launch, spaceflight and the plunge back through the atmosphere.
The flight was part of Rocket Cargo, an AFRL project studying whether large commercial rockets can move materiel around the world on tactical timelines, and the capsule carried sensors that recorded the temperature, shock and vibration the cargo experienced along the way. Engineers paid particular attention to how electronics and survival equipment came through the ride, and they also checked whether a UNI-PAC III life raft would fit inside the capsule for future tests, which hints at missions such as dropping rescue kits to downed aircrew or stranded sailors far from any base.
“Any day you launch a rocket is a good day, but today was more than just another big rocket launch,” said Brig. Gen. Douglas P. Wickert, Department of the Air Force Technology Executive Officer and AFRL commander. “Today’s launch was another demonstration of how AFRL is partnering with industry to burn down risk, collect hard data and deliver war-winning technologies for the operational force.”
Starfall is SpaceX’s new uncrewed reentry capsule, a squat disk about 3.1 meters (10 feet) across that weighs roughly 2,100 kg (4,600 pounds) and can bring back up to 1,000 kg (2,200 pounds) of payload under parachutes, with recovery planned in the Pacific Ocean. SpaceX flew the first Starfall demonstration in June, and regulatory documents describe the capsule as a way to support both rapid point-to-point cargo delivery and a commercial market for products made in orbit and returned to Earth.
The Air Force’s ambitions for Rocket Cargo are much bigger than a single capsule, since AFRL says the concept stands apart from other fast-delivery efforts because a large rocket could carry tens of tons per launch to places with no runways or roads. The service has said it wants rocket-delivered cargo to reach almost any point on Earth within about an hour and a half and eventually to move loads comparable to a C-17 transport, and in June it awarded Colorado-based Geneva Technologies $4.3 million to help design the rocket cargo system.
AFRL sees uses ranging from resupplying forces in contested areas and expeditionary operations to rescue missions, disaster relief and responding to chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear incidents, and it is working with a long list of companies to get there, including SpaceX, Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, Sierra Space, Anduril, Inversion Space and Outpost Space. In August, the Air Force expanded Blue Origin’s role in the program with a study contract now worth about $13 million.
“This was a critical achievement to demonstrate the potential of Rocket Cargo delivery for point-to-point rapid global mobility for the Future Force,” said Adam Remaly, director of the AFRL Technology Transition Office.
AFRL plans further tests with commercial rockets and reentry capsules as it gathers data on how cargo survives the trip, and it is also looking at how the military could benefit from commercial investment in capsules built to return products manufactured in space.

articles.title: Ukraine ready to freeze war along current front line: Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukraine is ready to freeze the conflict along the current front line and pursue diplomatic negotiations to end the war with Russia.
Speaking to Fox News on Wednesday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine would expect a ceasefire as the minimum from Russia, after which Kiev would seek security guarantees from the US and European countries.
“Yes. Right now we have to freeze, and I think this is a real way to end this war,” he said.
He said Kiev would then approach the US president and European leaders to seek security guarantees, stressing that peace and security were the most important priorities.
Asked whether Ukraine would surrender the Donbas region in exchange for an end to the war, Zelenskyy said Ukrainians were tired of the fighting but could not simply abandon their land.
He rejected suggestions that Russia was winning on the battlefield, saying Moscow was trying to pressure Kiev into withdrawing from its territory.
“In 2026, they didn't have success. They are not winning on the battlefield,” he said.
He reiterated that negotiations should begin from the current positions on the battlefield, with a peace plan to be developed through diplomacy.
Steps towards a ceasefire
Zelenskyy also described his meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo, Norway, on Tuesday as “productive”.
He thanked Norway’s prime minister for hosting the talks, which also involved European leaders and US officials, including Jared Kushner, who joined remotely.
The discussions focused on possible steps towards peace, Zelenskyy said, expressing hope that Witkoff’s meeting in Russia would provide further feedback.
He said initial steps towards de-escalation could include ceasefires covering food security, maritime activity and energy infrastructure.
Zelenskyy added that he had immediately backed US President Donald Trump’s proposal for an energy ceasefire.
“I hope that today, in some hours, we will have some results,” he said.

articles.title: Ukraine loses at least $1 mln worth of drones amid Starshield disruptions — newspaper
articles.body:
NEW YORK, October 21. /TASS/. The Ukrainian army lost dozens of drones worth at least $1 million due to restrictions on the Starshield military-grade satellite system in Ukraine, The New York Times reported.
A Ukrainian military commander told the newspaper that Starshield disruptions had forced the army to halt almost all operations for three days. The first reports of satellite communication problems emerged on October 14.
"Ukrainian officials fear that the Trump administration ordered the disruptions to punish Ukraine over its strikes on Russian oil refineries," the paper noted.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier, citing sources, that Elon Musk had ordered the slowdown of Starshield for Ukraine. The sources said that Musk and US President Donadl Trump and Musk had expressed anger at Ukraine for attacking Russian oil refineries. "Last week, Musk capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network, the people said, rendering some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless," The Wall Street Journal wrote. "Some US officials say that Musk acted unilaterally and that Trump didn’t specifically order any retribution against Ukraine," the paper added. However, one source said that Musk had talked to multiple senior administration officials, including Trump, before imposing the new speed cap.

articles.body:

The prime ministers of Poland and India have, after a meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies.
Donald Tusk’s visit, the first by a Polish prime minister to India in 16 years, follows the upgrading of bilateral ties between the two countries to a strategic partnership during Narendra Modi trip to Poland two years ago, which was the first by an Indian prime minister in almost five decades.
During a joint press conference with Tusk on Thursday, Modi said that his Warsaw visit had acted as a catalyst for the Polish-Indian relationship to “gain speed over the last two years”.
📍 New Delhi | Premier @donaldtusk spotkał się z Premierem Indii @narendramodi. pic.twitter.com/Y9HPLQsvf4
— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 22, 2026
Tusk added the two leaders had now reviewed the results of their cooperation so far and outlined priorities for the coming years. They discussed, among other things, ways to deepen economic, investment and technological ties between the two fast-growing economies.
Poland’s GDP is set to grow by 3.5% this year, the second-fastest rate in the European Union, while India will see economic growth of 7%. Poland’s economy is also on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to join the G20.
“The economic strength of both countries offers a wealth of opportunities for strategic partnership,” Modi said.
Tusk, meanwhile, underlined that “Poland and India are countries that have much in common and nothing that divides them…[with] no conflicting interests or historical grievances.”
Poland hopes that the boost to bilateral trade will come from an EU-India trade deal expected to be signed in December. The agreement is designed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on goods accounting for 96.6% of the value of EU exports to the Indian market.
Tusk said Poland wanted to capitalise on the opportunities created by the deal, with the ambition of becoming “India’s gateway to Europe”. Modi expressed confidence that Poland’s and India’s “shared goal” of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 “will certainly be achieved”.
“Today, trade between Poland and India totals just over $6 billion,” said Poland’s finance minister Andrzej Domański, who joined Tusk on the trip to India. “We want this trade to grow, and the conditions for that are very favourable.”
However, “it is no secret that we have a significant trade deficit with India”, Domański added. Last year, Poland exported goods worth €1.4 billion to India, with machinery, mineral products and metals the largest categories. Meanwhile, it imported €4.3 billion, in particular textiles, machinery and metals
The United States wants Poland to become a full member of the G20 "as soon as possible".
"Poland’s economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant," says the @StateDept https://t.co/OjpWly4FTw
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026
According to the Polish prime minister’s office, the EU-India agreement could also help increase Polish investment in India, particularly in advanced manufacturing, food processing, biotechnology and mobility.
To help facilitate such investments, Tusk travelled with almost 100 Polish business representatives, hoping the visit will help them to enter the large and rapidly growing Indian market. His office described the delegation as the largest of its kind in the history of Polish-Indian relations.
Modi said he was “particularly happy” with Tusk’s decision to bring a business delegation and announced plans to strengthen links between startups in both countries, including through technology hackathons for young people.
The countries plan to expand cooperation in critical minerals, raw materials and coal gasification, a process that converts coal into gas for energy and industrial use. Shipbuilding, defence, space and advanced technologies are also among the priority sectors.
Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS).
Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026
The leaders also highlighted historical ties and people-to-people exchanges as a foundation for closer relations.
Modi recalled the role of Indian Maharaja Jam Saheb Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji, known in Poland as the “Good Maharaja”, who provided shelter and care to around 1,000 Polish children evacuated from the Soviet Union during the Second World War.
“In 2022, Poland helped our Indian students, demonstrating that same spirit of humanity,” added Modi, referring to the support Poland provided to Indian students escaping from Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Modi said he hoped that the ongoing Jamsaheb Memorial Youth Exchange Programme, which recently took place for the second time, will “introduce the next generation to this Polish-Indian friendship”.
The strengthening of bilateral relations has also come amid a rapid rise in Indian migration to Poland in recent years. This year Indians became the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, numbering around 25,500, up almost 5% in a year.
