articles.title: Who is Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE nominee for UN General Secretary?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Who is Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE nominee for UN General Secretary?
The UAE has formally nominated veteran diplomat Lana Nusseibeh to become the next UN secretary-general, placing one of its most experienced international representatives in the race to succeed Antonio Guterres.
The nomination was submitted on Wednesday by UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in a letter to the presidents of the UN General Assembly and Security Council.
Nusseibeh, 48, is a former UAE ambassador to the UN who spent more than a decade in international diplomacy, including during the country's 2022-23 membership of the Security Council.
If successful, she would become the first woman to lead the UN and the second person from the Middle East and North Africa to hold the position, following Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
Who is Lana Nusseibeh?
Nusseibeh is the daughter of Zaki Nusseibeh, a senior Emirati presidential adviser who has served successive UAE leaders for decades. However, the Nusseibeh family are originally from Palestine and have longstanding connections to Jerusalem.
Her grandfather, Anwar Nusseibeh, was a prominent Palestinian politician and lawyer who served in senior government positions in Jordan.
She studied history at the University of Cambridge before obtaining a master's degree in Israeli and Jewish Diaspora Studies from the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS) in London.
Nusseibeh founded the UAE foreign ministry's Policy Planning Department in 2009, becoming its first director, and subsequently served as a joint special envoy to Afghanistan and Pakistan.
In September 2013, she became the first Emirati woman appointed as the country's permanent representative to the UN, a position she held until April 2024.
During her tenure, she served as president of the executive board of UN Women in 2017 and as a vice-president of the General Assembly. She also co-chaired negotiations concerning UN institutional reform.
Her most prominent diplomatic role came during the UAE's membership of the Security Council between 2022 and 2023, when she twice presided over the body.
During Israel's war on Gaza, Nusseibeh helped secure Security Council Resolution 2720 in December 2023, establishing a UN mechanism intended to facilitate humanitarian assistance to Palestinians.
She was also involved in securing resolutions condemning the Taliban's restrictions on Afghan women working for the UN and addressing the relationship between hate speech, discrimination and international security.
Following her departure from New York, she continued serving in senior positions within the UAE foreign ministry, becoming a minister of state in September 2025.
Can she become UN secretary-general?
Nusseibeh enters the contest as the organisation confronts financial pressures, questions over its effectiveness in responding to conflicts and growing divisions between major powers.
Her campaign programme, titled 'A United Nations for the Next Eighty Years', advocates strengthening conflict prevention, reducing institutional duplication and improving accountability.
Her extensive diplomatic experience could prove advantageous in a contest where leading candidates have struggled to secure the consensus required for appointment.
Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan, head of UN Trade and Development, and Argentina's Rafael Grossi, director-general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, are among her principal rivals.
However, Nusseibeh's candidacy could encounter geopolitical obstacles.
The UAE has faced serious allegations of supplying weapons and financial support to Sudan's Rapid Support Forces (RSF), whose members and allied militias were determined by the US in January 2025 to have committed genocide.
Amnesty International has documented weapons it believes reached the RSF through the UAE, while Abu Dhabi has consistently denied providing military support to either side in Sudan's war.
The controversy could complicate Nusseibeh's candidacy, although no evidence has been presented implicating her personally in the alleged arms transfers.
Regional rivalries, particularly the UAE's complicated relationship with Saudi Arabia, could also influence the contest, alongside expectations that the next secretary-general should come from Latin America.
Ultimately, her prospects will depend on securing at least nine Security Council votes without facing a veto from any of its five permanent members.
The successful candidate will take office on 1 January 2027, succeeding Guterres after two five-year terms.

articles.title: Some KC-135s Damaged by Iran Still in Depot: AFMC Boss
articles.body:
At least two KC-135 Stratotankers that were seriously damaged during Operation Epic Fury are still undergoing extensive maintenance depot repairs, the head of Air Force Materiel Command said Oct. 21.
Six of the Air Force’s six-decade-old refueling tankers received varying degrees of damage in the opening weeks of the war against Iran. One KC-135 was involved in a collision with another Stratotanker over western Iraq on March 12 and lost part of its tail. The other tanker in that collision was completely destroyed, killing all six Airmen aboard. Another five KC-135s were hit during an Iranian missile strike on Prince Sultan Air Base, Saudi Arabia.
During an event with the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, AFMC boss Lt. Gen. Linda Hurry said her command sent an aircraft battle damage repair team to the Middle East to make temporary repairs to some KC-135s and “get them back into the fight,” Hurry said. Others were patched up enough to fly back to depots in the U.S., she said. She did not specify how many planes fell into each category.
Photographs emerged online showing one KC-135 flying with a transplanted tail, and others landing in the United Kingdom with patches covering the fragmentation damage that peppered their skins.
At least two Stratotankers “received much more significant damage” and are still in depot, Hurry said. She applauded the work the repair team did on these planes to get them airworthy enough to get back to the U.S.
“One had many, many, many holes in the side,” Hurry said. The repair team was “able to patch it up and get the authority to have it [make] a one-time flight back to the depot. It was just phenomenal that they were able to actually save that aircraft. Now they’re rebuilding it.”
Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach told lawmakers in June that all of those salvageable KC-135s would eventually return to service, although the most heavily damaged could take a year or two to be completely fixed.
Tinker Air Force Base, Okla., serves as the main KC-135 depot.
Depot Hiring
In addition to Tinker, the Air Force has depots at Warner-Robins Air Force Base, Ga., and Hill Air Force Base, Utah. Officials have called them “national treasures” for their work in repairing critical assets, but there have been concerns about manning and funding for years now.
AFMC as a whole is seeing widespread manpower shortages, Hurry said, with about 8,200 billets—including maintainers, engineers and contracting professionals—currently vacant. The Air Force Sustainment Center, which is part of AFMC and oversees those depots, specifically has a shortage of 2,600 billets, she said.
In response, AFMC is looking to hire depot artisans—the most highly-skilled civilian mechanics, technicians, and engineers—and other maintainers to keep the depots fully staffed, Hurry said.
The command is trying to do more targeted and streamlined hiring to fill the gaps, including by hosting hiring events where they can extend temporary job offers “right there on the spot,” and getting new hires on the job faster, she said.
AFMC is also looking at offering retention benefits and targeted incentives to hold on to vital employees with critical skill sets, “to make sure we’ve got the right artisans to care for some of these airframes that are older than probably most of us on the line,” Hurry said.
But sometimes, Hurry said, the Air Force doesn’t have to wait for a plane to get to one of its three main depots to do some of that necessary work. Airmen have proposed ideas for “a speed line” to push maintainers forward to the field and get the work done on-site, she said.
That would not just help keep planes flying, Hurry said, but also could help with morale and retention.
“They can see what they’re doing would have a direct impact to [U.S. Central Command] operations or operations around the globe,” Hurry said. “It really, really makes a difference. The sense of pride, the sense of purpose, the sense of commitment to our mission has really helped some of our retention.”
When a plane like a KC-135 goes through the depot process, Hurry said, maintainers routinely tear it “down to its ribs to build it back up again, to send it back out to the fight.”
“It is amazing how far we break down the aircraft to build it back up again as part of the routine depot maintenance cycle,” Hurry said.

articles.title: NATO to allow Ukraine buy weapons, military equipment via its procurement agency — FT
articles.body:
LONDON, October 22. /TASS/. NATO will allow Ukraine to buy weapons, ammunition and military equipment via the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA), which could enable Kiev to receive supplies faster and at lower prices, the Financial Times (FT) reported.
NSPA Director of Support to Operations Jacqueline Borsboom told the newspaper that the agency would provide Ukraine with a structured framework for purchasing goods and access to the industrial base. According to the FT, last week NSPA held an event in Kiev for 150 Ukrainian companies, explaining how manufacturers could register to compete for contracts.
Russia has repeatedly said that arms supplies to the Kiev regime only prolong the Ukraine conflict.

articles.title: Hegseth Directs Air Force to Establish New Guard Special Tactics Squadron
articles.body:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has directed the Air Force to establish a new Special Tactics Squadron under the Florida Air National Guard, growing a small but elite group of special operators.
The Pentagon announced Hegseth’s order Oct. 21, releasing a brief Sept. 23 memo from Hegseth to Air Force Secretary Troy Meink, directing him to create the new squadron at Hurlburt Field “with an associated new organization at MacDill Air Force Base,” both in Florida.
Pentagon and Air Force spokespersons offered no further details. The Air National Guard did not immediately respond to a query.
Hurlburt is the headquarters of Air Force Special Operations Command, and MacDill is home to U.S. Special Operations Command. Connecting the new unit to both “creates an unparalleled ecosystem of combat-ready training and mission execution,” the Pentagon’s announcement states. “This move maximizes joint-force synergy, ensures seamless operational readiness, and provides the President with highly responsive, lethal options to counter pacing threats.”
Special tactics squadrons are some of the Air Force’s premier ground forces, consisting of combat controllers, pararescuemen, special reconnaissance, and Tactical Air Control Party specialists. They conduct a wide range of missions in covert, remote, or hostile areas, including combat search and rescue, airfield seizure, emergency air traffic controller, and coordination of close air support.
There are just a handful of special tactics squadrons across the Air Force, and only two in the Guard—the 123rd Special Tactics Squadron in Kentucky and the 125th Special Tactics Squadron in Oregon. The Florida Air National Guard has one special ops unit, the 249th Special Operations Squadron, which flies the CV-22 Osprey.
It is unclear how quickly the new unit will be established and be fully manned. Hegseth’s memo states that “any further resourcing for this direction, to include military construction, equipment, and manpower authorizations will be developed in the President’s Budget 2028 budget cycle.”
The memo also directs the National Guard Bureau and the Air Force to follow Air Force policy for establishing the new unit, “consistent with applicable DAF Strategic Basing process and environmental legal requirements.”
It is highly unusual—if not unprecedented—for the Secretary of Defense to direct the establishment of a squadron-level unit in any component.
Hegseth, a former Army officer, has praised special operations forces, seeing them as a model for innovation and acquisition reform, and they have played key roles in operations during his tenure, including Operation Absolute Resolve to seize Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January, Operation Rough Rider in Yemen in 2025, and the ongoing strikes against alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific.

articles.title: IN BRIEF: Kremlin spokesman comments on Putin-Witkoff meeting, trilateral talks on Ukraine
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. The outcome of the meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President’s Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, trilateral talks on Ukraine and cooperation with China were the main topics of Thursday’s briefing by Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov.
TASS has summarized the key statements made by the Kremlin spokesman.
On the president’s schedule
Russia has not yet decided whether President Vladimir Putin will travel to Miami for the Group of Twenty (G20) summit, but it will consider all circumstances when deciding whether to accept or decline the invitation: "There is an invitation to this summit, and it will be considered in light of all the circumstances."
On the Putin-Witkoff talks
Putin did not send any documents containing proposals for a settlement in Ukraine through US special envoy Steve Witkoff.
Mediation in a process as complex as the settlement of the conflict in Ukraine is difficult and is best conducted behind closed doors: "Of course not. Mediation in such a complex negotiation process is conducted behind closed doors."
"Megaphone diplomacy" and public discussion of proposals to settle the conflict in Ukraine can only harm the negotiation process: "Any kind of ‘megaphone diplomacy’ here can only be harmful. Public discussion of counterproposals can also only be harmful."
Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump are not currently planning a telephone conversation following the visit by US presidential special envoy Steve Witkoff. However, such a conversation could be arranged quickly: "At the moment, there are no plans for such a conversation. However, as you know, it can be arranged fairly quickly if necessary or if one of the parties desires it."
"The presidents constantly assure each other of their readiness to speak at a moment’s notice and at any time."
On the positions of third countries regarding Ukraine
The US is making substantial efforts to settle the situation around Ukraine, while European efforts are aimed at provoking further hostilities: "The US administration is doing a great deal to promote a peaceful settlement. European countries are doing nothing to foster a peaceful settlement and doing a lot to provoke further hostilities."
Russia has yet to hear any constructive statements from Europe indicating a willingness to de-escalate tensions: "We have not heard a single statement that would indicate such an intention."
At the same time, Russia sees a positive development in the willingness of some European capitals to seek to understand what is happening: "We do indeed see increased activity in some European capitals in terms of efforts to understand what is happening -- this is a positive development, rather. But, of course, it still seems a long way off from such objective statements [on de-escalation]."
On trilateral talks on Ukraine
Russian President Vladimir Putin has not yet decided on the composition of Russia’s negotiating team for trilateral talks on Ukraine: "As for the composition of the negotiating team, that will be the president’s decision. And it has not been made yet. Let us not forget that this was only announced yesterday."
There are currently no definite plans regarding Putin’s participation in a meeting with members of the Russian negotiating team during the resumed trilateral talks on a settlement of the conflict in Ukraine: "No, there’s still time before this trilateral meeting. There are no specific plans regarding the president on this matter as of yet."
On cooperation with China
Putin and Chinese Premier Li Qiang did not discuss preparations for the Power of Baikal gas pipeline deal during their meeting in St. Petersburg: "No, it was not discussed. The topic of cooperation in the energy sphere was highlighted in general."
Russia-China energy cooperation still has significant untapped potential: "This cooperation [in the energy sector] is truly extensive. It has horizons that have yet to be explored. Both sides will continue working to make fuller use of the potential that exists."
On foreign companies’ assets
Russia is guided exclusively by its own interests when making decisions concerning the assets of foreign companies: "In such conditions Russia, when making relevant decisions, is governed only by its own interests."

articles.title: Witkoff holds another meeting with Norwegian premier — NRK
articles.body:
STOCKHOLM, October 21. /TASS/. The US president’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, held another meeting with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store at Oslo Airport before returning to the United States, Norway’s NRK television reported.
According to the report, Witkoff briefed Store about his negotiations with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The talks lasted for an hour, and after that the US envoy immediately departed to his home country.
On October 20, a Ukrainian delegation headed by Vladimir Zelensky and Witkoff met in Oslo. On the American side, US president's son-in-law Jared Kushner participated via video link. The meeting was also attended by Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb. Next, Witkoff went to Russia for negotiations.
Witkoff’s talks with Putin, which took place in Russia’s second largest city of St. Petersburg, lasted around three hours and focused primarily on Ukrainian settlement.

articles.title: UK wants EU security council to complement NATO
articles.body:
Britain looks forward to hearing more detail about the proposed European Security Council while noting the importance of EU mechanisms complementing NATO structures, and will continue to deepen cooperation with the European Union in a way that reinforces NATO as the cornerstone of Euro-Atlantic security, according to answers given in Parliament.
James MacCleary, the Liberal Democrat member for Lewes, asked three separate questions on the subject, covering the assessment the department has made of the merits of establishing a European Security Council that includes the United Kingdom, the discussions the Secretary of State has had with Cabinet colleagues, and the discussions he has had with European counterparts.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, gave the same answer to all three: “Europe faces the most dangerous security environment since the Cold War, and we are stepping up alongside our allies to build a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO.
“The EU’s State of Union address is a welcome contribution. We look forward to hearing more detail about the proposed European Security Council whilst noting the importance for EU mechanisms to complement NATO structures.
“The UK will continue to deepen our cooperation with the EU in a way which reinforces NATO as the cornerstone of Euro Atlantic Security, including through the implementation of the UK-EU Security and Defence Partnership.”
Ursula von der Leyen set out the proposal in her State of the Union address in September, describing a forum that would bring the European Union together with the United Kingdom, Canada, Norway and Ukraine to coordinate against hybrid attacks and sabotage, and the idea has since been examined across Europe as either a new mechanism or a repackaging of the existing hybrid toolbox.
Britain has argued since leaving the European Union that new European defence machinery should not duplicate what the alliance already does, and should not create a decision-making layer that excludes the United States. Twenty-three EU members are also NATO members, and the two organisations already run parallel arrangements on crisis management.
The United Kingdom and the European Union signed a Security and Defence Partnership in 2025, which created a structured dialogue and opened the door to British participation in European defence industrial programmes.

articles.title: British submarine hunters delayed by Norway frigate sale
articles.body:
The Royal Navy will not meet its requirement for eight frigates fitted with the Sonar 2087 towed array until 2037 if two Type 26 frigates being built for Britain are sold to Norway, and the government appears to have taken a conscious decision to prioritise defence exports over sovereign capability, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, published its findings following an inquiry that took evidence between March and July this year and included visits to Norway, Denmark and Greenland.
Dhesi said: “The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the High North. Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and the UK, including the nuclear deterrent. Despite this, the Ministry of Defence has accepted a serious anti-submarine warfare gap. Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments in the High North.”
The report states: “Analysis suggests (Figure 4) Sonar 2087-towed array equipped frigate numbers could remain as low as five vessels for the next three years. This assumes two Type 26 frigates being built for the Royal Navy are sold to Norway, as the latter has ordered at least five Type 26s for £10 billion—which the government says will sustain 4,000 UK jobs. This reinforces the government’s goal to use defence exports to contribute to its Plan for Change, based around its three foundations of good government: economic stability, secure borders and national security.
However, Norway wants its first ship in service by 2029–30. Based on this scenario the Royal Navy will take until 2037 to meet its requirement for eight frigates to be equipped with the Sonar 2087 towed array sensor. In this case the government seems to have taken a conscious decision to prioritise defence exports over sovereign capability.”
A chart published with the report shows the combined Type 23 and Type 26 anti-submarine frigate line falling to two vessels in 2031 before recovering to eight by 2037.
Norway selected the Type 26 in 2025 to replace its Fridtjof Nansen class, in an agreement the Ministry of Defence valued at £10 billion and said would sustain four thousand British jobs. The ships are being built by BAE Systems at Govan and Scotstoun on the Clyde, and Britain’s own order is for eight.
The committee elsewhere records that the Royal Navy has a requirement for eight of its thirteen frigates to carry the Sonar 2087 towed array, that all five remaining Type 23 frigates are fitted with it, and that HMS Richmond and HMS Iron Duke were both decommissioned in mid-2026.
On the wider relationship with Norway, the report describes the 2025 Lunna House agreement and the Type 26 purchase as “therefore strategically more significant than a conventional defence export”, and says a joint class of British and Norwegian anti-submarine frigates “should improve NATO’s ability to detect and track Russian submarines moving from the High North into the North Atlantic”.
The committee’s recommendation asks the government to set out how major naval export programmes, including the Norway agreement and any future uncrewed maritime systems, will support High North deterrence while protecting Royal Navy capabilities, including an assessment of their effect on British delivery timelines, industrial capacity, shared training, sustainment, interoperability and the availability of critical anti-submarine warfare capabilities.
In written evidence to the inquiry the Ministry of Defence described anti-submarine warfare as a core strength of Britain’s armed forces. The government is expected to respond to the report within two months.

articles.title: Repeated Ukrainian attacks could lead to a major regional tragedy — Rosatom CEO
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. Ongoing attacks by the Ukrainian armed forces on the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) and Energodar could lead to a major regional tragedy, Rosatom CEO Alexey Likhachev told reporters.
"Constant strikes [by the Ukrainian armed forces on Energodar and the ZNPP], deliberate and calculated, targeting not military facilities but people and social infrastructure, have become part of everyday life," Likhachev said.
He stressed that the state nuclear corporation was continuing to seek a response from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and the international community to the situation. "We are drawing the attention of international organizations, countries and, as they say, all people of goodwill to the fact that this must stop; it is unacceptable. We are just a few steps away from a major regional tragedy," the Rosatom CEO said.

articles.title: Russia releases American jailed on mercenary charges after Trump’s request
articles.body:
Russia has released American citizen Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan who had been detained for more than four years after Russian forces captured him in Ukraine.
Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the release on Wednesday during a meeting with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, according to Russian media reports.
Witkoff thanked Putin for releasing Hubbard, praising the Russian president during the meeting.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanist,” Witkoff said, according to NBC News.
“You are also a humanist,” he told Putin.
U.S. President Donald Trump also confirmed Hubbard’s release on Wednesday in a post on his social media platform Truth Social. He said the release was not part of a prisoner exchange and that the United States was not releasing any Russians in return.
“Stephen is on his way home and will soon be back with his family,” Trump wrote.
Trump said Tuesday that he had asked Putin to release Hubbard.
“I have spoken with him for a long time. I have asked him to release him. Let’s see what happens,” Trump told journalists in Washington, according to AFP.
Hubbard had lived in the eastern Ukrainian city of Izium since 2014, according to CNN. He had worked as an English teacher outside the United States for decades.
Russian forces occupied Izium in February 2022, at the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Ukrainian forces recaptured the city in September that year, but Hubbard had been captured by Russian forces in the meantime.
Russian prosecutors accused him of fighting for Ukraine as a mercenary. In October 2024, he was sentenced to six years and 10 months in prison.
Hubbard’s sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, told CNN that the accusations against him were false.
Russian state media have reported that Hubbard admitted guilt, according to Reuters. However, the U.S. government classified him as “wrongfully detained.”
The circumstances surrounding his capture and detention have not been fully detailed in the information released about the case.

articles.title: Czech president: Trump's diesel deal derails peace progress between Ukraine, Russia
articles.body:
Czech President Petr Pavel stated that a truce between Russia and Ukraine was "very close" until President Donald Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel. He said this in an interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, which includes Politico.
"It will be much harder now. Russia uses this momentum to get out of pressure, and it’s kind of a moral boost for them," Pavel said, pointing out that coordinated U.S and European sanctions on Russian oil, oligarchs, and other industries had placed Russia "in a difficult position." However, the deal announced by Trump earlier this month, under which Russia was to supply hundreds of thousands of tonnes of diesel fuel to the U.S, gave Russia "time to breathe."
Pavel expressed support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who criticized the deal, stating that it "plays into Russia's hands" and allows Russia to "kill more people, conduct war longer, respect America even less, and cause the world even greater loss and damage."
"I believe that President Zelensky and the whole of Ukraine is a victim of a conflict. So, I would be probably the last to blame Ukraine for being guilty of the conflict. It was not Ukraine who attacked Russia. It was not Ukraine who was threatening Russia," Pavel said.
He added that Trump demonstrates a more open approach to Russia than any European leader.
"To some extent, he may be attracted by Vladimir Putin as a leader with authority, but I don’t think that … President Trump sees it from a position of a struggle between democracy and autocracies because he’s looking at it simply from the point of view of economic prosperity for the United States," he added.
Although Pavel expressed concern over the diesel deal, he declined to assert that the U.S had betrayed Ukraine or other European partners.
"I don’t know yet if we can call it betrayal, but I would call it a mistake. Because … it’s now giving Russia a new hope: New hope that they can disregard Europe, they can disregard Ukraine, they can focus on making a deal with the United States, potentially with China, and arranging all things up to their priorities and strategies. I believe that it’s clearly against our interest in Europe," he explained.
Pavel also did not rule out that European countries might buy Russian oil in the future, but added that "it will still take time."
"If one day Russia is a country respecting other countries’ sovereignty and borders, why not have regular business with such a country? But Russia is not there yet," he said.

articles.title: Trumps wants Russia-US-China meeting to address denuclearization as well
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, October 22. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump said that his potential trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping should focus, among other things, on denuclearization.
At Joint Base Andrews near Washington, reporters asked the president about the issue of a Ukrainian settlement at the potential trilateral meeting. "I can't tell you that because it's not just about that. That's about denuclearization. So it's not just about that. But we have a lot of steps. But I think it's the closest I've seen. You see what I see," Trump said as quoted by the White House press pool.
Reporters also asked the president what was next with the war, though they did not specify which conflict they were referring to. "We want to also settle the war, but we also want to keep it the way it is because Russia has not been involved very much, certainly in a very minimal way with respect to Iran," Trump responded.

articles.title: GM aims to develop vehicles in as little as two years with AI, software push
articles.body:
NEW YORK — General Motors plans to lean into artificial intelligence and vehicle software for future growth and development amid increasing competition abroad from Chinese automakers and a tougher U.S. market.
The Detroit automaker on Wednesday shared new details about a proprietary AI agent it's releasing under its OnStar brand, plans for a fourth generation of more efficient all-electric vehicles and a target to cut its vehicle development time in half.
GM also reconfirmed that by 2028, it wants to have eyes-off highway driving, or "personal autonomy," that will let drivers take their attention off the road. The automaker said that technology would start with the Cadillac Escalade IQ EV before rolling out to other, more high-volume models.
"All of these developments are building us the car of the future," CEO Mary Barra said Wednesday during an event laying out the plans, called "GM Forward," in downtown Manhattan.
The initiatives, which Barra, Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson and other executives discussed at the event, are designed to streamline the automaker's operations, while also improving the capabilities of its vehicles for customers.
"Over the last 12 months, we've evolved how we design, engineer and build our vehicles," said Anderson, who led the event and who has been tasked with overseeing GM's latest technology transformation.
GM said it is now targeting a vehicle development time of roughly two years from concept to production versus a traditional four- to five-year cycle. However, the company did not detail a timeline for reaching that goal.
The event comes as Chinese automakers are growing outside of the U.S. with rapid development times of new technologies and vehicles. Consulting firm AlixPartners said it believes China is currently bringing vehicles to market twice as fast as traditional automakers, with 40% to 50% less investment and a 30% cost advantage.
GM also continues to play catch-up to U.S. EV leader Tesla when it comes to delivering technology advancements through over-the-air updates and automated driving capabilities.
Anderson, a former Tesla executive, declined to speak specifically about how GM's technologies will compare to the EV maker, but said GM's systems will be able to visualize, or see, more things through the use of multiple types of sensors than a strictly camera-based system, which Tesla uses.
He also said the rapid development and new software architecture will help the company better compete against Chinese automakers abroad.
"There's inherent virtue to speed," Anderson told CNBC during an interview after the event. "Not just in being able to get a car out faster, it's being able to develop a system that's far more performant that you could have otherwise."
Next-generation vehicles
GM said Wednesday it has major plans for its next generation of EVs and traditional vehicles with internal combustion engines.
The company said those coming vehicles — regardless of type — will have 40 times the computing power and up to 50% faster cellular connectivity than prior systems.
That computing power is expected to help the automaker with over-the-air updates, onboard diagnostics and AI, as well as other technologies such as automated driving features.
The new brain of the vehicle will launch on the $130,000 Cadillac Escalade IQ EV in 2028 before rolling out to other models, including its next generation of EVs.
GM said the forthcoming EVs are expected to be 25% more aerodynamic and 15% lighter and feature electric motors and battery packs that are more compact.
GM President Mark Reuss said despite lackluster consumer adoption and the automaker pulling back billions of dollars in investments in EVs, it remains committed to producing them.
"We continue to develop our future EVs and work to reduce battery costs," Reuss said during the event. "And when the U.S. market is ready for EVs in large numbers, we will be there for them."
AI development
GM expects to achieve such targets through the use of AI in research and development.
The company said it is developing a "new operating approach for vehicle development" that leans into enterprise AI and virtualization to increase speed.
"This concurrent engineering model allows us to innovate faster, improve continuously, and scale new technologies across our lineup with incredible agility," the company said in a release.
GM used the development of its next-generation vehicles, including a new battery chemistry, as an example of how the new technologies are reshaping its vehicle development.
The company said it virtually tested more than 300,000 battery designs using its recently announced lithium manganese rich battery chemistry, or LMR, before building a single physical prototype.
Anderson said Wednesday that LMR will be the exclusive battery tech for its fourth-generation EVs. GM had previously said it wanted to use those batteries in full-size electric vehicles such as its Chevrolet Silverado and Escalade IQ beginning in 2028.
Anderson said GM is uniquely positioned to use AI compared to other automotive companies because of its more than 100 years in the industry as well as 30 years of OnStar.
"In the age of AI, data is currency," Anderson said. "For decades, GM's engineering, manufacturing and product teams have generated unparalleled body of data that we're now using to build industry-leading AI tools."
In-vehicle AI
The company is building on its internal use of AI to better shape its experiences for customers.
GM on Wednesday reconfirmed that it plans to launch a proprietary in-vehicle AI assistant through its OnStar technology brand.
The OnStar AI assistant is expected to launch in the coming months on the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq EV through an over-the-air update before expanding to other models.
GM currently uses Google's Gemini for its in-vehicle AI assistant. The company told CNBC earlier this year that the GM-developed AI will be more integrated with the vehicle.
The goal for OnStar AI, which will be available through a subscription, is to help customers be productive while in the car, especially if the vehicle has self-driving capabilities that don't require the driver or passengers to monitor the system.
GM on Wednesday also reiterated its plans to launch eyes-off highway driving in 2028. The automaker said a year ago that it wanted to launch that technology. It's been five years since Barra said she expected the automaker to offer personal autonomous vehicles this decade.
"Our vision is that eventually every vehicle should drive itself or its occupants anywhere, and we're investing across the self-driving stack to make that real," Anderson said.

articles.title: Russia and Türkiye back South Africa in G20 row with US
articles.body:
Russia and Türkiye back South Africa in G20 row with US
Russia and Türkiye have called for South Africa’s swift return to G20 activities after the US barred the country from participating during America’s presidency amid tensions over Pretoria’s domestic policies and foreign ties.
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Aleksandr Pankin and his Turkish counterpart, Berris Ekinci, discussed the issue during consultations in Moscow, according to a Russian Foreign Ministry statement released on Tuesday. They said any changes to G20 membership must be agreed on by consensus, with greater representation for countries of the Global South and East.
The diplomats also discussed preparations for the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta on October 30-31 and the leaders’ summit in Miami December 14-15. They stressed that the forum should remain a platform for equal dialogue on global economic challenges.
Russia and Türkiye are both members of the G20, which comprises 19 countries, the EU, and the African Union.
US President Donald Trump announced in November 2025 that South Africa would not be invited to the Miami summit, saying it demonstrated that it is “unworthy of membership.”
The Trump administration boycotted the G20 leaders’ summit in Johannesburg that month over allegations that the African country allows “horrific” abuses against its white minority, including killings and land confiscation, which Pretoria denies.
Trump also accused Pretoria of refusing to hand over the G20 presidency to a US Embassy representative. South Africa said it would breach protocol for President Cyril Ramaphosa to hand over to a junior diplomat. The transfer later took place at the Department of International Relations and Cooperation between officials of similar rank.
The South African presidency said US punitive measures are based on “misinformation and distortions.” Prior to the Johannesburg summit, Ramaphosa also rejected US pressure against issuing a joint declaration without Washington’s support. He told reporters on November 20 that South Africa “will not agree to be bullied.”
In December, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio extended the exclusion to all G20 meetings during America’s presidency. South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola rejected the move, saying no single member can unilaterally exclude South Africa, a founding member.
Relations have since deteriorated, with the US announcing visa restrictions in September against officials and people it accuses of enabling racial discrimination, uncompensated land seizures, and inciting violence against minorities in South Africa. US Ambassador Brent Bozell also criticized Pretoria’s ties with Russia, China, and Iran, pledging to challenge its “geostrategic drift” toward America’s competitors.
Ramaphosa warned on Monday that South Africa, which already faces steep US tariffs, must prepare for possible exclusion from America’s preferential trade program for African countries.

articles.title: British warship should ‘stand up’ to Russia in north
articles.body:
The government should prepare options for a British state-owned vessel to transit the Northern Sea Route in support of international freedom of navigation rights, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, sets out concern that Russia may seek to turn its control of the route into a de facto monopoly as it becomes more accessible.
Dhesi said: “The High North poses a major strategic challenge for the UK’s security. This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage.”
Its recommendation states: “The government should prepare options for a UK state-owned vessel to transit the Northern Sea Route in support of international freedom of navigation rights, including an assessment of the legal basis, operational risks and potential Russian response.”
The conclusion preceding it states: “As the Northern Sea Route becomes more accessible, Russia may seek to turn its control of the route into a de facto monopoly. A transit by a UK state-owned vessel through international waters could help uphold freedom of navigation rights under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, but this action would need to be carefully assessed against the operational and escalatory risks.”
The Northern Sea Route is a roughly 5,600 kilometre shipping lane running along Russia’s Arctic coast from the Kara Sea to the Bering Strait. Dr Marc De Vore, senior lecturer in international relations at the University of St Andrews, told the committee: “If we do not act to contest Russia’s illegal efforts to territorialise the northern sea route—these are their laws of 2012, 2018 and 2022—we will find after 2030, when the northern sea route becomes navigable all year long, that the Russians have set up a de facto monopoly on transit. They will make money off that, but they could also use it as a form of leverage—for example, if they do not like the level of support that Denmark is providing to Ukraine, they can cut off Maersk ships from sailing the northern sea route. Failing to contest that through freedom of navigation operations will give Russia a tremendous amount of both wealth and geopolitical leverage.”
The report records that in September 2018 the French Navy’s offshore support and assistance vessel Rhône transited the route from Tromsø in Norway to Dutch Harbor in Alaska without informing the Russian authorities. Russia subsequently stated that all foreign naval vessels would have to provide details of any proposed voyage at least forty-five days in advance and carry a Russian maritime pilot, and warned that if a voyage did not comply with Russian regulations it reserved the “right to take extraordinary measures including its forced halt, arrest and in extreme cases elimination.”
Freedom of navigation operations are actions taken by a country to sail or fly through contested international waters and airspaces to challenge maritime claims that break international law. The United States has conducted them in the Gulf of Sirte and the South China Sea, and Britain has done so near the Sea of Azov.
The committee notes such operations carry inherent risks, and in 2021 the Type 45 destroyer HMS Defender exercised its right of innocent passage through Ukrainian territorial waters off Crimea, which Russia had annexed in 2014, and Russia claims to have fired warning shots and dropped bombs near the vessel.
China is focused on using the route, with the sailing distance between Shanghai and Rotterdam approximately 25,500 kilometres via the Cape of Good Hope, 19,500 kilometres via the Suez Canal and 14,900 kilometres via the Northern Sea Route.

articles.title: Russia ready to act as mediator between US, Iran if they are interested in that — diplomat
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. Russia is ready to act as a mediator to settle the conflict between the United States and Iran if they are interested in that, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko said.
"If all the sides demonstrate such interest, we are ready [to act as mediators]," he said in an interview with the Izvestia daily. "We have already offered our services regarding how the Iranian nuclear program might be resolved, but so far our proposals have not received support."

articles.title: Lockheed Martin enters deal with US Defense Department for 850 F-35 Lightning II fighter jets
articles.body:
Lockheed Martin has entered into an initial production and sustainment agreement with the US Defense Department to deliver at least 850 F-35 Lightning II fighter jets over the next 10 years, the department said Thursday.
The defense contractor will self-fund at least $7 billion in initiatives that support the F-35 program, the department said in a statement.
The F-35, built with stealth technology that helps it evade enemy detection, is considered the world's most advanced fighter jet and sits at the core of Lockheed's aeronautics division, which accounts for nearly 40% of its quarterly revenue.
Under the agreement with the Defense Department, which US President Donald Trump calls the Department of War, Lockheed aims to maintain annual production at 156 aircraft.
The agreement is not an order but is considered a prearranged long-term contract.
"If granted multi-year authority in the coming months, the F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will work to finalize contract terms, pricing, and schedules through a formal contract award," the company said.
The agreement also covers international orders for the F-35, along with initial spares and modification kits, Arlington-based Lockheed said in a statement.
"We have fundamentally changed how we stabilize the American defense industrial base to produce at speed and scale," said Under Secretary of Defense Michael Duffey.
"This agreement with Lockheed Martin proves it. By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we are ensuring our warfighters are equipped with the lethal capabilities they need to fight and win."
Lockheed, defense industry, benefit from increased global defense spending
Lockheed and its peers across the US have benefited from increased global defense spending as geopolitical conflicts remain unabated.
Lockheed estimates the agreement will support 317,000 US jobs and generate nearly $79 billion in annual economic activity over the next decade.
It also expects the arrangement to lower production costs and ease supply-chain constraints from raw materials to finished parts.

articles.title: Trump, Putin and Xi can decide Ukraine’s fate without it: will there be a "Yalta 2.0"
articles.body:
Trump, Putin and Xi can decide Ukraine’s fate without it: will there be a "Yalta 2.0"
Kyiv • UNN
Steve Witkoff proposed a trilateral meeting of the leaders of the United States, Russia and China to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. An expert warned against negotiations without Kyiv.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff proposed that Russia hold a trilateral meeting involving China next month to discuss a plan to end the war in Ukraine. This is reported by Financial News, according to UNN.
Details
The proposal is for U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping to meet and reach a settlement on Ukraine.
The proposal is being compared to the Yalta Conference, when the top leaders of the United States, Great Britain, and the USSR gathered in Yalta on the Crimean Peninsula in February 1945 and agreed on the post-World War II world order. At that time, the division of Germany and Korea was also discussed
Additionally
The president of the International Institute for Security Studies, Oleksii Buriachenko, said in a comment to UNN that only the Kremlin is interested in possible trilateral talks between Russia, the United States, and China. In particular, it wants to raise the possibility of resolving Russia’s war against Ukraine without the participation of Kyiv and Europe. For the United States and China, other issues remain priorities.
According to him, the possibility of trilateral talks arose against the backdrop of preparations for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, which is to be held in China this year.
In the expert’s view, it is precisely the location of the summit that creates conditions for a potential meeting between Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and Xi Jinping, but this does not mean that Russia’s war against Ukraine will become the main topic of the talks, because, according to the expert, the initiative to discuss it in such a format is primarily beneficial to Moscow.
Despite this, the political scientist does not believe that the potential meeting itself will have direct political consequences for Ukraine. In his view, the main risk is that discussing the war without Kyiv could gradually come to be perceived as an altogether acceptable format of international politics. Therefore, it is important for Ukraine not only to state that such talks are unacceptable, but also to seek partners who will likewise support this position.

articles.title: Russian, Indian military pilots train to coordinate at Indra 2026 exercise
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. Crews of the Russian Aerospace Forces and the Indian Air Force practiced coordinated operations involving Su-30SM aircraft during the Russian-Indian Indra 2026 cross-branch exercise, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Within the Indra 2026 exercise, crews of the Russian Aerospace Forces and the Indian Air Force conducted joint flights of Su-30SM aircraft to practice engaging small, low-flying targets and eliminating carriers of short-and medium-range air-launched weapons, and practiced elements of maneuvering air combat at medium and low altitudes," the ministry said in a statement.
The Russian Aerospace Forces and the Indian Air Force crews operating Mi-8 army aviation helicopters rehearsed deploying special operations units, as well as conducting search and rescue operations for crews in distress in difficult terrain.
